back: A list of potentially inappropriate medications for older persons. It is organised by body system and therapeutic category, and gives the rationale and quality of evidence for each entry.

front: What do the START and STOPP tools do in prescribing for older patients?
back: START lists evidence-based prescribing indicators by body system, to alert the prescriber to the right treatment. STOPP identifies potentially inappropriate medicines in older persons' prescriptions and is used for medication review.

front: What does the Medication Appropriateness Index check for each prescribed drug?
back: Whether the drug is indicated, whether it is effective, whether the dose is appropriate, whether it is cost-effective, and whether it duplicates another therapy.

front: What parameters make up the Child-Pugh score, and what are the classes?
back: The score uses bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites and encephalopathy. Class A (mild) is 5-6 points, class B (moderate) 7-9 points and class C (severe) 10-15 points. Class B and C patients have decompensated cirrhosis.

front: Why is ponesimod not recommended in some patients with liver disease?
back: It is not recommended for patients with moderate or severe hepatic impairment, that is Child-Pugh class B or C.

front: How is the starting dose of obeticholic acid set according to liver disease stage?
back: Used when there is no adequate response to ursodeoxycholic acid after at least 1 year, or when it is not tolerated. Non-cirrhotic or Child-Pugh A: start 5 mg once daily for 3 months, then 10 mg once daily at most. Child-Pugh B or C, or a prior decompensation event: start 5 mg once weekly for 3 months, then 5 mg twice weekly, at most 10 mg twice weekly (doses at least 3 days apart).

front: Why is succinylcholine unsafe in hepatic failure?
back: Plasma pseudocholinesterase, which the liver synthesises, breaks down succinylcholine. In hepatic failure this enzyme is deficient, so the drug is not safe. It is also unsafe in renal failure.

front: Which antitubercular drugs are safe in liver disease, and which is most hepatotoxic?
back: Streptomycin and ethambutol are safe in liver disease. Pyrazinamide is the most hepatotoxic, then isoniazid, then rifampicin. In TB with liver damage, the book starts streptomycin, levofloxacin and ethambutol, and reintroduces the other drugs as transaminases normalise, in the order rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide.

front: Which fluoroquinolones are removed in bile and avoided in liver disease?
back: Pefloxacin, moxifloxacin and trovafloxacin. They are not excreted in urine, are removed in bile, are hepatotoxic and are contraindicated in liver disease. Trovafloxacin has been banned because of hepatotoxicity.

front: How is the dose calculated for an exceptionally obese or lean adult?
back: On a body weight basis: individual dose = (body weight in kg / 70) x average adult dose. The average adult dose refers to a person of medium build. Body surface area has been argued to be a more accurate basis.

front: How does haemodialysis change the vancomycin dosing schedule?
back: With non-high-flux dialysis membranes, about 1 g (around 15 mg/kg) every 5 to 7 days typically gives adequate levels. With intermittent high-efficiency or high-flux dialysis, maintenance doses are needed after each dialysis session.

front: Why can metered-dose inhalers and solid dosage forms be a problem in young children?
back: Young children find solid dosage forms and metered-dose inhalers difficult to administer.

front: Trace catecholamine synthesis from phenylalanine and name the rate-limiting enzyme.
back: Phenylalanine is hydroxylated to tyrosine, tyrosine hydroxylase converts it to DOPA (the rate-limiting step), and DOPA decarboxylase gives dopamine. Dopamine enters the storage vesicle, where dopamine beta-hydroxylase converts it to noradrenaline. In adrenal medullary cells, phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), induced by the high local cortisol level, methylates noradrenaline to adrenaline.

front: Which drug blocks catecholamine synthesis, and where is it used?
back: Metyrosine (alpha-methyl-p-tyrosine) inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase and depletes catecholamines. It is used to reduce catecholamine output in pheochromocytoma before surgery and in inoperable cases.

front: How is noradrenaline stored in the nerve terminal, and how does reserpine act?
back: It is held in vesicles, complexed with ATP (about 4:1) and bound to chromogranin. VMAT-2 pumps amines into the vesicle in exchange for H+. Reserpine blocks VMAT-2, so transmitter leaks into the cytoplasm, is destroyed by MAO, and the stores become depleted.

front: Compare uptake-1 and uptake-2 for catecholamines.
back: Uptake-1 is the Na+-coupled norepinephrine transporter (NET) in the neuronal membrane. It recaptures 75 to 90 percent of released noradrenaline, is blocked by cocaine and desipramine, and is the main way neuronal action ends. Uptake-2 is an extraneuronal transporter in other tissues. It is Na+-independent, prefers adrenaline, is not blocked by cocaine, and is quantitatively minor.

front: Which enzymes metabolise catecholamines, and why does metabolism matter little for neuronally released noradrenaline?
back: MAO acts first on the intraneuronal and leaked pool; COMT acts first on circulating amines in liver and other tissues. Aldehyde reductase, dehydrogenases and ADH take part in the intermediate steps. Urinary products are VMA, MOPEG, metanephrines and DOMA, mostly conjugated. Metabolism is slow compared with reuptake, so it contributes little to ending neuronal action.

front: Using the Ahlquist classification, compare the potency order of adrenaline, noradrenaline and isoprenaline at alpha and beta receptors.
back: Alpha: adrenaline greater than or equal to noradrenaline, both much greater than isoprenaline. Beta: isoprenaline greater than adrenaline, which is greater than or equal to noradrenaline. Ahlquist (1948) used these two distinct rank orders of agonist potency to divide adrenoceptors into alpha and beta; the split was later confirmed by selective antagonists.

front: Compare alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors: location, transducer, effector and selective drugs.
back: Alpha-1 is postjunctional on effector organs. It acts through Gq, IP3/DAG and calcium, causing vasoconstriction, mydriasis and contraction of the bladder trigone and prostate. Phenylephrine is the selective agonist and prazosin the selective antagonist. Alpha-2 is mainly prejunctional, where it inhibits transmitter release, and is also found in the brain and platelets. It acts through Gi, lowering cAMP. Clonidine is the selective agonist and yohimbine the antagonist.

front: Where are beta-1, beta-2 and beta-3 receptors found, and which selective drugs act on them?
back: Beta-1: heart and juxtaglomerular cells; dobutamine is the relatively selective agonist, and metoprolol or atenolol the antagonists. Beta-2: bronchi, blood vessels, uterus, liver, skeletal muscle; salbutamol and terbutaline are agonists, ICI 118551 an antagonist. Beta-3: adipose tissue and bladder detrusor; mirabegron is the agonist used in overactive bladder.

front: Dobutamine: receptor action, clinical dose and why it is useful as an inotrope.
back: It is a dopamine derivative with no dopamine-receptor activity. Its main action is a relatively beta-1 selective agonism. At 2 to 8 mcg/kg/min IV it raises contractility and output with little change in peripheral resistance or BP, and less tachycardia than isoprenaline. It is less arrhythmogenic than adrenaline. Uses: pump failure after MI or cardiac surgery, short-term severe heart failure, and pharmacological stress testing.

front: Describe ephedrine: mechanism, duration and why its use is now restricted.
back: A mixed-acting sympathomimetic: it releases noradrenaline and also acts directly on alpha and beta receptors. It resists MAO, so it is orally active and lasts 4 to 6 hours, but it is about 100 times less potent than adrenaline, and tachyphylaxis develops on repeated doses. Its use is restricted because it lacks selectivity and its efficacy is low. Remaining uses: hypotension during spinal anaesthesia, mild chronic bronchial asthma, and occasionally postural hypotension.

front: What is the drug of choice in anaphylactic shock, what is the dose, and why?
back: Adrenaline, injected intramuscularly without delay: 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1 in 1000) in adults, 0.3 mL for children 6 to 12 years and 0.15 mL up to 6 years; repeat every 5 to 10 minutes if there is no or only transient improvement. It raises BP, counters bronchospasm and laryngeal oedema, acts fast, and also suppresses mediator release from mast cells. IV adrenaline is used only for immediately life-threatening shock, diluted and infused slowly with monitoring. H1 antihistamines and IV hydrocortisone are adjuncts only.

front: What is the vasomotor reversal of Dale, and why does noradrenaline not show it?
back: After alpha blockade, adrenaline's pressor effect turns into a fall in BP. Adrenaline at ordinary doses causes alpha-1 vasoconstriction and beta-2 vasodilatation. Blocking alpha leaves only the beta-2 vasodilatation. Noradrenaline has no beta-2 action, so its pressor effect persists after alpha blockade.

front: Classify: uses of selective beta-2 agonists
text: Selective beta-2 agonists are used in {{bronchial asthma}} and COPD, to delay {{preterm labour}} (ritodrine), and in {{familial hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis}}.

front: Why do alpha-1 blockers cause postural hypotension?
back: They block alpha-1 mediated constriction of arterioles and veins, so peripheral resistance and venous tone fall and blood pools in capacitance vessels. Venous return and cardiac output drop, and the postural reflex that normally compensates on standing is impaired, so BP falls on standing and dizziness or syncope can follow.

front: Describe phenoxybenzamine: mechanism, duration and uses.
back: A halogenated alkylamine that forms a reactive intermediate and covalently binds alpha receptors. The blockade is irreversible and non-equilibrium and lasts 3 to 4 days until new receptors are made. Its main effects are postural hypotension, nasal stuffiness, miosis and failure of ejaculation. It is used mainly in pheochromocytoma and occasionally in peripheral vascular disease. Oral dose 20 to 60 mg/day; i.m. and s.c. injection is painful and should be avoided.

front: What is phentolamine used for, and what does its diagnostic test involve?
back: It is a short-acting, nonselective alpha-1 and alpha-2 antagonist; alpha-2 block increases noradrenaline release, so reflex tachycardia is marked. Uses: hypertensive episodes in pheochromocytoma, clonidine withdrawal or cheese reaction, local infiltration for extravasation of noradrenaline or dopamine, and intracavernosal injection with papaverine. Book test: 5 mg IV over 1 minute; a fall above 35 mm Hg systolic or 25 mm Hg diastolic suggests pheochromocytoma, but false results occur. Katzung notes it is now rarely used, and diagnosis rests on raised plasma or urinary catecholamines and metanephrines.

front: Prazosin: selectivity, first-dose effect and why it replaced phenoxybenzamine.
back: It is a selective alpha-1 blocker (about 1000 times more selective for alpha-1 than alpha-2) that blocks all alpha-1 subtypes equally. Sparing prejunctional alpha-2 keeps reflex tachycardia mild. The first-dose effect (postural syncope) is reduced by starting with a low dose at bedtime, and tolerance to it develops. Being competitive and short acting (half-life 2 to 3 h, effect 6 to 8 h), it is easier to control than irreversible phenoxybenzamine. Uses: hypertension, BHP and Raynaud's phenomenon.

front: Tamsulosin: receptor profile, advantages and key adverse effects in BHP.
back: It is a uroselective alpha-1A/1D blocker. The 1A subtype dominates in the prostate and bladder base, so it relieves BHP symptoms with little change in BP or heart rate and little postural hypotension. It lacks the apoptosis-promoting effect seen with terazosin and doxazosin. Side effects: retrograde ejaculation and dizziness. Floppy iris syndrome is a concern during cataract surgery. It is given once daily as a modified-release capsule.

front: Why do alpha-1 blockers relieve BHP faster than finasteride, and what do they not do?
back: BHP obstruction has a static part (enlarged gland) and a dynamic part (alpha-1 mediated tone of the bladder neck and prostate). Alpha-1 blockers relax the dynamic part and give relief within about 2 weeks. Finasteride acts on the static part and takes around 6 months. Alpha-1 blockers do not reduce prostate size, and the benefit stops when the drug is stopped.

front: Alfuzosin: duration, indication and key drug interaction.
back: A short-acting prazosin congener (half-life about 3 to 5 hours), nonselective among alpha-1 subtypes. It is indicated only for symptomatic BHP and is not approved as an antihypertensive. It is metabolised by CYP3A4, so strong inhibitors such as erythromycin, ketoconazole and ritonavir should be avoided. Dose: 10 mg OD as extended release.

front: Labetalol: receptor action, clinical niche and main side effect.
back: It blocks alpha-1 and nonselectively blocks beta receptors, with beta blockade about 3 to 5 times stronger than alpha. Its fall in BP comes from alpha-1 block plus beta-2 vasodilatation. Heart rate is usually unchanged and limb blood flow increases. It is used in pheochromocytoma, clonidine withdrawal, pregnancy-induced hypertension and hypertensive emergencies (20 to 40 mg IV repeated). Its main side effect is postural hypotension.

front: Propranolol: why does the antihypertensive effect appear only after some weeks?
back: Acutely, propranolol lowers cardiac output, and total peripheral resistance rises, so BP changes little. With chronic use, resistance vessels adapt to the lower output, peripheral resistance falls and BP drops. Other contributions: less renin release (beta-1 mediated), less noradrenaline release, and central effects of lipophilic agents.

front: Which beta-blockers have intrinsic sympathomimetic activity, and what advantages does it give?
back: Pindolol, acebutolol and celiprolol. They partly activate beta receptors, so resting bradycardia and cardiac depression are minimal, exercise tachycardia is still blocked, rebound after withdrawal is less likely, and plasma lipids are less affected. Limitations: they are not useful for migraine prophylaxis (they dilate cerebral vessels) and are not suited to secondary prevention after MI.

front: Esmolol: why is it so short acting, and where is it used?
back: It is a cardioselective beta-1 blocker without partial agonist or membrane-stabilising action. Blood esterases hydrolyse it rapidly, so plasma half-life is under 10 minutes and the effect ends 15 to 20 minutes after stopping the infusion. It is given as a 0.5 mg/kg loading dose, then 0.05 to 0.2 mg/kg/min. Uses: supraventricular tachycardia, intraoperative arrhythmias, control of HR and BP during cardiac surgery and aortic dissection, and early MI.

It lowers intraocular pressure by 20 to 35 percent within an hour, for about 12 hours. Systemic absorption through the nasolacrimal duct can cause bronchospasm and bradycardia, so pressure on the inner canthus is advised after instillation.

front: How do competitive and depolarising neuromuscular blockers differ at the end plate?
back: Competitive blockers occupy the nicotinic receptor without activating it, so ACh cannot open the channel. Depolarising blockers (succinylcholine, decamethonium) activate the receptor like ACh, but they resist acetylcholinesterase and keep the end plate depolarised until it becomes inexcitable.

front: Phase I and phase II depolarising block: how do they differ?
back: Phase I (classical) block: rapid onset, fasciculation then flaccid paralysis, no fade on train-of-four. Phase II (desensitisation) block: slow recovery, fade present, partly reversed by anticholinesterases. Phase II appears with high or infused doses, after fluorinated anaesthetics, or in atypical pseudocholinesterase.

front: How is train-of-four monitoring done, and what does the ratio tell you?
back: Four supramaximal stimuli at 2 Hz are applied to the ulnar nerve and adductor pollicis responses recorded. The TOF ratio is the fourth response divided by the first. Competitive block shows fade, with the ratio falling in proportion to the depth of block; depolarising (phase I) block reduces all four twitches equally, without fade. During recovery from competitive block the ratio climbs back towards 1.0: a ratio above 0.7 usually allows spontaneous breathing, but full clinical recovery needs a ratio above 0.9 (Katzung).

front: Succinylcholine: dose, onset, duration and how it is terminated.
back: IV dose: Katzung gives 0.75 to 1.5 mg/kg (KDT quotes a lower range); fasciculations over the chest and abdomen appear within about 30 s, followed by paralysis lasting about 5 to 10 min. It is hydrolysed rapidly by plasma pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) to succinylmonocholine and then succinic acid and choline, so recovery is spontaneous. Neostigmine does not reverse the block and may worsen it.

front: What happens to succinylcholine in atypical (deficient) pseudocholinesterase?
back: An abnormal genetic variant of plasma cholinesterase hydrolyses succinylcholine poorly. Homozygotes (roughly 1 in 3000) develop prolonged block (phase II) with apnoea lasting hours, which needs continued mechanical ventilation. The dibucaine number identifies the variant: dibucaine inhibits the normal enzyme by about 80% but the abnormal one by only about 20%. Testing is not routine but is indicated with a family history. Mivacurium is also prolonged, but that block can be reversed by neostigmine, unlike succinylcholine paralysis.

front: Sugammadex: what does it bind, how does it reverse block, and what is its advantage?
back: A modified gamma-cyclodextrin that encapsulates (chelates) rocuronium and, less so, vecuronium into an inactive complex excreted unchanged by the kidney, so it should be avoided in severe renal impairment. It does not inhibit acetylcholinesterase, so there are no muscarinic effects. Katzung doses: 2 mg/kg for shallow block (second twitch has returned), 4 mg/kg for deep block, 16 mg/kg for immediate reversal after a single 1.2 mg/kg dose of rocuronium. Adverse effects: altered taste, nausea, hypersensitivity and occasional anaphylaxis (about 0.3% with the 16 mg/kg dose). It can also bind progesterone-based contraceptives, reducing their effect.

It blocks RyR1 calcium-release channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle and prevents calcium-induced calcium release. Excitation-contraction coupling fails although the membrane still depolarises, so end-plate transmission is unaffected. Cardiac and smooth muscle channels (RyR2) are only weakly affected. Fast twitch fibres are affected more than slow antigravity fibres.

front: Dantrolene in malignant hyperthermia: why it works, the dose, and what limits its oral use
back: Malignant hyperthermia is persistent calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in genetically susceptible people, triggered by fluorinated anaesthetics and succinylcholine. Dantrolene blocks the RyR1 calcium-release channel, so IV dantrolene is the drug of choice. Dose in the owner's books: 1 mg/kg IV, repeated as needed up to a maximum of 10 mg/kg (KDT, Katzung). Oral use for spasticity is limited because the muscle weakness it causes offsets the benefit, and long-term use causes dose-related hepatotoxicity (a black-box warning).

front: Why can rocuronium replace succinylcholine for rapid tracheal intubation?
back: Rocuronium is a non-depolarising aminosteroid blocker with the fastest onset in its class, so it is the alternative to succinylcholine for tracheal intubation. It causes no fasciculation and no potassium release, has minimal cardiovascular effects, and is used for maintenance as well. Even profound block can be reversed by sugammadex (16 mg/kg reverses a 1.2 mg/kg dose within a few minutes). It depends on liver and biliary elimination, so its action is prolonged in liver disease.

front: Atracurium versus cisatracurium: elimination and side effects.
back: Atracurium undergoes spontaneous Hofmann elimination as well as ester hydrolysis, so its action is not prolonged in hepatic or renal failure. It releases histamine in a dose-related way, causing hypotension. Its breakdown product laudanosine has a long half-life, crosses the blood-brain barrier and at high levels can cause seizures, a concern during long ICU infusions. Cisatracurium, its potent stereoisomer, depends less on hepatic inactivation, forms less laudanosine and is much less likely to release histamine; it is preferred in liver or kidney disease and the elderly and has largely replaced atracurium.

front: How do local anaesthetics block the axonal Na+ channel?
back: The unionised base crosses the membrane and re-ionises inside the axon. The cation binds a receptor in the inner pore of the Na+ channel (segment S6 of domain IV), stabilises the inactivated state, and so raises the threshold and stops conduction. Blockade is use-dependent: it builds faster at higher firing frequencies, and higher extracellular Ca2+ reduces it.

front: Why does the pKa of a local anaesthetic determine its onset?
back: Only the unionised base crosses the nerve membrane. Lidocaine (pKa about 7.6 to 7.8) has 30 to 40% unionised at pH 7.4, so onset is fast. Bupivacaine, tetracaine and procaine (pKa 8.1 to 8.9) have 15% or less unionised, so onset is slow. Chloroprocaine is an exception: rapid onset despite a high pKa.

front: Why is epidural bupivacaine popular for labour analgesia?
back: At low concentration (0.25%), bupivacaine blocks sensory fibres more readily than motor fibres, giving pain relief with little leg weakness. The mother can push during contractions. In postoperative continuous epidural analgesia, the same separation allows early walking and exercise. Ropivacaine gives a similar sensory-motor separation.

Ester types (procaine, chloroprocaine, tetracaine, benzocaine) are hydrolysed by plasma pseudocholinesterase, act for shorter periods and cause more hypersensitivity; allergy cross-reacts among esters. Amide types (lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, prilocaine) are broken down in the liver, act longer and more intensely, rarely cause allergy, and do not cross-react with esters. Methylparaben preservative is a common allergen.

front: Why is adrenaline added to local anaesthetic solutions, and where should it be avoided?
back: Adrenaline (1 in 50,000 to 1 in 200,000) slows absorption from the injection site: the block lasts longer and is more intense, systemic toxicity falls and the field is less bloody. Classical teaching avoids it in ring blocks of fingers, toes, penis and pinna, where collateral flow is poor; Katzung notes some now question this rule. Use with caution in ischaemic heart disease, arrhythmia, uncontrolled hypertension, thyrotoxicosis, and with beta-blockers (unopposed alpha effect) or tricyclic antidepressants.

front: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity: CNS and cardiovascular features and management
back: CNS: early circumoral numbness, tongue tingling, dizziness, tinnitus; then restlessness, twitching, convulsions, coma and respiratory arrest. Cardiovascular: bradycardia, hypotension, arrhythmias, asystole and vascular collapse; bupivacaine is the most cardiotoxic. Management: stop injection, secure airway, give oxygen and ventilate, treat convulsions with diazepam or midazolam, support circulation, and give IV lipid emulsion, which has been shown to resuscitate bupivacaine cardiotoxicity.

front: Lidocaine versus bupivacaine: how do they compare?
back: Lidocaine: relative potency 1, fast onset, duration about 60 to 120 min, relatively low cardiotoxicity; also used as an antiarrhythmic. Bupivacaine: about 4 to 5 times as potent, slower onset, long duration (about 120 to 360 min), markedly more cardiotoxic, and avoided in IV regional block. Its sensory-selective epidural use at low concentration is its main advantage. Levobupivacaine is less cardiotoxic.

front: What is EMLA and how is it used?
back: A eutectic mixture of local anaesthetics: lidocaine 2.5% and prilocaine 2.5% form a mixture with a lower melting point, made into a 5% cream that can penetrate keratinised skin. Applied under an occlusive dressing for about 1 hour, it numbs intact skin to about 5 mm, lasting 1 to 2 hours after removal. Used before venepuncture or IV cannulation (especially in children), skin graft harvest and superficial procedures. A prilocaine metabolite can cause methaemoglobinaemia.

front: Why is cocaine no longer used as a local anaesthetic?
back: Its only classical indication was ocular surface anaesthesia, but it constricts conjunctival vessels and can cloud and even slough the cornea, so even this use is not justified. It blocks reuptake of noradrenaline and adrenaline, causing vasoconstriction, hypertension, tachycardia and mydriasis. It is a powerful CNS stimulant with high abuse potential. It must never be injected, because it is a protoplasmic poison that causes tissue necrosis.

front: Spinal anaesthesia: injection site, site of action and level of block.
back: The drug is injected into the subarachnoid space at L2-3 or L3-4, below the end of the cord, so it acts mainly on cauda equina nerve roots. Spread depends on dose, volume, specific gravity and posture; hyperbaric (glucose) solutions move to the dependent part. Sympathetic block is about 2 segments higher than the sensory level and motor block about 2 segments lower. The level becomes fixed about 10 min after injection.

text: Maximum doses for nerve block are about {{300 mg}} for lidocaine, {{150 mg}} for bupivacaine and {{200 mg}} for ropivacaine; the highest peak blood levels follow {{intercostal}} block, so limits are respected most carefully there.

front: What are the four cardinal features of general anaesthesia?
back: Loss of all sensation, especially pain; unconsciousness with amnesia; immobility with muscle relaxation; and abolition of somatic and autonomic reflexes.

front: What is MAC, and what changes it?
back: MAC is the minimum alveolar concentration that prevents movement in response to a surgical incision in 50% of patients. It is the standard measure of inhalational potency (the lower the MAC, the more potent the agent). It declines progressively beyond about 50 years of age, is lowered by sedative or opioid premedication, and is additive when two agents are combined (for example, 0.5 MAC of nitrous oxide plus 0.5 MAC of isoflurane gives about the effect of 1 MAC isoflurane).

front: Second gas effect and diffusion hypoxia.
back: Second gas effect: a high-concentration gas such as nitrous oxide (70 to 80%) draws in extra gas volume, so a simultaneously given potent agent such as halothane reaches blood faster. Diffusion hypoxia: when nitrous oxide is stopped, its rapid outflow dilutes alveolar oxygen. It is prevented by giving 100% oxygen for a few minutes after stopping nitrous oxide.

front: Describe Guedel's four stages of anaesthesia.
back: Stage I, analgesia: from start of inhalation to loss of consciousness. Stage II, delirium: excitement until regular breathing returns; no stimulus should be given. Stage III, surgical anaesthesia: regular breathing to cessation of spontaneous breathing, with four planes. Stage IV, medullary paralysis: breathing and circulation fail. These stages are blurred in modern practice.

front: Which receptors do nitrous oxide and ketamine act on, and how does this differ from volatile agents?
back: Nitrous oxide and ketamine mainly inhibit NMDA glutamate receptors, which gate Ca2+ channels. Volatile agents, barbiturates, propofol and benzodiazepines potentiate GABA-A chloride currents; some volatile agents and barbiturates also inhibit neuronal nicotinic channels. General anaesthetics mainly depress synaptic transmission, unlike local anaesthetics, which block axonal conduction.

front: Thiopentone: why is its action short, and what are its main risks?
back: It is highly lipid-soluble, so it reaches the brain within one arm-to-brain circulation time (about 15 to 20 s). Redistribution into muscle and fat ends the effect in 6 to 10 min, while slow hepatic metabolism (half-life 8 to 12 h) leaves residual sedation for over 12 h. Risks: apnoea, hypotension, laryngospasm, poor analgesia; contraindicated in porphyria. Extravasation or inadvertent intra-arterial injection causes intense pain, necrosis and gangrene. It must not be mixed with succinylcholine in the same syringe.

A 1% emulsion; induction 2 mg/kg IV, maintenance 100 to 200 µg/kg/min. Recovery is fast with little nausea (it has antiemetic activity), so it suits day-case surgery; it is also used in asthmatics. Drawbacks: pain on injection (reduced by lidocaine or an opioid), induction apnoea, dose-related hypotension from vasodilatation and dose-dependent respiratory depression. Prolonged high-dose infusion can cause metabolic acidosis, lipaemia and heart failure (propofol infusion syndrome); unexplained tachycardia during propofol anaesthesia should prompt a check for acidosis.

front: Ketamine: dissociative anaesthesia and when to avoid it.
back: It blocks NMDA receptors, giving dissociative anaesthesia: profound analgesia and amnesia while the eyes stay open and airway reflexes persist. It preserves respiration and dilates bronchi, but raises heart rate, BP, cerebral blood flow and oxygen demand. Emergence delirium and hallucinations are common. Avoid in hypertension, ischaemic heart disease and heart failure; it suits hypovolaemic patients and asthmatics. It has traditionally been avoided with raised intracranial pressure, though Katzung notes the cerebral effects may be blunted by keeping CO2 normal. Its S-isomer, esketamine, is given intranasally for depression.

front: Remifentanil: why does its effect end so quickly?
back: It is hydrolysed rapidly by plasma and tissue esterases rather than by the liver or kidney, so its effect fades within about 10 to 15 min even after prolonged infusion. This titratability and quick recovery suit short, intensely painful procedures and infusion techniques. It still causes respiratory depression and can cause chest wall rigidity.

front: Halothane: main adverse effects and why it has declined.
back: It causes dose-related depression of myocardial contractility and a fall in BP, and sensitises the heart to adrenaline, which can cause arrhythmias. It depresses respiration and reduces urine output by lowering GFR. About 20% is metabolised; immune reactions against trifluoroacetylated liver proteins can cause halothane hepatitis (about 1 in 10,000 exposures, about 50% fatal), presenting days after surgery with fever, nausea, rash and eosinophilia. It triggers malignant hyperthermia. Low cost keeps it in use in developing countries, but newer agents have replaced it elsewhere.

text: Nitrous oxide has a MAC of about {{105%}} and so cannot produce surgical anaesthesia alone; {{halothane}} has a MAC of about {{0.75%}}, {{isoflurane}} about {{1.2%}} and {{desflurane}} about {{6%}}.
Stage I is {{analgesia}}, stage II is {{delirium}}, stage III is {{surgical anaesthesia}} with four planes, and stage IV is {{medullary paralysis}}.

{{Thiopentone}} is an ultrashort {{thiobarbiturate}}; {{propofol}} is given as a {{1%}} emulsion; {{etomidate}} is a briefly acting inducing agent with little cardiovascular depression; {{midazolam}} is the water-soluble benzodiazepine.

{{Glycopyrrolate}} is about {{twice}} as potent as atropine with no central effects; {{ondansetron}} is the {{5-HT3}} blocker used as antiemetic of choice; {{ranitidine}} is an H2 blocker that raises gastric pH.

front: Dexmedetomidine: mechanism, advantages and adverse effects
back: The active S-enantiomer of medetomidine, a centrally acting selective alpha-2A agonist (clonidine-like action). Given by IV infusion, it produces sedation and analgesia with little respiratory depression, amnesia or anaesthesia, and blunts the sympathetic response to stress. Uses: sedation of ventilated ICU patients, sedation during endoscopy and regional anaesthesia, and as an adjunct that lowers the dose of inhalational anaesthetic. Rapid hepatic metabolism, half-life 2 to 3 h. Side effects resemble clonidine: hypotension, bradycardia and dry mouth.

front: Neostigmine reversal of competitive neuromuscular block: how it works and its limits
back: Neostigmine inhibits cholinesterase, so acetylcholine builds up at the end plate and overcomes the competitive blocker. KDT dose: 0.5 to 2 mg (30 to 50 µg/kg) IV, given almost routinely after long- and intermediate-acting blockers, preceded by atropine or glycopyrrolate (about 10 µg/kg) to block muscarinic effects such as bradycardia, hypotension and bronchospasm. Reversing residual block matters because residual weakness causes hypoventilation and hypoxia in recovery. It does not reverse depolarising (phase I) succinylcholine block; it worsens it. Sugammadex is an alternative for rocuronium.

front: What are the three main mechanisms that generate cardiac arrhythmias?
back: Enhanced or ectopic automaticity (a steeper phase-4 slope or abnormal pacemaker sites); triggered activity from early or delayed after-depolarisations; and re-entry, where an impulse recirculates because of conduction block or slowing (circus movement or functional re-entry).

front: What is the Vaughan Williams classification?
back: A four-class scheme based on the main electrophysiological action: class I sodium channel blockers (subclasses IA, IB and IC), class II beta blockers, class III drugs that prolong repolarisation (mainly potassium channel blockers), and class IV calcium channel blockers. Many drugs act in more than one class, so the scheme is only a guide.

front: Class IA antiarrhythmics: name the drugs and their main electrophysiological effects.
back: Quinidine, procainamide and disopyramide block open-state sodium channels and dissociate with intermediate (moderate) kinetics. They prolong the action potential, refractoriness and QT interval, widen the QRS, and depress conduction. Their proarrhythmic risk, including torsades de pointes, is significant.

front: Why is lidocaine a class IB drug, and what is it used for?
back: It preferentially blocks inactivated sodium channels, so it acts mainly on depolarised or ischaemic tissue. It suppresses ectopic automaticity and ventricular arrhythmias, and it has practically no effect on atrial action potentials, so it is ineffective in atrial arrhythmias. It is given only intravenously because of high first-pass metabolism, and it has the lowest proarrhythmic potential of the antiarrhythmics.

front: Class IC drugs: name the two main examples and explain why their use is restricted.
back: Flecainide and propafenone are the most potent sodium channel blockers, with very slow recovery. They markedly slow conduction and widen the QRS, and they can be proarrhythmic. The CAST trials found excess sudden death with class IC drugs after myocardial infarction, so they are avoided in structural heart disease and ischaemia. Propafenone also has beta-blocking activity and is metabolised by CYP2D6.

front: How do beta blockers suppress arrhythmias, and which arrhythmias respond best?
back: They block adrenergically driven automaticity and after-depolarisations, and they prolong AV nodal refractoriness, which slows AV conduction. They work best in sympathetically mediated arrhythmias, inappropriate sinus tachycardia and AV-node-dependent tachycardias, and they control ventricular rate in AF and flutter. Long-term beta blockade reduces sudden cardiac death after myocardial infarction.

front: Amiodarone: list its main electrophysiological actions and its long-term benefit.
back: It prolongs the action potential and QT interval by blocking delayed rectifier potassium channels. It also blocks inactivated sodium channels, partly blocks L-type calcium channels, and has non-competitive adrenergic blocking activity; its torsades risk is low despite QT prolongation. Its half-life is weeks. KDT notes that, apart from propranolol, it is the only antiarrhythmic shown to reduce long-term sudden cardiac death; however, its modest mortality benefit in heart failure seen in a meta-analysis was not confirmed in the SCD-HeFT trial.

front: Adenosine: dose, route and mechanism in PSVT.
back: Given as a rapid intravenous bolus over 1 to 3 seconds, usually 6 to 12 mg of adenosine (or 10 to 20 mg of ATP). It acts on A1 receptors to hyperpolarise SA and AV nodal fibres and reduce calcium current, which interrupts AV-node re-entry. More than 90% of AV-node-dependent PSVT episodes terminate within about 30 seconds. Its half-life in blood is about 10 seconds.

front: Which drugs modify the response to adenosine, and why does it matter clinically?
back: Theophylline and caffeine block A1 receptors and blunt its effect, so heavy tea or coffee drinkers may need higher doses. Dipyridamole inhibits its cellular uptake and potentiates it. Patients on carbamazepine have a greater risk of heart block.

front: What are the main adverse effects of IV adenosine, and when is verapamil preferred?
back: Transient dyspnoea, chest discomfort, flushing and a fall in BP are common. Brief asystole or ventricular fibrillation can occur and usually resolves quickly. It can precipitate bronchospasm, so verapamil is preferred in asthma. Its action is too brief for prophylaxis. Unlike verapamil, it is safe in wide-QRS tachycardia and in patients with hypotension or heart failure.

front: Verapamil: which cardiac actions make it useful in PSVT, and why is it contraindicated in broad-QRS WPW tachycardia?
back: It blocks L-type calcium channels, slows SA nodal firing and markedly prolongs AV nodal refractoriness, which terminates AV-node re-entry. A dose of 5 mg IV is given over 2 to 3 minutes. It is contraindicated in broad-QRS WPW tachycardia, where it can shorten the accessory pathway refractory period and speed conduction. Avoid it with IV beta blockers, in hypotension or heart failure, and in VT, where it may precipitate VF.

front: Classify: Adenosine effects on the heart

front: Classical (stable) angina and variant (Prinzmetal) angina: how do their causes and drug approaches differ?
back: Classical angina is caused by fixed atherosclerotic narrowing of epicardial arteries. It is provoked by exertion or emotion and relieved by rest, so drugs that reduce cardiac work help. Variant angina is due to recurrent coronary vasospasm, occurs at rest or during sleep, and needs drugs that prevent or relieve spasm, such as nitrates and calcium channel blockers.

front: How do organic nitrates relax vascular smooth muscle?
back: They are denitrated inside the smooth muscle cell to release nitric oxide, which activates soluble guanylyl cyclase. The rise in cGMP activates protein kinase G, which reduces myosin light-chain kinase activity and relaxes the muscle. Veins contain more of the mitochondrial enzyme that generates NO from GTN (aldehyde dehydrogenase), which may explain their venodilator preference.

front: What are the main haemodynamic effects of nitrates in angina?
back: Venodilatation pools blood and lowers preload, end-diastolic volume and wall tension, which reduces myocardial oxygen demand. Mild arteriolar dilatation lowers afterload. Large epicardial coronary arteries dilate, which can redistribute flow to the ischaemic subendocardium. They have no direct effect on heart rate or contractility, but a large fall in BP can cause reflex tachycardia.

front: Nitrate tolerance: when does it occur, and how is it prevented?
back: Continuous exposure, especially with oral, transdermal, infusion or sustained-release therapy, blunts the haemodynamic and anti-ischaemic effects. Tolerance wears off within hours of stopping and is cross-tolerant between nitrates. Oxidative stress from denitration impairs the NO-generating enzyme, and neurohormonal compensation contributes. The main preventive measure is a daily nitrate-free interval. Intermittent sublingual GTN causes no significant tolerance.

front: Sublingual GTN for an acute attack: onset, duration and key dosing points.
back: The tablet acts within 1 to 2 minutes and peaks in 3 to 6 minutes because it is absorbed straight into the systemic circulation, bypassing the liver. Plasma half-life is about 2 minutes, and duration depends on how long the tablet stays in the buccal mucosa. A usual dose is 0.5 mg sublingual at the onset of pain or before exertion. Pain not relieved after three tablets 5 minutes apart needs urgent review, since IV GTN may be started in acute coronary syndrome.

front: When must GTN be withheld in suspected myocardial infarction?
back: When systolic BP is below 90 mm Hg, when heart rate is below 50 or above 100 per minute, and when right ventricular infarction is suspected. It must also be withheld if sildenafil was taken in the previous 24 hours. Nitrate-induced hypotension can also prevent the use of beta blockers, which have stronger long-term benefit.

front: Why must nitrates be avoided after sildenafil?
back: Sildenafil and other PDE-5 inhibitors raise cGMP, the same second messenger that nitrates act through. The combination can cause profound hypotension, and MI and death have been reported. Nitrates should not be given within 24 hours of a PDE-5 inhibitor, and a longer gap is needed after tadalafil because of its long half-life. If hypotension occurs, fluids and alpha-agonists are used for support. Other vasodilators add to the hypotension.

front: Beta blockers in stable angina: how do they help, and which should be preferred?
back: They lower heart rate, contractility and BP, cutting myocardial oxygen demand, especially during exercise. A slower heart prolongs diastole, which improves subendocardial perfusion. Total coronary flow falls slightly, but flow to the ischaemic region is not reduced. Cardioselective agents (atenolol, metoprolol) are preferred, since nonselective agents can worsen vasospastic angina. They reduce mortality after a recent MI and in heart failure, and in stable angina trials they gave better outcomes than calcium channel blockers. Abrupt withdrawal should be avoided.

front: Ranolazine: mechanism, effect on heart rate and BP, and key safety issues.
back: It inhibits the late sodium current, which indirectly reduces calcium overload during ischaemia and helps preserve myocardial function. It does not change heart rate or BP, and it prolongs exercise duration. It prolongs the QT interval, so it must not be combined with other QT-prolonging drugs, and CYP3A4 inhibitors should be avoided. It can be used with sildenafil.

front: Trimetazidine: how does it work, and why is it not a haemodynamic drug?
back: It inhibits long-chain 3-ketoacyl-CoA thiolase (LC3-KAT), a key enzyme of fatty acid oxidation. Myocardium shifts toward glucose oxidation, which needs less oxygen per unit of ATP. It has no effect on heart rate or BP at rest or on exercise, yet it reduces angina frequency and increases exercise capacity. Side effects include GI upset; it can cause movement disorders such as parkinsonism, especially in elderly patients with reduced renal function, so the EMA restricts it to second-line add-on use in stable angina. It is not approved in the USA.

front: Nicorandil: mechanism and main adverse effects.
back: It opens ATP-sensitive potassium channels in smooth muscle, causing hyperpolarisation, and it also acts as a nitric oxide donor that raises cGMP. It lowers preload and afterload and increases coronary flow, with no significant effect on contractility or conduction. Adverse effects include flushing, headache, palpitation and painful oral aphthous ulcers. Concurrent PDE-5 inhibitors are contraindicated, and it does not cause nitrate-type tolerance.

front: How do the major guidelines define hypertension and set treatment thresholds (NICE 2011, JNC 8, ACC/AHA 2017, ESC 2018)?
back: NICE 2011 (as in KDT): stage I 140 to 159/90 to 99, stage II 160 to 179/100 to 109, severe 180/110 mm Hg or more. JNC 8 (2014): treat from 140/90, except in people aged 60 or over, where the systolic threshold and goal are 150 mm Hg (diastolic stays 90). ACC/AHA 2017: normal below 120/80, elevated 120 to 129/below 80, stage 1 130 to 139/80 to 89, stage 2 140/90 or more; so hypertension in the USA starts at 130/80 and the target is below 130/80, with drugs in stage 1 only if there is atherosclerotic disease or a 10-year risk of 10% or more. ESC 2018: hypertension remains 140/90 or more, with a systolic target below 140 and close to 130. The lower targets followed SPRINT, where a systolic target of 120 rather than 140 mm Hg cut cardiovascular events and total mortality by about 25%.

front: Thiazide diuretics: the usual antihypertensive dose and why higher doses are avoided.
back: Low-dose hydrochlorothiazide (12.5 to 25 mg/day) or chlorthalidone is preferred. Maximal antihypertensive effect is reached at 25 mg/day, which gives the best benefit-risk ratio; higher doses mainly add adverse effects. Higher doses cause hypokalaemia, glucose intolerance, dyslipidaemia and hyperuricaemia without much further BP fall. Thiazides are ineffective in advanced chronic kidney disease.

front: ACE inhibitors in hypertension: where are they preferred, and what is the main limiting adverse effect?
back: They are first-line in most grades of essential and renovascular hypertension, except bilateral renal artery stenosis. They are preferred with diabetes, nephropathy, left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, angina and after MI. Dry, persistent cough, from raised bradykinin, is the most common reason to stop them. They are contraindicated in pregnancy.

front: ARBs compared with ACE inhibitors: practical advantages, and which combination is discouraged?
back: ARBs block the angiotensin receptor without raising kinin levels, so the ACE inhibitor cough is avoided; angioedema and taste disturbance are rare. They share the metabolic and prognostic benefits of ACE inhibitors. JNC 8 and NICE advise against combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB. ARBs are also avoided in pregnancy.

front: Calcium channel blockers in hypertension: which agents are used, and what are their main advantages?
back: Dihydropyridines, mainly amlodipine, are used most; verapamil and diltiazem are equally effective but less used. They lower BP by reducing peripheral resistance without reducing cardiac output or causing fluid retention. Advantages include no CNS effects, no sexual dysfunction, neutral effects on lipids, uric acid and electrolytes, and suitability in asthma, peripheral vascular disease and pregnancy. Short-acting nifedipine is not used for hypertension.

front: Beta blockers in hypertension: why are they no longer first-line?
back: They are mild antihypertensives, and in primary prevention they are less effective than diuretics, ACE inhibitors or ARBs for stroke and MI. Nonselective agents raise triglycerides and worsen quality of life, and rebound hypertension and angina can follow abrupt withdrawal. They remain indicated for compelling reasons such as post-MI, stable heart failure or high coronary risk.

front: Clonidine: mechanism of action and the withdrawal syndrome.
back: Clonidine is a central alpha-2A agonist that reduces sympathetic outflow from the medulla, lowering BP and heart rate. Stopping it abruptly, especially after missed doses, can cause severe rebound hypertension with tachycardia, anxiety, sweating and headache, resembling phaeochromocytoma. It is treated with an alpha plus beta blocker, nitroprusside, or clonidine itself. Tricyclic antidepressants antagonise its effect.

front: Methyldopa: active metabolite, site of action, and why it is used in pregnancy.
back: Methyldopa is converted in the body to alpha-methylnoradrenaline, a central alpha-2 agonist that lowers sympathetic tone and reduces total peripheral resistance more than heart rate or output. It is now used mainly in pregnancy because of its long safety record. Sedation and mental slowing are common. A positive Coombs test is common, but haemolytic anaemia is rare.

front: Hydralazine: mechanism, reflex effects, and main limitations.
back: It is a direct arteriolar vasodilator with little venous action, so it lowers diastolic BP more than systolic. Baroreflex activation causes tachycardia, higher cardiac output and renin release, leading to salt and water retention and tolerance unless a diuretic or beta blocker is added. It can provoke angina. Prolonged use above 100 mg/day can cause a lupus-like syndrome, more often in women and slow acetylators.

front: Reserpine: mechanism and why it is no longer used as an antihypertensive.
back: Reserpine irreversibly inhibits the vesicular monoamine transporter (VMAT2), so noradrenaline, dopamine and serotonin are gradually lost and degraded. The effect outlasts the drug for weeks. Central depletion causes sedation, depression and extrapyramidal symptoms. It has been replaced by safer agents and is now used mainly as a pharmacological tool.

front: Sodium nitroprusside: why it suits hypertensive emergencies, and what limits its use.
back: It acts within seconds and wears off within minutes, so BP can be titrated by the infusion rate. It dilates both arterioles and veins, and its NO release does not produce nitrate-type tolerance. Cyanide and thiocyanate toxicity, lactic acidosis, and the need for an infusion pump and arterial monitoring limit its use. It should be avoided in stroke and in eclampsia.

front: Resistant hypertension: common causes and drug approach
back: Many patients need two, three or four drugs at optimal doses. Common reasons for apparent resistance are inadequate doses, poor adherence, combining drugs that act by the same mechanism, high salt intake and salt retention caused by vasodilators (so diuretic therapy is often inadequate), and interfering drugs: NSAIDs, sympathomimetic decongestants, ciclosporin, erythropoietin, ephedra, liquorice, cocaine and amphetamines. Many resistant patients have primary hyperaldosteronism and respond to adding spironolactone 25 to 50 mg daily; alternatives at this step are another diuretic, an alpha-1 blocker or a beta blocker. Renal denervation may help selected patients with well-defined resistant hypertension.

front: Which histamine receptor types are clinically relevant, and what is the role of H3 and H4?
back: H1 and H2 are the main clinically targeted types. H3 is mainly a presynaptic autoreceptor in the brain that limits histamine release; KDT lists no H3 drug in use, but GG14 notes pitolisant, an H3 inverse agonist, is approved for narcolepsy. H4, cloned in 2001, is on eosinophils, mast cells and basophils and promotes their chemotaxis.

front: What are the signalling pathways of H1 and H2 receptors?
back: H1 is Gq-coupled: PIP2 hydrolysis gives IP3 and DAG, releasing intracellular Ca2+ and activating protein kinase C. H2 is Gs-coupled: adenylyl cyclase is stimulated and cAMP rises.

front: Describe the triple response produced by intradermal histamine.
back: Red spot from intense capillary dilatation; wheal from fluid leaking out of capillaries and venules; flare, a surrounding redness from arteriolar dilatation that is driven by an axon reflex.

front: Why is histamine inactive when given orally?
back: It is rapidly broken down by oxidation and methylation, and the liver degrades all histamine absorbed from the intestine before it reaches the circulation.

front: Why are first-generation H1 antihistamines sedating, and which ones are the most sedating?
back: They cross the blood-brain barrier and block central H1 receptors that help maintain wakefulness. Diphenhydramine, promethazine, hydroxyzine and dimenhydrinate are the highly sedating members, while chlorpheniramine and clemastine are only mildly sedating.

front: Why were terfenadine and astemizole withdrawn, and how does fexofenadine avoid this problem?
back: Both caused torsades de pointes through blockade of cardiac delayed rectifier K+ channels, especially at higher doses or with CYP3A4 inhibitors. Fexofenadine, the active metabolite of terfenadine, blocks these channels only weakly and is minimally metabolised, so it does not prolong the QTc interval.

front: Why are H1 antihistamines ineffective in bronchial asthma?
back: Leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4) and PAF are more important mediators of human asthma than histamine. Also, the antihistamine may not reach concentrations high enough to block the large amounts of histamine released locally in the bronchi.

front: Why is adrenaline, not an antihistamine, the life-saving drug in anaphylactic shock?
back: H1 antihistamines act slowly and only block histamine effects. In anaphylaxis, leukotrienes and PAF contribute substantially to the fall in blood pressure, so adrenaline is the first-line drug and antihistamines play a secondary role.

front: What is betahistine, what is it used for, and what are its contraindications?
back: An orally active histamine analogue with some H1 selectivity, used for vertigo in Meniere's disease, probably by improving blood flow in the inner ear. It is contraindicated in patients with asthma and peptic ulcer.

front: What additional actions does cyproheptadine have beyond H1 blockade, and what are its uses?
back: It also blocks 5-HT2A receptors and is sedating. Uses include pruritus, appetite stimulation (including off-label use in underweight patients), and control of carcinoid intestinal symptoms and SSRI-induced priapism.

front: Describe the synthesis and degradation of 5-HT.
back: 5-HT is made from L-tryptophan: tryptophan hydroxylase forms 5-hydroxytryptophan, which is decarboxylated to 5-HT. It is degraded mainly by MAO-A to 5-hydroxyindole acetic acid. It is taken up into platelets and nerve endings by the serotonin transporter, which SSRIs and tricyclics inhibit, and its vesicular storage (VMAT-2) is blocked by reserpine.

front: How are the 5-HT receptor families classified by their signalling?
back: 5-HT1 receptors (Gi/Go) reduce cAMP. 5-HT2 receptors (Gq) generate IP3 and DAG. 5-HT4, 5-HT6 and 5-HT7 (Gs) raise cAMP. 5-HT3 is not G-protein coupled but a ligand-gated cation channel that depolarises nerve endings quickly.

front: Which 5-HT receptor do triptans act on, and what does it do in cranial vessels?
back: 5-HT1B/1D. Stimulation constricts dilated cranial vessels, including carotid arteriovenous shunts, and reduces release of inflammatory neuropeptides from perivascular nerves. Sumatriptan is the prototype selective agonist.

front: What is the role of 5-HT1A agonists such as buspirone?
back: Buspirone, gepirone and ipsapirone are azapirones that act as partial agonists at 5-HT1A receptors. They are anxiolytics that do not cause sedation.

front: Which receptor mediates the emetic reflex, and which antagonist is the prototype?
back: 5-HT3 receptors on nerve endings in the gut wall (myenteric plexus), in the area postrema and in the nucleus tractus solitarius. Ondansetron is the prototype selective 5-HT3 antagonist, used against vomiting from highly emetic cytotoxic drugs and radiotherapy.

Acting on 5-HT2A receptors it changes platelet shape and causes weak aggregation, but it does not induce the release reaction. Platelets store and release 5-HT, which amplifies aggregation with collagen and other mediators.

front: Why was methysergide withdrawn, and what was it used for?
back: It is a potent 5-HT2A/2C antagonist used for migraine prophylaxis, carcinoid and postgastrectomy dumping syndrome. It was withdrawn because it caused fibrosis in the abdomen, lungs and endocardium.

front: Why are ergot alkaloids poorly suited to oral migraine treatment?
back: Oral bioavailability of the amino-acid ergots (ergotamine) and their hydrogenated derivatives is below 1 percent, due to slow and incomplete absorption and high first-pass metabolism. Caffeine improves absorption of ergotamine.

Oral 50 to 100 mg at the onset of an attack; may be repeated once within 24 hours, but not if the first dose failed. SC 6 mg (acts in 10 to 20 min, also repeatable once in 24 h) when oral use is impractical or pain builds quickly; nasal spray is an alternative. Contraindicated in ischaemic or vasospastic coronary disease, stroke or TIA, peripheral vascular disease, hemiplegic or basilar migraine, ischaemic bowel disease and uncontrolled hypertension. Do not give within 24 hours of an ergot or another triptan, or within 2 weeks of an MAO inhibitor; combining with SSRIs or SNRIs risks serotonin syndrome.

front: What is the first-line treatment for a mild migraine attack, and what adjunct is useful for nausea?
back: Simple analgesics such as paracetamol (0.5 to 1 g) or aspirin (300 to 600 mg) taken at the first sign of an attack. Metoclopramide, given orally or by injection, relieves the nausea and gastric stasis that delay absorption.

front: Name the precursor and the two main enzymatic pathways for eicosanoid synthesis.
back: The precursor is arachidonic acid (a 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid), released from membrane phospholipids by phospholipase A2. The cyclooxygenase pathway makes prostaglandins, thromboxanes and prostacyclin. The lipoxygenase pathway (5-LOX) makes leukotrienes. Eicosanoids are not stored; they are made when needed.

front: How do COX-1 and COX-2 differ in function?
back: COX-1 is expressed constitutively in most cells and makes prostanoids for housekeeping functions: gastric mucosal protection, platelet TXA2 and renal function. COX-2 is induced by cytokines, shear stress and growth factors and is the main source of prostanoids in inflammation (pain, fever) and cancer. The split is not absolute: COX-2 also contributes constitutively in some tissues, such as gastric epithelium. Selective COX-2 inhibitors include celecoxib and etoricoxib.

front: How does aspirin differ from other NSAIDs in inhibiting COX?
back: Aspirin acetylates a serine residue on COX and inhibits it irreversibly. Other NSAIDs are competitive and reversible. Because platelets cannot make new COX-1 and the vessel wall can, low-dose aspirin inhibits platelet thromboxane for days.

front: What are the opposing actions of platelet TXA2 and endothelial PGI2?
back: TXA2, made by platelets, promotes aggregation and vasoconstriction. PGI2, made by the endothelium, inhibits aggregation and causes vasodilatation. The two act as a balanced system that keeps blood flowing and allows plugging when a vessel is injured.

front: Which prostanoids constrict bronchi, and which dilate them?
back: PGF2alpha, PGD2 and TXA2 constrict bronchi, more strongly than histamine. PGE2 is a powerful bronchodilator and PGI2 a mild one. Inhaled PGE2 is not clinically useful because it irritates the airway and its action is brief.

front: What are the gastroprotective actions of PGE2?
back: PGE2 reduces basal and stimulated acid and pepsin secretion, suppresses gastrin release, and increases mucus and bicarbonate secretion and mucosal blood flow. The ulcer-causing effect of NSAIDs is attributed to losing this protection.

front: Which leukotriene receptor antagonists are used in asthma, and what do they block?
back: Montelukast and zafirlukast block the cysLT1 receptor, which is mainly on bronchial and intestinal smooth muscle and binds LTD4 more avidly than LTC4. They are useful antiasthmatic drugs.

front: What is platelet activating factor chemically, and how is it made?
back: It is acetylglyceryl ether phosphorylcholine, with an ether-linked alkyl chain of 16 or 18 carbons. It is made on demand from membrane phospholipids, with the second step rate-limiting. It is active at subnanomolar concentrations.

front: Carboprost: what is it, and how is it used in postpartum haemorrhage?
back: Carboprost is 15-methyl PGF2-alpha; the methyl group prolongs its action. For PPH from uterine atony not responding to oxytocin and ergometrine: 0.25 mg (250 mcg) IM, repeated every 30 to 120 minutes if needed (KDT); Katzung cites about 80% success. It is also used for second-trimester and missed abortion. Adverse effects: vomiting, diarrhoea, fever, flushing and transient bronchoconstriction.

front: Which PGF2alpha analogues are first-line for open-angle glaucoma and how do they work?
back: Latanoprost, travoprost and bimatoprost are FP receptor agonists. They lower intraocular pressure by increasing uveoscleral and trabecular outflow of aqueous humour, and are non-irritating compared with the parent PGF2alpha.

front: Where is most of the body's iron, and where is the stored fraction kept?
back: An adult carries about 3.5 g of iron. Roughly 62% is in haemoglobin and about 25% is stored as ferritin and haemosiderin, mainly in reticuloendothelial cells in liver, spleen and marrow. The rest is in myoglobin and iron-containing enzymes.

front: Compare the absorption of haeme iron with that of inorganic dietary iron.
back: Haeme iron is absorbed best (up to about 35%) through a haeme carrier protein, without needing to be freed from its complex first. Inorganic iron averages about 5%: it must be reduced to the ferrous form, then enters the enterocyte through DMT1 and leaves the cell through ferroportin.

front: Which substances impair the absorption of non-haeme iron, and which help it?
back: Impairing: antacids and other alkalis (keep iron insoluble and block its reduction), phytates in cereals, phosphates, tetracyclines (chelation), and a heavy mixed meal in the stomach. Helping: gastric acid, reducing agents such as ascorbic acid and sulfhydryl amino acids, and meat, which adds haeme iron and stimulates acid.

front: What is the mucosal block (ferritin curtain) and when is it overcome?
back: Iron entering the enterocyte can be trapped as ferritin, which is lost when the cell is shed after 2 to 4 days. This limits absorption. The block is weakened in iron deficiency or brisk erythropoiesis, when more iron passes into plasma, and is overwhelmed by a gross excess of iron.

front: What oral elemental iron dose gives the maximal haemopoietic response, and what is the prophylactic dose?
back: KDT: about 200 mg of elemental iron a day in three divided doses gives the maximal haemopoietic response; about 30 mg a day is prophylactic. GG14 adds that a single dose of about 65 mg elemental iron (one 325 mg ferrous sulfate tablet) every other day maximises the fraction absorbed. Doses are always counted as elemental iron, not salt weight.

front: When is parenteral iron indicated instead of oral iron?
back: When oral iron is not tolerated, when it is not absorbed (malabsorption, inflammatory bowel disease, chronic inflammation), when the patient does not take it, in severe deficiency with ongoing blood loss, and in chronic kidney disease patients on erythropoietin who need iron faster than oral intake can supply.

front: Iron dextran: what makes it unusual, and what are its main risks?
back: It is the only iron preparation that can be given both i.m. and i.v. About 25% extra is added to the calculated dose because some stays locally bound at the injection site. It has the highest rate of hypersensitivity, including anaphylactoid collapse, because dextran is antigenic. A test dose is no longer recommended, and resuscitation facilities must be ready before any i.v. dose.

front: Which newer intravenous iron products are the most convenient and safest, and why?
back: Ferric carboxymaltose and iron isomaltoside 1000 are considered the two most convenient and safest i.v. options. Ferric carboxymaltose can be given as a single infusion of up to 1000 mg in saline (not glucose) and must not be given i.m. Iron isomaltoside 1000 allows a single 1 to 2 g infusion over 15 to 30 minutes, because its tight matrix releases little labile iron.

front: Which drug is the chelator of choice in acute iron poisoning, and why is dimercaprol (BAL) avoided?
back: Desferrioxamine (deferoxamine). It is given when plasma iron exceeds the total iron-binding capacity, and the IV route is used to chelate iron already absorbed; early chelation has cut the mortality of iron poisoning sharply. BAL (dimercaprol) is avoided because its iron complex is itself toxic.

front: Which clotting tests explore the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways, and what does each test?
back: The aPTT explores the intrinsic (contact-activation) pathway and the common pathway. The prothrombin time (PT) explores the extrinsic (tissue factor) pathway and the common pathway. The extrinsic route activates factor X within seconds; the intrinsic route is slow and takes minutes.

front: How does vitamin K take part in blood clotting?
back: Vitamin K is a cofactor for the hepatic enzyme gamma-glutamyl carboxylase, which adds carboxyl groups to glutamate residues of factors II, VII, IX and X. This lets them bind calcium and phospholipid surfaces. Protein C, protein S and osteocalcin use the same step.

front: How do coumarin anticoagulants block clotting?
back: They inhibit vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKOR), so reduced vitamin K cannot be regenerated. The liver then makes under-carboxylated, inactive factors II, VII, IX and X. Coumarins work only in vivo and act with a delay of 1 to 3 days, because already-circulating factors must decay.

front: On warfarin, which clotting factor falls first, and why does the effect take days to appear?
back: Factor VII has the shortest half-life (about 6 h), so it falls first, followed by factor IX (about 24 h), factor X (about 40 h) and prothrombin (about 60 h). Synthesis slows within hours, but the full effect appears over 1 to 3 days as circulating factors decline. A larger loading dose only slightly hastens it.

front: Which drugs and conditions increase the effect of warfarin, and by what mechanism?
back: Broad-spectrum antibiotics reduce gut vitamin K production; ceftriaxone and cefoperazone add a direct hypoprothrombinaemic effect; aspirin adds platelet inhibition and GI bleeding; sulfonamides, phenytoin and indomethacin displace warfarin from albumin; chloramphenicol, erythromycin, metronidazole, amiodarone, cimetidine and allopurinol inhibit its metabolism. Liver disease, malnutrition and hyperthyroidism also increase the effect.

front: Which drugs reduce the effect of warfarin, and why is stopping them dangerous?
back: Barbiturates (not benzodiazepines), carbamazepine, rifampicin and griseofulvin induce warfarin metabolism; oral contraceptives raise clotting factor levels. If an inducer is withdrawn while warfarin continues, the INR can rise sharply, and fatal bleeding has occurred.

front: What INR ranges are used for warfarin therapy?
back: INR 2 to 3 for most indications, such as venous thromboembolism and atrial fibrillation. A higher range of 2.5 to 3.5 is used for mechanical heart valves in the mitral position, or mechanical valves in another position with atrial fibrillation or a prior stroke. Intracranial bleeding risk rises steeply above INR 4. The INR corrects the prothrombin time for the sensitivity of the thromboplastin used, so results are comparable between laboratories.

front: How is excess anticoagulation or bleeding on warfarin managed?
back: No bleeding, raised INR: hold warfarin and restart at a lower dose once the INR is in range; if the INR is 10 or more, give oral vitamin K1 2.5 to 5 mg, which lowers the INR within 24 to 48 h without causing warfarin resistance. Serious bleeding: four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus vitamin K1 10 mg by slow IV infusion (IV vitamin K can cause anaphylactoid reactions). Vitamin K acts slowly because factors must be resynthesised, and high doses make the patient unresponsive to warfarin for several days.

Heparin binds antithrombin III and greatly speeds its inhibition of factors Xa, IIa (thrombin), IXa, XIa and XIIa, but not VIIa. Its long chain also acts as a scaffold that brings thrombin and antithrombin together. The effect is immediate in vivo and in vitro.

front: Why does low-concentration heparin prolong aPTT more than PT?
back: At low concentration heparin mainly blocks factor Xa-driven thrombin generation, which amplifies the intrinsic pathway, so aPTT rises while PT barely changes. At high concentration it also blocks the common pathway, and PT is prolonged.

front: What is the standard i.v. heparin regimen and the monitoring target?
back: Continuous IV infusion after a bolus: GG14 gives a 5000 U fixed or weight-adjusted bolus, then 800 to 1600 U/h (KDT: 5000 to 10000 U bolus, then 750 to 1000 U/h). Titrate to an aPTT of 1.5 to 2.5 times control (about 50 to 80 s). Intermittent IV bolus dosing is no longer recommended.

front: How is heparin reversed with protamine, and what are its limits and dangers?
back: Protamine, a basic protein, neutralises heparin about 1 mg per 100 U. It does not reverse fondaparinux and only partly reverses low molecular weight heparins. Inject it slowly (about 5 mg/min); rapid injection causes flushing and breathlessness. It can itself act as an anticoagulant and can cause hypersensitivity.

front: What is danaparoid, and when is it used?
back: A heparinoid preparation consisting mainly of heparan sulfate from pig gut mucosa. Its anticoagulant action is weaker than heparin's. It is used in patients with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

front: How does aspirin inhibit platelets, and why does its effect last for days?
back: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates platelet COX-1, which stops thromboxane A2 synthesis. Platelets have no nucleus and cannot make new enzyme, so the effect lasts until new platelets are formed; bleeding time stays prolonged for 5 to 7 days. Low daily doses accumulate. Daily doses of 100 mg or less are used for most indications; higher doses also inhibit vascular prostacyclin and add bleeding without extra benefit.

front: Dabigatran: how is it given, and how is it reversed?
back: Dabigatran etexilate is an oral prodrug converted to dabigatran, a reversible direct thrombin inhibitor. About 80% of absorbed drug is excreted unchanged by the kidney, so the dose is reduced in severe renal impairment. It has no CYP3A4 interaction, but it is a P-glycoprotein substrate. Idarucizumab, a humanised antibody fragment, is the specific reversal agent. It must not be used with mechanical heart valves or triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome.

front: What roles do chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL and HDL play in lipid transport?
back: Chylomicrons carry dietary triglyceride from the gut. VLDL carries liver-made triglyceride. Its remnant, IDL, loses more triglyceride and becomes LDL, which carries cholesterol to tissues and liver. HDL removes excess cholesterol from tissues. Raised LDL and VLDL are atherogenic; HDL is protective.

front: How do statins lower LDL cholesterol?
back: They competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis. Hepatic cholesterol falls, which increases LDL receptor expression on liver cells, so more IDL and LDL are cleared from blood. Over the long term, feedback partly restores synthesis, leaving a dose-dependent lowering of LDL.

front: Why are statins given at bedtime, and which statins are exceptions?
back: Cholesterol synthesis by HMG-CoA reductase peaks around midnight, so statins are given at night for maximal effect. Atorvastatin and rosuvastatin have long half-lives and can be taken at any time of day.

front: Statin myopathy: how common is it, and which drugs raise the risk?
back: Muscle aches are common, but true myopathy is rare (under 1 in 1000) and rhabdomyolysis deaths are on record. Risk rises with gemfibrozil and nicotinic acid, and with CYP3A4 inhibitors (macrolides such as erythromycin, azole antifungals, cyclosporine, nefazodone, HIV protease inhibitors, amiodarone). Pravastatin, fluvastatin and rosuvastatin are not extensively metabolised by CYP3A4, so they carry less interaction risk. Simvastatin 80 mg is not advised; simvastatin should not exceed 20 mg with amlodipine or amiodarone, or 10 mg with diltiazem or verapamil.

front: Which fibrate is preferred alongside a statin, and why should gemfibrozil be avoided with statins?
back: Fenofibrate interferes least with statin handling, so it is preferred when a fibrate must be combined. Gemfibrozil blocks hepatic uptake of the active statin acids through the OATP1B1 transporter (called OATP2 in KDT) and competes for the glucuronidation that clears most statins, nearly doubling statin levels and raising the risk of myopathy; avoid the combination.

front: How does ezetimibe lower LDL cholesterol, and what is its main role?
back: It blocks NPC1L1, the intestinal transporter for dietary and biliary cholesterol and phytosterols, lowering LDL by about 15 to 20%. It is mainly an add-on to a statin, with a synergistic effect. Its extra outcome benefit is small, about 2% in IMPROVE-IT with simvastatin.

front: Why are bile acid sequestrants seldom used, and what do they do to triglycerides?
back: Cholestyramine, colestipol and colesevelam bind bile acids in the gut, which increases hepatic LDL receptor expression and lowers LDL by about 15 to 25%. Triglycerides are not lowered and may rise. They are seldom used because they are unpalatable, need large doses, cause flatulence and GI upset, bind other drugs, and are poorly accepted.

front: How do fibrates work, and what lipid changes do they produce?
back: They activate PPAR-alpha, which increases lipoprotein lipase and fatty acid oxidation and reduces hepatic triglyceride synthesis. Triglycerides fall by 20 to 50%, LDL falls by 5 to 15%, and HDL rises by 10 to 20%. Their main use is severe hypertriglyceridaemia.

front: Why is nicotinic acid useful, and what limits its use?
back: It is the most effective drug for raising HDL, and it also lowers triglycerides, LDL and lipoprotein(a). It inhibits adipocyte lipolysis and hepatic VLDL production. Flushing (mediated by prostaglandin D2) limits use; aspirin before a dose reduces it. Dyspepsia, hyperglycaemia, hyperuricaemia and liver damage are other limits, and doses above 2 g a day are poorly tolerated. Added to statins it gave no outcome benefit (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE), and in 2016 the FDA withdrew approval of extended-release niacin as statin add-on therapy.
