back: Any preventable event that may cause or lead to inappropriate medication use or patient harm while the medication is in the control of the health professional, patient or consumer (NCC MERP definition). It may arise in prescribing, order communication, labelling, packaging, naming, compounding, dispensing, distribution, administration, education, monitoring or use. Most are latent errors, "accidents waiting to happen", whose causes can be found and fixed.

front: How common are medication errors compared with adverse drug events, and what approach reduces them?
back: They are estimated to be 50 to 100 times more common than adverse drug events. Reduction needs a system-based approach covering prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, administering and monitoring, with trained staff and mandatory, redundant checkpoints.

front: Complete: the "five rights" of drug administration
text: Give the right {{dose}} of the right {{drug}} to the right {{patient}} at the right {{time}} by the right {{route}}.

front: How is the medication error rate calculated, and what rate signals a systemic problem?
back: Number of errors observed divided by the opportunities for error (all doses observed being given plus doses ordered but not given), multiplied by 100. A rate of 5% or more indicates a systemic problem in the facility's drug distribution system.

"QD" is misread as QID
"OD" should mean only right eye
Do not abbreviate drug names (e.g. AZT misread as azathioprine or aztreonam)
e.g. methotrexate and metolazone, apixaban and aripiprazole
Write the indication on the prescription

front: Give examples of errors of omission in hospital chart orders.
back: Vague orders such as "resume pre-op meds" (assumes an accurate list exists), "continue present IV fluids" (no fluid, volume or rate) or "continue eye drops" (no eye, drug, strength or frequency); failing to stop a previous drug when a new one starts; not stating regular versus long-acting form or strength; and "as needed" orders that do not say what condition justifies a dose.

front: Define polypharmacy and distinguish appropriate from inappropriate polypharmacy.
back: Concurrent use of many medicines, commonly taken as five or more (some say six or more) a day. Appropriate: every drug serves an agreed therapeutic goal that is being or can be met, ADR risk is minimised and the patient is willing and able to take them. Inappropriate: one or more drugs are not or no longer needed because there is no evidence-based indication, the goal is not met, the drugs cause or risk ADRs, or the patient cannot or will not take them.

A cause of polypharmacy in which an adverse drug reaction is misread as a new illness and treated with another drug, exposing the patient to further adverse effects from an unnecessary medicine. Other causes include multiple diseases, multiple prescribers, transitions of care, poor diagnostic skill and self-medication with OTC products and supplements.

front: Classify: tools to detect inappropriate prescribing in older patients
text: {{Beers}} criteria list potentially inappropriate medicines in older persons by body system; {{STOPP}} screens older persons' prescriptions for inappropriate drugs; {{START}} alerts doctors to the right treatment that is missing; the {{Medication Appropriateness Index}} checks indication, effectiveness, dose, cost and duplication; {{anticholinergic burden}} scales add up anticholinergic load; {{ARMOR}} is a stepwise Assess-Review-Minimize-Optimize-Reassess approach.

front: Complete: SAIL and TIDE techniques to reduce polypharmacy
text: SAIL: keep the regimen {{Simple}}, know the {{Adverse effects}}, give every drug an {{Indication}}, and keep a shared {{List}}. TIDE: give enough {{Time}}, {{Individualise}} doses ("start low, go slow"), avoid {{Drug-drug and drug-disease interactions}}, and {{Educate}} patient and carer.

front: What is medication reconciliation, when is it done, and how?
back: Comparing the patient's new medication orders with everything the patient has been taking, to catch omissions, duplications, dosing errors and interactions. It is done at every transition of care (admission, transfer, discharge, change of prescriber) and at office visits. Steps: obtain the best possible medication history (e.g. "brown bag" review of all medicines brought in, confirmed with carers), list intended prescriptions, compare the two lists, decide on changes, and communicate the new regimen with counselling.

front: Define deprescribing and list its steps.
back: The systematic identification and withdrawal of drugs whose actual or potential harm outweighs benefit for that patient's goals, function, life expectancy, values and preferences. Steps: full medication reconciliation; estimate overall risk of drug harm; check each drug for eligibility to stop; prioritise; carry out the withdrawal plan and monitor for withdrawal effects. Tools include Medstopper and deprescribing.org guidelines.

front: What are the goals of a hospital antimicrobial stewardship programme (ASP)?
back: ASPs are ongoing institutional efforts to optimise antimicrobial use in inpatients. Goals: achieve clinical cure while limiting toxicity and resistance by avoiding misuse and overuse; choose the right drug, dose, duration and route, and de-escalate in time; and cut costs without lowering quality of care. Appropriate prescribing and education of patients and doctors achieve these goals.

front: What is the pharmacologist's role in antibiotic policy?
back: The pharmacologist is a core member in formulating national drug policy and the hospital antibiotic policy; in hospitals the clinical pharmacologist drafts the antibiotic policy together with the clinical microbiologist and the head of critical care medicine.

front: What is a prescription (drug) audit and what does it aim to achieve?
back: A regular review of physicians' prescriptions, typically led by a pharmacologist, to check that therapy is safe, effective and affordable and that hospital practice is evidence-based. It aims to reduce polypharmacy, medication errors and cost to the patient. WHO includes supervision, audit and feedback among its key interventions for rational drug use.

front: Define compliance (adherence) and give the four types of noncompliance.
back: The extent to which patients follow treatment instructions. Noncompliance: (1) the prescription is never obtained (about one-third of patients in some studies); (2) the drug is taken wrongly (dose, frequency, timing, route, duplication, wrong purpose); (3) the drug is stopped early, e.g. when symptoms improve or the bottle is empty; (4) the drug is taken inappropriately, e.g. shared with others.

front: Short note: Drug counselling to improve adherence

Label carries drug name, purpose and duration; avoid "take as directed"
Symptomless disease (e.g. hypertension)
Frequent dosing (once daily is followed better than four times daily)
Living alone, hard-to-open packs, cost, transport, beliefs
Better communication; assess social and economic situation
Link doses to daily routine (e.g. meals)
Pill organisers, alarms, compliance packaging, refill reminders
Teach the patient to monitor effects; involve the patient actively

front: How can a hospital use pharmacoeconomic analysis when it prepares its formulary?
back: It can apply pharmacoeconomic methods (cost-minimisation, cost-effectiveness, cost-benefit and cost-utility) to compare treatments when preparing its formulary of essential medicines. The same analysis helps decide and fix the prices of old and new drugs and supports reimbursement.

front: On what does the empirical antibiotic choice for adult hospital-acquired infection depend, according to Katzung?
back: The local antibiogram and the severity of illness. Katzung's empirical regimen adds vancomycin or linezolid for MRSA only when MRSA is a concern.

front: How does growth hormone act, and why do its growth effects depend on IGF-1?
back: GH binds a JAK-STAT-linked cytokine-type receptor on most cells, which alters gene transcription. Its growth-promoting and nitrogen-retaining effects are mostly indirect, carried by IGF-1 (somatomedin), made mainly in the liver. GH itself promotes lipolysis and gluconeogenesis and reduces glucose uptake, so it raises blood glucose.

front: List the main therapeutic uses of somatropin (recombinant GH).
back: GH deficiency in children (pituitary dwarfism), Turner syndrome (with timed oestrogen and androgen), growth failure from chronic renal insufficiency in children, adult GH deficiency and AIDS-related wasting. Use in idiopathic short stature is debated, and its use by athletes is banned.

front: What adverse effects limit somatropin therapy?
back: Injection-site pain and lipodystrophy, glucose intolerance, hypothyroidism (by unmasking central TSH deficiency), salt and water retention, myalgia, hand stiffness and headache. Intracranial pressure can rise in a few patients. Immunogenicity is low, so allergy and resistance are uncommon.

front: Why is native somatostatin unsuitable as a drug for acromegaly?
back: Its half-life is only 2 to 3 minutes. It is not selective: it also suppresses insulin, glucagon, TSH, gastrin and gut secretions. Stopping it causes GH rebound. Long-acting analogues (octreotide, lanreotide) are used instead.

front: How does octreotide differ from somatostatin, and what are its uses?
back: A synthetic octapeptide about 40 times more potent than somatostatin at suppressing GH, with a half-life of about 90 minutes. It is only a weak inhibitor of insulin. Uses: acromegaly, secretory diarrhoea (carcinoid, AIDS, chemotherapy or diabetes related) and IV control of variceal bleeding. Adverse effects: gallstones, steatorrhoea and abdominal pain.

front: How does pegvisomant work, and when is it used?
back: It is a pegylated mutant GH. One of its two receptor-binding sites binds more tightly and the other more weakly than native GH, so it allows receptor dimerisation but blocks the conformational change needed for signalling: a GH receptor antagonist. Pegylation slows clearance. Daily s.c. treatment normalises IGF-1 in most patients with acromegaly. It does not reduce GH secretion (GH levels may rise), so response is followed by IGF-1. KDT lists it for acromegaly due to small adenomas; it is used when GH excess persists after surgery.

front: What controls prolactin secretion, and which drugs raise prolactin levels?
back: Dopamine (prolactin-inhibiting factor) keeps prolactin low by acting on D2 receptors of lactotrope cells. Dopamine blockers (chlorpromazine, haloperidol, metoclopramide) and the dopamine-depleting drug reserpine raise prolactin. Suckling keeps levels high after delivery, and prolactinomas are a common cause of hyperprolactinaemia.

front: Outline the steps in thyroid hormone synthesis and where TSH acts.
back: Iodide is trapped by the Na+/iodide symporter, a step TSH increases. Thyroid peroxidase oxidises it (using H2O2) and attaches it to tyrosyl residues of thyroglobulin as MIT and DIT. Coupling of two DIT gives T4; MIT plus DIT gives T3. Stored colloid is re-endocytosed and proteolysed, releasing T4 and T3; MIT and DIT are deiodinated and the iodide reused. TSH stimulates trapping, organification, coupling and release.

front: Why is T4 called a prohormone of T3?
back: T4 is secreted in larger amounts and is bound much more tightly to plasma proteins, so it acts as a circulating reserve. About a third of T4 is converted to T3 by deiodinases in the liver, kidney and target tissues. T3 is the active form: it binds the nuclear receptor more strongly, acts faster and is about five times more potent.

front: Which deiodinase is inhibited by propylthiouracil, and which antiarrhythmic inhibits both D1 and D2?
back: Propylthiouracil inhibits type 1 deiodinase (D1), found mainly in liver, kidney and thyroid, but not D2. Amiodarone inhibits both D1 and D2. Carbimazole does not. High-dose propranolol and glucocorticoids also reduce T4 to T3 conversion, except in brain and pituitary.

front: How do thyroid hormones increase heart rate and contractility?
back: They act directly on the heart by increasing the myosin isoform with higher Ca2+-ATPase activity. They also raise beta-adrenergic receptor numbers and coupling, so catecholamines have a greater effect. The result is tachycardia, a bounding pulse, higher systolic pressure and atrial fibrillation. Thyroid hormones can also precipitate heart failure or angina.

front: Why is levothyroxine preferred over liothyronine?
back: Liothyronine (T3) acts faster, but its action is short and it carries a higher risk of arrhythmia and angina. Levothyroxine gives a more sustained and uniform effect, and its oral bioavailability is about 75 percent. Liothyronine is not freely available in India and is used IV with T4 only in selected cases such as myxoedema coma.

A medical emergency, best managed in intensive care, as intubation and ventilation may be needed. Give everything IV because absorption by other routes is poor. Drug of choice is an IV loading dose of levothyroxine (Katzung: 300 to 400 µg; KDT: 200 to 500 µg), then 50 to 100 µg IV daily until oral therapy is possible. IV T3 can be added, but it is more cardiotoxic; use lower doses in older or cardiac patients. Give IV hydrocortisone if adrenal or pituitary insufficiency may coexist, give IV fluids cautiously (risk of water intoxication), and treat the precipitating infection or heart failure.

front: Which drugs reduce levothyroxine absorption, and which speed its clearance?
back: Absorption is reduced by sucralfate, iron, calcium and proton pump inhibitors, and by food, so levothyroxine is taken on an empty stomach. Enzyme inducers (rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) speed T4 metabolism and may need a higher dose. Severe hypothyroidism itself reduces absorption.

front: When is subclinical hypothyroidism treated with thyroxine?
back: Subclinical hypothyroidism means raised TSH with normal thyroid hormone levels. Treatment is individualised. Levothyroxine is generally advised when TSH is above 10 mU/L. For milder TSH elevations, close TSH monitoring is appropriate; KDT adds that treatment for TSH 6 to 10 mU/L is optional and preferable if cardiovascular risk factors are present.

front: Name drugs that cause hypothyroidism or goitre, and the mechanism of each.
back: Lithium inhibits hormone release. Amiodarone blocks peripheral T4 to T3 conversion and interferes with hormone action. Sulfonamides and para-aminosalicylic acid impair iodination and coupling. Phenobarbitone, phenytoin, carbamazepine and rifampicin speed T4 breakdown. Iodides and radioiodine can also cause hypothyroidism.

front: What is the pathogenesis of Graves' disease, and why is TSH low in it?
back: An IgG thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin binds the TSH receptor and drives long-lasting thyroid stimulation. The excess hormone suppresses TSH through negative feedback. Stimulation of TSH receptors in periorbital tissue appears to cause exophthalmos. Toxic nodular goitre is TSH-independent, is more common in older people and usually lacks eye signs.

front: How do type 1 and type 2 diabetes differ in cause and insulin levels?
back: Type 1 results from loss of beta cells, usually autoimmune, so circulating insulin is low or absent and ketosis is common. Type 2 involves insulin resistance with impaired beta-cell secretion; insulin levels are normal or high and genetic predisposition is strong. Type 2 accounts for over 90 percent of cases.

front: How does glucose trigger insulin release from beta cells?
back: Glucose is phosphorylated by glucokinase and metabolised, which raises ATP. ATP closes ATP-sensitive K+ channels, depolarising the cell. Calcium enters and insulin granules undergo exocytosis. Oral glucose gives a stronger response than IV glucose because gut incretins (GLP-1, GIP) amplify secretion.

front: What is the mechanism of metformin's glucose-lowering effect?
back: Metformin does not stimulate insulin release, but it needs insulin to act. Its main effect is suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis and glucose output, through AMPK activation that follows changes in cellular energy status. It also improves insulin-mediated glucose uptake in muscle and fat, and slightly reduces intestinal glucose absorption.

front: How do sulfonylureas lower blood glucose, and why is hypoglycaemia their main risk?
back: They bind the SUR1 subunit of the beta-cell KATP channel and close it. Depolarisation and calcium influx increase insulin release, mainly the second phase, and this happens even at low glucose. Because insulin is released regardless of meals, they can cause severe, unpredictable hypoglycaemia. They need functioning beta cells, so they do not work in type 1 diabetes.

front: Why must insulin be injected, and what is its plasma half-life?
back: Insulin is a peptide that is broken down in the gut, so it is ineffective orally. It is distributed only in extracellular fluid, and its plasma half-life is about 5 to 9 minutes. Nearly half of pancreatic insulin is cleared by the liver on first pass.

front: What are the onset, peak and duration of regular insulin, and how should it be timed?
back: KDT: onset 30 to 60 minutes, peak 2 to 3 hours, duration 6 to 8 hours (Katzung: effect within 30 min, peak about 2 h, lasts 5 to 7 h). Because absorption from the s.c. site is slow, it is optimally injected about 1 hour before a meal (KDT); injected just before eating it gives early post-meal hyperglycaemia and late hypoglycaemia. It is unsuitable for basal cover. Given IV its action is prompt, and it is the insulin used for IV infusion in DKA.

front: Name the rapid-acting insulin analogues and how they are timed.
back: Insulin lispro (B28 and B29 residues reversed), insulin aspart (B28 proline replaced by aspartate) and insulin glulisine. They act within about 15 minutes, peak at 1 to 2 hours and last 3 to 5 hours. Lispro is given 0 to 20 minutes before a meal, giving better meal-time control and fewer late hypoglycaemic episodes than regular insulin.

front: What is insulin glargine, and how is it given?
back: A long-acting analogue that forms a depot after injection and releases a steady, peakless level for up to 24 hours. It is given once daily, often at bedtime, for basal cover; it does not control meal-time glucose. It is acidic and cannot be mixed with other insulins. It causes fewer night-time hypoglycaemic episodes than NPH.

front: How do DPP-4 inhibitors lower blood glucose?
back: They block DPP-4, the enzyme that breaks down GLP-1 and GIP, so incretin levels rise. This increases glucose-dependent insulin release and reduces glucagon, so hypoglycaemia risk is low and the drugs are weight neutral. Vildagliptin and saxagliptin bind DPP-4 covalently; sitagliptin binds without a covalent bond. Adverse effects: nasopharyngitis and upper respiratory infection, hypersensitivity (angioedema, Stevens-Johnson syndrome), possible pancreatitis, joint pains; saxagliptin and alogliptin have been linked to heart failure.

front: How do GLP-1 receptor agonists lower glucose, and what are their main adverse effects?
back: Exenatide is based on exendin-4, a lizard peptide that DPP-4 does not degrade. Liraglutide is GLP-1 with a C16 fatty acid chain; albumin binding hinders DPP-4 access and slows absorption, giving a half-life of about 12 hours and once-daily dosing (GG14 calls it DPP-4 resistant). Semaglutide is resistant through a position-2 substitution and binds albumin tightly (half-life 7 days; weekly injection or daily oral form). All act on GLP-1 receptors: glucose-dependent insulin release, less glucagon, slower gastric emptying and less appetite, so weight falls. Adverse effects: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea; pancreatitis risk; avoid with medullary thyroid carcinoma (GLP-1 receptors on C cells).

front: How do SGLT-2 inhibitors act, and what are their main safety concerns?
back: They block SGLT2 in the proximal tubule, lowering the renal threshold for glucose and causing glycosuria. This lowers HbA1c by about 0.5 to 1%, with weight loss and little hypoglycaemia. They reduce heart failure hospitalisation and slow diabetic kidney disease, so they are used early in patients with cardiovascular disease, heart failure or nephropathy. Risks: genital mycotic and urinary infections, volume depletion and hypotension, ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose. Glucose-lowering efficacy falls with renal impairment: not recommended for glycaemic control below eGFR 45 and contraindicated below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2.

front: How does pioglitazone work, and what limits its use?
back: It is a PPAR-gamma agonist acting mainly in fat and muscle, where it enhances insulin-responsive gene expression and GLUT4 translocation. It improves insulin sensitivity without raising insulin levels, and it lowers triglycerides and raises HDL. Limitations: fluid retention, weight gain, heart failure, fractures and the need for liver monitoring. A possible bladder cancer link has been reported, though large studies disagree. It is contraindicated in heart failure and liver disease.

front: How do you treat an episode of insulin-induced hypoglycaemia?
back: Give 15 to 20 g of oral glucose or sugar, and repeat after 15 to 20 minutes if there is no improvement. In severe cases give 30 to 50 mL of 50 percent glucose IV over about 10 minutes. If the patient cannot take sugar and IV glucose is not available, glucagon 0.5 to 1 mg can be given as a stopgap; a 3 mg nasal glucagon device is now available. KDT also lists adrenaline 0.2 mg s.c. as a less desirable option. Continue oral carbohydrate because hypoglycaemia may recur.

front: How is insulin given in diabetic ketoacidosis?
back: Regular insulin IV only, alongside aggressive IV hydration (normal saline first) and potassium replacement. The usual starting infusion is about 0.1 U/kg/h; KDT precedes it with an IV bolus of 0.1 to 0.2 U/kg and doubles the rate if glucose has not fallen significantly in 2 hours (a fall of about 10% per hour is adequate). When glucose reaches about 300 mg/dL (usually in 4 to 6 h), KDT reduces the infusion to 2 to 3 U/h and adds 5% glucose, continuing until the patient is fully conscious and can start s.c. insulin.

{{Insulin}} is the drug of choice for diabetes in pregnancy. {{Metformin}} has been shown to be safe and effective in gestational diabetes, though it is not FDA-approved for it. {{Pioglitazone}} should not be used in pregnancy, and the safety of {{sulfonylureas}} is not established, so patients are switched to insulin.

front: Tirzepatide: what is it, and how does it compare with GLP-1 agonists?
back: A dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist, built on the GIP sequence with a fatty diacid chain that binds albumin, allowing once-weekly s.c. injection. Started at 2.5 mg weekly and raised in 2.5 mg steps every 4 weeks up to 15 mg. It lowered HbA1c by about 1.9 to 2.6% with weight loss of about 6 to 13 kg, and improved lipids, blood pressure and fatty liver. Safety resembles GLP-1 agonists: dose-related nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea, and a slightly higher pancreatitis rate.

A humanised monoclonal antibody against CD3, the main signalling part of the T-cell receptor, which modulates the autoimmune attack on beta cells. It is given as a daily infusion for 14 days to people aged 8 and above at high risk of type 1 diabetes (two positive autoantibodies with impaired glucose tolerance, stage 2). It delays the onset of clinical (stage 3) type 1 diabetes by about 25 months. Adverse effects: transient fall in white cells and lymphocytes, rash, headache.

front: Short note: Milestones that shaped research ethics and GCP

points: US Federal Food and Drugs Act: against adulterated or misbranded food and drugs
Sulphanilamide elixir tragedy: untested solvent (an antifreeze) killed over 100 people
Nuremberg Code after Nazi camp experiments: informed consent, right to withdraw
Promoted for morning sickness; babies born without limbs or with severe deformities
Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association): ethical base of ICH-GCP
Belmont Report (US National Commission, under the National Research Act 1974)
CIOMS guidelines applying Helsinki to modern research
ICH-GCP finalised 1996, effective 1997

front: What did the Nuremberg Code establish?
back: Drawn up in 1947 after unethical experiments on prisoners in Nazi camps during World War II, it established that research subjects must give informed consent and must be free to withdraw from an experiment at any time.

front: What is the Declaration of Helsinki and why does it matter for trials?
back: A statement of ethical principles for medical research on human subjects, issued by the World Medical Association in 1964 and regularly updated. It sets the widely accepted ground rules for human research and forms the ethical base of ICH-GCP: trials must be conducted according to its principles.

front: What do the CIOMS guidelines add to the Declaration of Helsinki?
back: The Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences (guidelines first published 1993) gives detailed guidance on applying Helsinki to present-day research: HIV/AIDS research, post-study availability of treatment, women as subjects, confidentiality, compensation for adverse events and consent, while avoiding unnecessary suffering and weighing risk against benefit.

front: Complete: the four principles of medical ethics (Beauchamp and Childress)
text: {{Autonomy}}: the person's right to make choices and hold views; {{beneficence}}: do good and contribute to welfare; {{non-maleficence}}: do no intentional harm; {{justice}}: treat everyone equally and share benefits fairly.

front: What are the cardinal principle and the principle of precaution in research on human participants?
back: The cardinal principle is respect for the dignity of persons. Precaution and risk minimisation require care at every stage so that participants and affected communities face minimum risk and no known irreversible harm. All guidelines demand both ethical and scientific review and informed consent.

front: How do ICH-GCP and WHO-GCP differ?
back: ICH-GCP was designed to harmonise technical requirements for drug registration across the US, Japan and EU and has 13 principles. WHO-GCP was written as a teaching tool for countries without their own guideline and has 14 principles (its principles 5 and 6 are combined in ICH-GCP). Both aim to promote good clinical practice.

Staff qualified by education, training and experience
Records allow accurate reporting and verification

front: What are the Indian GCP guidelines and what is the principle of essentiality?
back: CDSCO set up an expert committee that produced India's first GCP document in 2001, modelled on WHO, US FDA, ICH and EU guidelines. It lists 10 ethical principles in line with Helsinki, including informed consent, community agreement, non-exploitation, privacy and confidentiality, risk minimisation, and accountability and transparency of investigators and sponsors. Essentiality means human subjects should be used only when absolutely necessary and no alternative exists. The NDCT Rules 2019 define "GCP guidelines" as the CDSCO guidelines adopted by the Drugs Technical Advisory Board.

front: What role do the ICMR ethical guidelines play in Indian research?
back: ICMR issued Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research on Human Subjects in 2000, with planned periodic revision to keep researchers updated on bioethics. Ethics committees for biomedical and health research (as opposed to drug trials) are constituted under ICMR's National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants. Standard guidelines also make studies comparable across centres and help prevent duplicated research.

front: Complete: categories of ethics committee review by risk
text: Proposals with less than minimal risk (e.g. research on educational practice) may be {{exempted}} from review; those with minimal risk (e.g. studies of already approved drugs or devices) get {{expedited}} review; those with more than minimal risk, or involving {{vulnerable}} groups such as children or psychiatric patients, need {{full}} committee review. The {{member secretary}} screens and categorises proposals.

front: What kinds of ongoing review does an ethics committee carry out after approval?
back: Periodic review of ongoing research at intervals of 6 months to 1 year; continuing review of any new information and adverse events; and interim review in special circumstances by a sub-committee, re-examined by the full committee as needed (e.g. quarterly).

front: What decisions can an ethics committee reach, and how are records kept?
back: Approval (only minor changes), approval with modifications, resubmission with more information, or outright disapproval. Decisions are preferably by consensus; invited subject experts give opinions but do not decide. Minutes are approved and signed by the chair, documents are confidential, and records are kept for 5 years after the trial ends.

front: What is clinical equipoise and why does it matter ethically?
back: Genuine uncertainty among experts about which treatment is better. It justifies randomising patients, because the trial is done precisely because doubt exists. Placebo-controlled trials are argued to violate equipoise and the principle of beneficence when a proven effective therapy is already available.

front: What does the Declaration of Helsinki say about placebo controls?
back: It discourages placebo controls when an alternative treatment is available, since patients randomised to placebo would in effect be denied treatment; every patient, including controls, should get the best proven methods and not suffer unnecessary pain. Where an available treatment prevents death or irreversible harm, a placebo control is generally inappropriate.

front: Short note: When is a placebo-controlled trial ethically justified?

points: No proven or approved therapy exists
Existing therapy is of doubtful or modest, inconsistent efficacy with frequent adverse effects, and the new drug is not expected to be better
Patients fully informed, autonomy kept, close monitoring, rescue treatment available, GCP followed
Existing therapy is highly and consistently effective: use an equivalence or non-inferiority design
Existing therapy prevents death or irreversible morbidity
Add-on design so all receive standard care
Minimal placebo exposure; early-escape and withdrawal rules
Smaller placebo arm; DSMB interim review

front: What must the consent form of a placebo-controlled trial tell participants?
back: What "placebo" means, in lay language; that they may receive it; why a placebo is used and what alternatives exist; how long they may be on placebo and the likely discomfort; the harm of not receiving or delaying effective treatment and that the condition may worsen; and that they may withdraw at any time.

front: When is it ethical to use a placebo in clinical practice?
back: Only with the patient's welfare as the sole motive, to relieve suffering, when the condition has an unpredictable course, standard treatment fails or is not tolerated, or no effective therapy exists. It must never replace effective treatment, must be stopped if ineffective, and the doctor should answer honestly if asked about it; if it helps and nothing better exists, stopping it is unethical.

front: What is a conflict of interest in research, and how should a reader handle it?
back: A situation where personal factors (e.g. funding or financial gain) could influence professional judgement or responsibilities. Such conflicts are common; what matters is whether they were recognised and managed. When appraising a paper, check the declared funding source and any statement on how a conflict was handled. Ethics committee members must also declare conflicts.

front: How does ICD-11 define burnout, and what are its three dimensions?
back: A syndrome from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, marked by (1) exhaustion or energy depletion, (2) mental distance from the job, negativism or cynicism, and (3) reduced professional efficacy.

front: What is the pharmacologist's role in medical education?
back: Teaching undergraduates (pharmacology is a second-year MBBS and BDS subject), postgraduates (including thesis guidance), and nursing and pharmacy students. Content includes rational drug use and essential drugs, drug classes, effects, toxicity, ADRs and interactions, telling real drug information from promotional claims, dose calculation by age, sex and health status, and correct routes. Pharmacologists also educate practising doctors on rational use, new drugs, ADR reporting, drug audit and generic prescribing.

front: How are pharmacology competencies organised in India's competency-based undergraduate curriculum (CBME)?
back: Each competency is a coded statement of what the student should be able to do, numbered with the prefix PH (e.g. PH1.2 evidence-based medicine and TDM, PH1.43 rational antimicrobial use and stewardship, PH1.55 national health programmes, PH1.64 drug development, trial phases and GCP). Katzung's Indian edition maps each PH competency to the chapter that covers it.

front: How does GG14 use the Belmont Report's justice principle in the debate on foreign drug trials?
back: The Belmont Report says research should not unduly involve groups unlikely to benefit from its later applications. Some ethicists argue that testing drugs abroad in populations who cannot afford the approved product breaches this principle. Defenders reply that such trials also bring medical care to underserved people.

front: Which two WHO rational-use interventions relate to medical education?
back: Problem-based pharmacotherapy training in undergraduate curricula, and continuing in-service medical education made a requirement for licensure.

front: Besides guiding treatment, procurement and reimbursement, what else does Sarkar say an essential medicines list identifies?
back: The 'must know' drugs for the teaching and training of health care professionals.

front: Which receptor does histamine use to switch on acid secretion by the parietal cell, and what does it do?
back: H2 receptors on the basolateral membrane. Activation raises cAMP, which switches on the H+/K+ ATPase proton pump, the final step of acid secretion. Histamine is the dominant physiological stimulus; gastrin and acetylcholine act partly by releasing histamine from ECL cells.

front: Why do H2 blockers also reduce acid responses to gastrin and acetylcholine?
back: Histamine plays a permissive role. The cAMP made by H2 activation is needed for a full secretory response to gastrin and cholinergic agonists, so H2 blockade weakens the response to almost every secretagogue.

front: Compare cimetidine, ranitidine and famotidine on potency and antiandrogen effects.
back: Ranitidine is about 5 times as potent as cimetidine, and famotidine about 5 to 8 times as potent as ranitidine. Only cimetidine has antiandrogenic effects (gynaecomastia, loss of libido), raises prolactin and slows hepatic breakdown of estradiol. GG14 notes that some ranitidine and nizatidine preparations have been withdrawn because of contamination.

text: Omeprazole irreversibly inhibits the {{H+/K+ ATPase}} proton pump, and it is converted to its reactive form only in the acidic {{canaliculus}} of the parietal cell.

front: Why are PPIs swallowed whole and taken before a meal?
back: They are acid labile, so they are given as enteric-coated forms that must not be crushed or chewed. Taken on an empty stomach, the drug is in the blood when a meal switches the pumps on, and food lowers bioavailability.

front: Why does a PPI take 3 to 4 days to reach full acid suppression?
back: Each dose blocks only the pumps that are actively secreting, and the drug is cleared within 1 to 2 hours. Repeated dosing blocks more pumps until a plateau is reached at about 3 to 4 days, with 80 to 98 percent of 24-hour acid output suppressed. Secretion takes 3 to 4 days to return after stopping.

front: What are the main concerns with long-term high-dose PPI therapy?
back: Compensatory hypergastrinaemia with ECL-cell hyperplasia, fundic gland polyps and atrophic gastritis (tumour risk appears very low), and rebound acid hypersecretion on stopping. Loss of the acid barrier raises the risk of infections such as hospital-acquired pneumonia, community-acquired Clostridium difficile and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Reduced vitamin B12 absorption, hypomagnesaemia, and osteoporosis-related fractures are also reported, as are interstitial nephritis and, with omeprazole, gynaecomastia and erectile dysfunction.

front: Why does omeprazole matter with clopidogrel, and which PPI has the fewest interactions?
back: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, the enzyme that activates clopidogrel, which can blunt its antiplatelet effect. Omeprazole also raises levels of warfarin, diazepam and phenytoin. Pantoprazole has the lowest affinity for cytochrome P450 and the least interaction risk.

front: Why is misoprostol seldom used for ulcers now?
back: It is a synthetic PGE1 analogue that lowers acid output, but the effect lasts only about 3 hours, it relieves ulcer pain poorly, and it needs four times daily dosing. Diarrhoea, cramps and uterine bleeding are common, and it can cause abortion. Its main remaining role is preventing NSAID-induced ulcers.

front: How does sucralfate protect an ulcer without neutralising acid?
back: Below pH 4 it polymerises into a sticky gel that binds to the ulcer base and forms a physical shield against acid, pepsin and bile. It has no acid-neutralising action and is barely absorbed. Antacids must not be given with it, because they stop it polymerising.

front: What is colloidal bismuth subcitrate, and why is it not an antacid?
back: A colloidal bismuth compound that heals ulcers without raising gastric pH. It precipitates below pH 5. Its benefit may come from protecting the ulcer base, raising mucosal prostaglandin, mucus and bicarbonate, and acting directly on H. pylori. It causes black tongue and stools, and milk or antacids must be avoided with it.

front: Why should every H. pylori-positive ulcer patient be offered eradication?
back: Eradication is standard care in every H. pylori-positive gastric or duodenal ulcer: unless the patient keeps taking NSAIDs, it almost abolishes recurrence. H. pylori also drives chronic gastritis and contributes to gastric adenocarcinoma and gastric MALT lymphoma, which can regress after eradication. KDT adds that where testing is unavailable, failed or relapsing ulcers should still receive eradication therapy.

front: Which H. pylori eradication regimens are listed in the textbooks?
back: GG14 (newest): triple therapy for 10 to 14 days, a PPI twice daily with clarithromycin 500 mg and amoxicillin 1 g twice daily (metronidazole 500 mg can replace amoxicillin); bismuth quadruple therapy for 10 to 14 days, a PPI with bismuth, tetracycline and metronidazole four times daily; sequential therapy (PPI + amoxicillin for 5 days, then PPI + clarithromycin + tinidazole or metronidazole for 5 days); or PPI + amoxicillin + levofloxacin for 10 days. Where resistance to clarithromycin and metronidazole is common, a 14-day quadruple regimen is advised. KDT cites the older US-FDA regimen: lansoprazole 30 mg + amoxicillin 1 g + clarithromycin 500 mg, all twice daily for 2 weeks (86 to 92 percent eradication).

front: Where is the chemoreceptor trigger zone, and why can blood-borne drugs act on it?
back: In the area postrema, which lies outside the blood-brain barrier, so circulating drugs, toxins and hormones can act on it directly. It relays signals to the nucleus tractus solitarius, which drives the vomiting centre in the medulla.

front: How do cytotoxic drugs and radiation trigger vomiting through serotonin?
back: Gut cell damage releases 5-HT from enterochromaffin cells. It activates 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents, which carry the signal to the nucleus tractus solitarius and the chemoreceptor trigger zone. Substance P acting on NK1 receptors adds to the signal.

front: What is an effective IV ondansetron schedule for highly emetogenic cisplatin?
back: KDT: 8 mg IV given slowly over about 15 minutes, starting about 30 minutes before the cisplatin infusion, then two more 8 mg doses 4 hours apart; a single 24 mg dose on day 1 has also been used, and 8 mg orally twice daily for 3 to 5 days for delayed vomiting. GG14 gives the adult dose as 8 to 16 mg IV or 16 to 24 mg orally. Ondansetron alone is weak against delayed vomiting, so it is combined with dexamethasone and an NK1 antagonist.

front: Why is palonosetron preferred for delayed chemotherapy-induced vomiting?
back: It has the highest 5-HT3 receptor affinity and the longest half-life in its class (about 40 hours), so it controls delayed vomiting (days 2 to 5) better than ondansetron and keeps its efficacy in repeat cycles. Dose: 250 microgram (0.25 mg) by slow IV injection 30 minutes before chemotherapy, not repeated within 7 days. GG14 notes that, unlike first-generation 5-HT3 antagonists, it does not appear to prolong the QT interval.

front: What does aprepitant add to a standard antiemetic regimen, and what are its key interactions?
back: It is a selective NK1 antagonist that blocks substance P in the brain. Added to ondansetron and dexamethasone for cisplatin, it mainly improves protection against delayed vomiting. It is metabolised by CYP3A4, so it can raise dexamethasone levels and alter warfarin effect, and those doses need adjusting.

front: Which receptors does metoclopramide use in the gut to speed gastric emptying?
back: It is a 5-HT4 agonist on myenteric neurones, which increases acetylcholine release and so improves propulsive contraction and lower oesophageal sphincter tone. Its D2 blockade in the gut and weak 5-HT3 block add to this at higher doses. Atropine blocks the 5-HT4 effect.

front: What are the adverse effects of metoclopramide, and which are most important in children?
back: Sedation, dizziness, loose stools and extrapyramidal effects: acute dystonias (more common in children and young adults, often after IV use and possibly after a single dose) and parkinsonism after weeks of use. Tardive dyskinesia can follow chronic use and may be irreversible. Hyperprolactinaemia causes galactorrhoea and gynaecomastia; QT prolongation and methaemoglobinaemia in neonates are also reported.

front: How does domperidone differ from metoclopramide?
back: Domperidone is a D2 antagonist that barely crosses the blood-brain barrier, so extrapyramidal effects are rare and it does not oppose levodopa in Parkinson disease. Its prokinetic action is not reversed by atropine. It still acts on brain areas outside the barrier: the chemoreceptor trigger zone (antiemetic) and prolactin control (galactorrhoea, gynaecomastia). It carries a risk of serious ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death, especially above 60 years and at doses over 30 mg/day.

front: Why was cisapride withdrawn from most markets?
back: It blocks cardiac delayed-rectifier potassium channels, which prolongs the QT interval and risks torsades de pointes. The risk rises with CYP3A4 inhibitors such as azole antifungals and macrolides. It was banned in India in 2011.

front: Which antiemetic class is first choice for motion sickness, and when should it be taken?
back: Drugs with anticholinergic and antihistaminic action: hyoscine (the most effective, but short acting, so suited to short journeys) and H1 antihistamines such as promethazine, dimenhydrinate and meclozine. They work best when taken about 1 hour before the journey. Dopamine blockers and 5-HT3 antagonists are less effective.

Central substance P and dopamine D2 pathways
Acute and delayed phases

Benzodiazepines for anticipatory vomiting
Cannabinoids for resistant cases
Metoclopramide or prochlorperazine as rescue, with antidystonic cover
Constipation and headache with 5-HT3 antagonists; QT prolongation with first-generation agents
Dystonia and sedation with dopamine blockers
Assess the response and adjust the regimen in later cycles

front: Essay: Prokinetic drugs and their place in gastrointestinal disorders

points: Coordinated propulsion rather than tonic contraction
Effects on gastric emptying and LES tone
Metoclopramide: central and peripheral action; extrapyramidal effects and prolactin rise
Domperidone: peripheral; fewer CNS effects; arrhythmia on rapid IV injection
Cisapride: effective, but withdrawn for QT prolongation and arrhythmia
Mosapride: 5-HT4 agonist with minor 5-HT3 block; no extrapyramidal effects; later reports of QT prolongation with CYP3A4 inhibitors
Gastroparesis, functional dyspepsia, adjunct in GERD

Check interacting drugs and QT-prolonging co-medication
Use for symptom control with a clear review point

text: Metoclopramide acts as a {{5-HT4}} agonist in the gut and as a {{D2}} antagonist in the chemoreceptor trigger zone.
Phenothiazines such as {{prochlorperazine}} and butyrophenones such as {{haloperidol}} block {{D2}} receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone.
The NK1 antagonist {{aprepitant}} blocks the action of {{substance P}}, while the 5-HT3 antagonist {{ondansetron}} blocks {{5-HT}} signals on vagal afferents.
Ursodiol dissolves small cholesterol gallstones by {{lowering}} the cholesterol content of bile; its plasma half-life is about {{4 days}} because of enterohepatic cycling.

front: Why must bulk-forming laxatives be taken with plenty of water, and what do they not do?
back: They swell by absorbing water, which softens stool and speeds transit. Without enough fluid they can cause impaction, and ispaghula must never be swallowed dry. They take several days for full effect and do not soften stool already in the rectum, so they prevent constipation rather than treat it.

front: Why are stimulant laxatives such as bisacodyl and senna contraindicated in pregnancy and in bowel obstruction?
back: They can stimulate the gravid uterus reflexly, and they increase propulsion and fluid secretion, which is dangerous with an obstruction. Regular use causes hypokalaemia and colonic atony, and senna can cause melanosis of the colon.

front: How does lactulose lower blood ammonia in hepatic encephalopathy?
back: Colonic bacteria break lactulose down into acidic, osmotically active products. The lower stool pH turns ammonia into the ionised, non-absorbable ammonium form, and the laxative effect clears it. Blood ammonia can fall by 25 to 50 percent. Lactitol works similarly.

front: What are prucalopride and lubiprostone, and what is the key safety point for each?
back: Prucalopride is a 5-HT4 agonist that boosts colonic propulsion. It is used for chronic constipation in women when other laxatives fail, and appears to lack the cardiovascular risk that ended tegaserod. Lubiprostone is a prostaglandin analogue that opens chloride channels to draw fluid into the gut; nausea is its commonest side effect, and it is reserved for patients who have failed at least two other laxative classes.

front: What are the components and total osmolarity of the WHO low-osmolarity oral rehydration solution?
back: Sodium 75 mmol/L, glucose 75 mmol/L, potassium 20 mmol/L, chloride 65 mmol/L and citrate 10 mmol/L, with a total osmolarity of 245 mOsm/L. The older standard formula (310 mOsm/L, higher sodium) caused periorbital oedema in children and produced more stool and vomiting.

front: What is the role of zinc in acute childhood diarrhoea, and how is it given?
back: Given with low-osmolarity ORS, zinc shortens and reduces the severity of the episode and lowers recurrence for 2 to 3 months. It is given for 10 to 14 days: 20 mg per day for children aged 6 to 60 months and 10 mg per day under 6 months.

front: Why does loperamide cause few central effects, and when must it be avoided?
back: It is a peripheral mu-opioid agonist (40 to 50 times as potent as morphine as an antidiarrhoeal) that is poorly absorbed and barely enters the brain, so at normal doses it has no analgesic action and little abuse liability. GG14 warns that exceeding the recommended dose can cause torsades de pointes, cardiac arrest and death. Avoid it in invasive diarrhoea (fever, blood or mucus; risk of toxic megacolon and systemic spread), in severe colitis, and in young children (KDT: under 4 years; GG14: not recommended under 2 years).

front: How does racecadotril reduce diarrhoea without slowing the gut?
back: It is a prodrug converted to thiorphan, an enkephalinase inhibitor. By protecting natural enkephalins it lowers mucosal cAMP and cuts intestinal secretion, but leaves motility alone. It is not contraindicated in children; the usual dose is 100 mg three times daily for up to 7 days.

front: In acute diarrhoea, which features suggest an invasive cause that needs an antibiotic?
back: Blood and mucus in the stool, fever, urgency and cramps, with only mild dehydration, point to colonic invasion (for example Shigella, EPEC, Campylobacter or Salmonella typhimurium). Watery diarrhoea with vomiting and little fever points to a noninvasive cause, where oral rehydration is the mainstay.

points: Laxative: soft formed stool; purgative: stronger, more fluid evacuation
Ispaghula, methylcellulose, bran: water-holding, fermentable fibre
Docusate: anionic detergent that draws water into stool
Liquid paraffin: lubricant; avoid regular use (granulomas, lipid pneumonia, fat-soluble vitamin loss)
Bisacodyl and sodium picosulfate: act on colonic mucosa and enteric neurones
Senna and cascara: anthraquinone glycosides activated by colonic bacteria; act in 6 to 8 hours
Magnesium and sodium salts: bowel preparation, poisoning, tapeworm clearance
Lactulose and lactitol: fermented to acidic osmotic products
Prucalopride (5-HT4 agonist), lubiprostone (chloride channel activator)

front: Short note: Constipation, rational treatment and purgative abuse

Functional: spastic (hard stool, irritable bowel) or atonic (age, debility, laxative abuse)
Secondary: obstruction, hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, opioids, anticholinergics, oral iron, clonidine, verapamil
Diet, fluids, exercise and regular habits first
Spastic: soluble fibre; atonic: bulk or osmotic agent; stimulants last
Enema preferred to treat impaction
Keep stool soft in hernia, cardiovascular disease and perianal surgery
Bowel preparation: saline purgative, bisacodyl or senna
Hypokalaemia, steatorrhoea, protein-losing enteropathy, spastic colitis

Avoid antibiotics in enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (haemolytic uraemic syndrome)

Bulking colloids such as ispaghula; kaolin and pectin adsorbents are banned in India

Octreotide: somatostatin analogue for carcinoid or VIP tumour diarrhoea; given subcutaneously
Loperamide: potent peripheral opioid, most suitable antimotility drug for adults
Diphenoxylate with atropine: CNS effects; contraindicated under 6 years
Codeine: not used for diarrhoea because of dependence
Avoid antimotility drugs in invasive diarrhoea, severe colitis and young children

points: Ulcerative colitis: continuous mucosal disease of the colon, spreading up from the rectum

Extraintestinal features in up to half of patients

Mesalazine, olsalazine, balsalazide: deliver 5-ASA to the colon with fewer side effects; 5-ASA not useful in Crohn's

Budesonide (delayed-release) targets ileal or colonic disease with fewer systemic effects
Azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine for steroid-dependent or resistant disease; check TPMT status

Tofacitinib: oral JAK inhibitor

front: Essay: Oral rehydration therapy in acute diarrhoea

points: Sodium absorption coupled to glucose by the sodium-glucose cotransporter survives in diarrhoea
Secreted fluid contains no glucose, so it cannot be reabsorbed
Isotonic or slightly hypotonic: osmolarity 200 to 310 mOsm/L
Glucose equal to or slightly above sodium, not above 110 mM
Potassium 15 to 25 mM and a base such as citrate 8 to 12 mM

Frequent drinks; replace stool losses; aim to restore hydration within about 6 hours
Nasogastric drip if a weak child refuses

text: Colonic bacteria split the {{azo}} bond of sulfasalazine to release {{5-aminosalicylic acid}}, the active anti-inflammatory part, and {{sulfapyridine}}, which causes most side effects.
Azathioprine is converted to {{6-mercaptopurine}}; patients deficient in the enzyme {{TPMT}} are at high risk of severe bone marrow toxicity.
Diphenoxylate is a synthetic {{opioid}} given with {{atropine}} to discourage abuse, and it is contraindicated below {{6}} years of age.

front: Isotretinoin: why is it restricted in women of reproductive age?
back: It is highly teratogenic. Up to about a quarter of exposed fetuses have birth defects, mainly craniofacial, cardiac and CNS abnormalities. It is contraindicated in women who may become pregnant during treatment and for one month after stopping.

front: Isotretinoin: where is it used and what is the usual course?
back: Oral 13-cis retinoic acid for severe cystic acne that has not responded to other treatment. The usual dose is 0.5 to 1 mg/kg daily for about 20 weeks, and relapses can be treated by repeating the course. Half-life is about 18 hours, and unlike acitretin it does not accumulate in fat.

front: Acitretin: indications and its pregnancy and alcohol precautions.
back: Oral synthetic retinoid for severe psoriasis, lichen planus and severe ichthyosis. It is highly teratogenic and accumulates in body fat, so elimination takes months. Avoid conception during treatment and for 3 years after stopping, and avoid alcohol during treatment and for 3 months after.

front: Benzoyl peroxide in acne: how does it act and what are its limits?
back: In the presence of water it releases oxygen, which kills P. acnes and other anaerobic or microaerophilic bacteria. It also has keratolytic and comedolytic action, and bacteria do not develop resistance. It causes irritation and dryness, bleaches hair and fabric, and must not be applied together with tretinoin because it breaks the tretinoin down.

front: Calcipotriol: mechanism and place in psoriasis.
back: A synthetic vitamin D analogue that has little systemic effect on calcium when used topically. It binds the vitamin D receptor in keratinocytes, reducing proliferation and promoting differentiation. Response takes 4 to 8 weeks, efficacy is comparable to a moderate-potency steroid, and combining it with a steroid works better than either alone.

front: Keratolytics: salicylic acid and urea, concentrations and uses.
back: Salicylic acid at 10 to 20% (in alcohol or propylene glycol) dissolves corns and works better under an occlusive dressing; 3 to 5% is used in other conditions. Urea at 5 to 20% acts as a humectant that softens keratin in ichthyosis and hyperkeratotic lesions, and it enhances penetration of a topical steroid applied with it.

front: Short note: Isotretinoin in acne vulgaris

points: Reduces sebum output and corrects abnormal follicular keratinisation
Bacterial numbers fall secondarily
Severe cystic acne that has not responded to other therapy
About 20 weeks at 0.5 to 1 mg/kg daily
Cheilitis, dry skin, eyes, nose and mouth, epistaxis
Raised serum lipids, raised intracranial pressure, musculoskeletal pain
Highly teratogenic; contraindicated in women who may conceive during therapy
Also avoid pregnancy for one month after stopping
Corticosteroids: start high potency, then step down; occlusion speeds response
Calcipotriol (vitamin D analogue) and tazarotene (retinoid prodrug)
PUVA: oral methoxsalen, then UVA exposure 1 to 2 hours later
Risks include skin cancer, cataract and premature skin ageing
Oral acitretin; PUVA for severe disease
Methotrexate weekly for moderate-to-severe psoriasis (avoid with liver disease; watch interacting drugs); cyclosporine microemulsion (monitor BP and creatinine)
Apremilast, an oral PDE4 inhibitor
Biologics: TNF inhibitors (etanercept, adalimumab, infliximab), IL-17 blockers (secukinumab, ixekizumab), IL-12/23 blocker ustekinumab, IL-23 blockers (guselkumab, risankizumab)
Controls lesions but does not cure; relapse is common on stopping

front: Essay: Acne vulgaris: pathogenesis and drug management

points: Androgen-driven sebum excess in follicles
P. acnes colonisation; bacterial lipases release irritant free fatty acids
Comedones form and may rupture into inflammation and pustules
Benzoyl peroxide: antibacterial and comedolytic; bacteria do not become resistant
Retinoids: tretinoin, adapalene, tazarotene; benzoyl peroxide inactivates tretinoin, so do not apply together
Topical antibiotics (clindamycin, erythromycin) for inflamed papules, combined with benzoyl peroxide to improve efficacy and limit resistance; azelaic acid
For extensive acne or acne not controlled by topical therapy
Oral tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline) or macrolides
Isotretinoin for severe nodulocystic acne, with strict teratogenicity precautions
Tretinoin: start at a low strength; response takes 6 to 10 weeks
Long-term tetracyclines can cause raised intracranial pressure

text: Chemical sunscreens such as {{PABA}} absorb UVB, {{benzophenones}} block UVA, and physical sunscreens such as {{zinc oxide}} and {{titanium dioxide}} scatter UV and visible light. SPF is the UVB dose causing minimal erythema on protected skin divided by the dose on unprotected skin.

Potent: {{clobetasol propionate}}, betamethasone valerate and fluocinolone acetonide 0.025%; moderately potent: {{mometasone}} and fluticasone; mild: {{hydrocortisone}}. Potency depends largely on the {{lipophilicity}} of the compound, which governs how deeply it penetrates the skin.
{{Hydroquinone}} is a weak agent that inhibits {{tyrosinase}} and needs months of use in melasma; {{monobenzone}} destroys melanocytes and can cause {{permanent depigmentation}}.

front: Define disinfection and sterilisation, and state the difference.
back: Sterilisation kills all microbes, including spores. Disinfection reduces pathogenic microbes to a level that does not endanger a person with normal defences, so it does not necessarily kill everything. Antiseptics are used on living tissue and disinfectants on inanimate objects.

front: Hexachlorophene: why was its use restricted?
back: A chlorinated phenol that is odourless, non-staining and persists on skin, but it is narrow spectrum: it kills gram-positive bacteria, not gram-negative bacteria or spores. A 3% bath for infants cut staphylococcal infection but caused brain damage in premature neonates, and preparations above 2% have been banned.

front: Chlorhexidine: class, mechanism and main uses.
back: A cationic biguanide that disrupts bacterial membranes and denatures proteins. It is more active against gram-positive bacteria and persists on skin. Used for surgical scrub, neonatal bath, obstetric and general skin antisepsis, and as a 0.12 to 0.2% mouthwash for gingivitis; repeated use can stain teeth brown.

front: Ethanol as an antiseptic: effective concentration and limits.
back: Effective at 40 to 90%, fastest near 70%, because it precipitates bacterial proteins. It does not kill spores and promotes rusting of instruments. It irritates mucosa, the scrotum and open wounds, where it forms a coagulum that can shelter bacteria. Alcohol-based rubs are used for hand hygiene.

front: Povidone-iodine: what is it, and how does it differ from tincture iodine?
back: An iodophore: iodine bound to polyvinylpyrrolidone that releases free iodine slowly. It is non-irritant, non-staining and long-acting, and it does not blister when covered with a dressing. Tincture iodine (2% in alcohol) stings on abrasions. Povidone-iodine is used on boils, burns, ulcers, tinea, vaginitis, surgical scrubs and endoscope disinfection.

front: Permethrin: why is it the first-choice drug for scabies?
back: A pyrethroid that paralyses the insect nervous system. Human toxicity is very low, systemic absorption is minimal and resistance is rare. A single application cures most scabies and lice, including cases that did not respond to lindane. For scabies, 5% cream is applied over the body except face and scalp and washed off after 8 to 12 hours.

points: Broad-spectrum insecticide that enters the chitinous cover and affects the nervous system
Effective against lice and scabies after one treatment
Lice: applied to scalp for 12 to 24 hours; repeat after one week if needed
Scabies: applied below the neck, scrub bath 12 to 24 hours later
Lipid soluble, so absorbed through skin, especially from oily vehicles and in children
Resistance reported; less effective than permethrin
CNS stimulation, convulsions and cardiac arrhythmias
Avoid in infants, young children and pregnancy

front: Short note: Ivermectin in scabies and lice

points: Anthelmintic that is also effective against ectoparasites
The only oral drug used for ectoparasitosis; used less often because good topicals exist
Single oral dose of 0.2 mg/kg (about 12 mg in adults)
Cures roughly 91 to 100% of scabies cases, including patients with AIDS
Not for children under 5 years, pregnant women or breastfeeding women
Very few side effects
Contagious mite infestation that burrows through the epidermis and causes intense itch
Finger webs are the usual entry site; spreads to forearms, trunk, genitals and legs
Permethrin 5% cream: single application, first choice
Benzyl benzoate: second-line; contraindicated in children due to neurological effects
Lindane: effective but systemic toxicity risk; avoid in children and pregnancy
Crotamiton: lower cure rate; a 5-day course is used in children
Sulfur: cheap but messy and malodorous; largely superseded
Oral ivermectin when topical drugs are unsuitable
Treat family contacts together; wash garments and bed linen in hot water

text: First choice: {{permethrin}}; second line: {{benzyl benzoate}} and {{crotamiton}}; older agents: {{sulfur}} and {{DDT}}; oral option: {{ivermectin}}.

front: Classify: oxidising agents, aldehydes and halogens
text: {{Potassium permanganate}} and {{hydrogen peroxide}} are oxidising agents; {{glutaraldehyde}} is less irritant than {{formalin}}, which is a 37% solution of {{formaldehyde}}.

{{Silver nitrate}} 1% is used for {{ophthalmia neonatorum}} because it is highly active against {{gonococci}}; {{silver sulfadiazine}} is used on burns because it is highly active against {{Pseudomonas}}.

front: What features make a chelating agent clinically useful?
back: It must form a stable ring with the metal, ideally a 5 to 7 membered ring with two or more ligand groups. It should bind the toxic metal more strongly than calcium and the body's own ligands, distribute into the same compartments as the metal, and be water soluble. Its efficacy falls as the gap between exposure and treatment increases.

front: Dimercaprol: which metals does it treat, and what is the main contraindication?
back: It treats arsenic, mercury, gold, bismuth, nickel and antimony poisoning, and is an adjuvant with calcium EDTA in lead poisoning and with penicillamine in copper poisoning. It is contraindicated in iron and cadmium poisoning, because its complexes with these metals are themselves toxic.

front: Calcium disodium EDTA: main use, route and key toxicity.
back: Given intravenously because it is not absorbed orally and does not enter the brain. It is the mainstay for lead poisoning and also treats iron, zinc, copper, manganese and some radioactive metals, but not mercury. Its main toxicity is proximal tubular necrosis, which is reduced by keeping urine flow high.

front: Disodium EDTA: why must it be infused slowly?
back: It is a potent calcium chelator, so rapid intravenous injection causes tetany. A slow infusion avoids this because calcium is drawn from bone. For emergency hypercalcaemia bisphosphonates are preferred.

front: Penicillamine: which isomer is used, and what are its main indications?
back: The D-isomer, because the L-isomer and the racemate cause optic neuritis. Indications are Wilson's disease (0.5 to 1 g daily, taken 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals), copper or mercury poisoning, cystinuria and cystine stones, and scleroderma. Prolonged use causes skin, renal, haematological and collagen toxicity.

front: Desferrioxamine: what is it used for and what is its chelating capacity?
back: An iron chelator derived from an actinomycete. One gram binds about 85 mg of elemental iron. It removes loosely bound iron and iron from ferritin and haemosiderin, but not iron in haemoglobin or cytochromes. Used in acute iron poisoning (mainly children) and transfusion siderosis; it is given parenterally because little is absorbed orally.

Two SH groups bind metals that inactivate sulfhydryl enzymes; 2:1 complexes are most stable
Arsenic, mercury, gold, bismuth, nickel and antimony poisoning
Adjuvant with calcium EDTA in lead poisoning and with penicillamine in copper poisoning
Intramuscular 5 mg/kg stat, then 2 to 3 mg/kg every 4 to 8 hours for 2 days
Then once or twice daily for 10 days; start early and alkalinise urine
Dose-related rise in BP, tachycardia, vomiting, burning, sweating and headache
An antihistamine given 30 minutes before reduces the reactions
Acute iron poisoning, mainly in children
Transfusion siderosis in thalassaemia and other chronic iron overload
Parenteral; histamine release causes flushing, hypotension and urticaria
Repeated use can cause lens and retinal changes
Oral; somewhat less effective than desferrioxamine but cheaper and more convenient
Anorexia, vomiting, joint pain and reversible neutropenia; agranulocytosis rare
Oral once daily on an empty stomach; iron complex excreted in bile
High affinity for iron, low for copper and zinc; GI bleeding and renal failure reported

points: Chelators form stable ring complexes that the body excretes
Early treatment matters: efficacy falls as the delay increases

Copper: penicillamine; iron: desferrioxamine, deferiprone or deferasirox
Dimercaprol intramuscular; calcium EDTA intravenous only; succimer and deferasirox oral

Dimercaprol: dose-related hypertension and pain; antihistamine pre-treatment helps
Calcium EDTA: proximal tubular necrosis and febrile reactions
Penicillamine: skin, renal and haematological toxicity on long-term use

text: Dimercaprol and {{succimer}} treat arsenic and mercury; {{calcium disodium edetate}} treats lead; {{penicillamine}} treats copper in Wilson's disease; {{desferrioxamine}} treats iron overload.
Rapid intravenous {{disodium edetate}} causes {{tetany}} by chelating calcium; {{calcium disodium edetate}} can cause {{proximal tubular necrosis}}, which is reduced by high {{urine flow}}.
{{Deferiprone}} is an oral option that can cause reversible {{neutropenia}}; {{deferasirox}} is given once daily on an empty stomach and is excreted in {{bile}}.

front: Fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins: how do they differ in storage and toxicity?
back: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored for long periods, so regular large doses can accumulate to toxic levels. Water-soluble vitamins (B complex and C) are poorly stored and excess is excreted, so toxicity is rare. Water-soluble vitamins mostly act as cofactors for enzymes.

Xerophthalmia, Bitot's spots, corneal softening (keratomalacia) and night blindness progressing to total blindness. Also dry rough skin with follicular papules, increased infection, diarrhoea, urinary stone formation, impaired spermatogenesis and growth retardation. Common in infants and children in developing countries.

front: Vitamin A: chronic and acute toxicity.
back: Chronic: about 100,000 IU daily for months causes nausea, dermatitis, hair loss, bone pain, raised intracranial pressure and liver disease; it is also teratogenic, so daily intake should stay under about 20,000 IU. Acute: over 1 million IU gives headache, drowsiness, vomiting and skin shedding; treat by stopping intake and giving vitamin E. Excess carotenoids do not cause toxicity.

front: Vitamin E: why is antioxidant use for heart disease and cancer not justified?
back: Large observational studies and meta-analyses have not shown fewer cardiovascular events or cancers in well-nourished people, and high doses (over 400 mg/day of tocopherol) have been linked to heart failure. No clear human deficiency syndrome exists. Its recognised uses are narrow: supplementation for at-risk patients, G6PD deficiency and acanthocytosis.

front: Isoniazid and vitamin B6: what is the interaction and how is it handled?
back: Isoniazid combines with pyridoxal and increases renal loss of pyridoxine, which can cause deficiency and peripheral neuropathy. Pyridoxine at 10 to 100 mg/day prevents or treats these effects and is routinely given with anti-MDR-TB regimens. Hydralazine, cycloserine and penicillamine also interfere with pyridoxine.

front: Pellagra: classic features and which niacin form is preferred for treatment?
back: The three Ds: dermatitis (a sunburn-like rash that darkens and peels), diarrhoea with glossitis and stomatitis, and dementia. Treatment is 200 to 500 mg/day in divided doses. Nicotinamide is preferred, especially by injection, because nicotinic acid causes flushing and other side effects.

Mainly polyneuritis: numbness, weakness, wrist drop or foot drop
Mental changes, poor memory and constipation
Cardiovascular: palpitation, high-output heart failure and ECG changes
Oedema from heart failure, worsened by protein deficiency

Beriberi: 100 mg/day intramuscular or intravenous, then oral maintenance; prophylaxis 2 to 10 mg/day
Needed for hydroxylation of proline and lysine in collagen
Also needed for carnitine, catecholamine and steroid synthesis, and for folate conversion

Seen in malnourished infants, the elderly, alcoholics and drug users
Scurvy: 0.5 to 1.5 g/day; prevention 50 to 100 mg/day
Improves iron absorption; acidifies urine in urinary tract infection
Rebound scurvy after stopping long-term mega-doses

front: Classify: vitamins and their coenzyme forms
text: Thiamine forms {{thiamine pyrophosphate}}; riboflavin forms {{FAD}} and {{FMN}}; niacin forms {{NAD}} and {{NADP}}; pyridoxine forms {{pyridoxal phosphate}}.

Scurvy reflects a {{connective tissue}} defect; {{angular stomatitis}} and corneal vascularisation point to riboflavin deficiency; {{seborrhoeic dermatitis}} and glossitis suggest pyridoxine deficiency.
Vitamin C improves {{iron}} absorption by keeping it in the {{ferrous}} state; abrupt stopping of large doses can cause {{rebound scurvy}}.

front: Active versus passive immunity: which products give each, and which gives immediate protection?
back: Vaccines give active immunity by stimulating the recipient's own antibody or cell-mediated response, which takes weeks. Antisera and immunoglobulins give passive immunity with ready-made antibodies, so protection is immediate but short-lived. Only antisera are also curative for an established infection.

front: Live attenuated vaccines: who must not receive them?
back: People with impaired defences: leukaemia or other malignancy on cytotoxic chemotherapy, systemic lupus, those on corticosteroids, and those with AIDS or other immunodeficiency. Two live vaccines not given together should be separated by about one month. Vaccines are also deferred during pregnancy and acute infection.

front: Sabin (OPV) versus Salk (IPV) polio vaccine: which is preferred for children and for adults?
back: OPV (live, Sabin) is the vaccine of choice for children in KDT: easy to give, it induces intestinal as well as systemic immunity and limits carriage, which is the basis of pulse polio campaigns. It is shed in stool, so it can spread to contacts, and rarely (about 1 per million doses) causes vaccine-associated paralysis; the USA stopped using it in 2000. IPV (inactivated, Salk) mainly induces humoral immunity, does not spread or cause paralysis, and is preferred for adults, immunocompromised people (OPV is contraindicated in primary immunodeficiency), pregnant women and children with symptomatic HIV.

front: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis: intradermal (Thai) regimen and intramuscular schedule.
back: KDT (Thai regimen, notified in India in 2006): 0.1 ml of PCEV or PVRV, or 0.2 ml of HDCV, intradermally at two sites on days 0, 3 and 7, then one site on day 28 and one on day 90; about one-fifth of the i.m. vaccine dose. GG14 (i.m.): four doses on days 0, 3, 7 and 14, with rabies immunoglobulin on day 0, part infiltrated into the bite and the rest i.m. RIG is needed for category III bites because the vaccine takes 10 to 14 days to produce antibodies. A previously vaccinated person needs only two doses (days 0 and 3) and no RIG.

front: Human versus equine antisera: which is preferred for rabies and tetanus?
back: Human immunoglobulin is preferred. Human rabies immunoglobulin (20 IU/kg on day 0, infiltrated around the bite) and human tetanus immunoglobulin (250 to 500 IU prophylaxis) have longer half-lives and rare serum sickness. Equine rabies serum (40 IU/kg) and tetanus antitoxin (1500 to 3000 IU) are used only when the human product is unavailable.

front: Polyvalent antisnake venom: which venoms does it neutralise, and how is it given?
back: Each ml neutralises standard venom of Indian cobra, Russell's viper, saw-scaled viper and common krait. Give 20 ml intravenously at about 1 ml/min, repeated every 1 to 6 hours until signs of envenomation stop. Viper bites may need up to about 300 ml; some serum is also infiltrated around the bite to limit local gangrene.

front: Vitamin K: forms, mechanism, main uses, and why menadione is avoided.
back: K1 (phytonadione, phytyl side chain) is from plants, K2 (menaquinones) is made by gut bacteria, and K3 (menadione) is synthetic. It is a cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues in prothrombin and factors VII, IX and X (also proteins C and S), letting them bind calcium. Uses: deficiency from diet, antibiotics or obstructive jaundice; haemorrhagic disease of the newborn (1 mg i.m. at birth); and, most important, overdose of oral anticoagulants, for which K1 is preferred because it acts fastest (avoid unnecessarily high doses, which cause warfarin resistance for days). I.v. emulsified K1 can cause severe anaphylactoid reactions. Menadione causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency and neonates and can precipitate kernicterus.

front: Vitamin B12: causes of deficiency, features and treatment.
back: Causes: pernicious anaemia (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor), other gastric damage or gastrectomy, intestinal malabsorption or resection, blind-loop bacteria or fish tapeworm, and (less often) a strict vegetarian diet. Features: megaloblastic anaemia with hypersegmented neutrophils, glossitis, and neurological damage (subacute combined degeneration, peripheral neuritis). Treatment is by injection when intrinsic factor is lacking; hydroxocobalamin is preferred because it is more protein-bound and better retained (e.g. 1 mg i.m. daily or alternate days for 2 weeks, then every 1 to 3 months). Add folic acid and iron, because brisk haemopoiesis can unmask their deficiency. Neurological recovery is slow and may be incomplete.

front: Folic acid: uses, and why it must never be given alone in vitamin B12 deficiency.
back: Uses: megaloblastic anaemia from poor intake, malabsorption, pregnancy and other high-demand states, and antiepileptic therapy (avoid large doses, which can weaken anticonvulsant control); therapeutic dose 2 to 5 mg/day orally. Routine supplementation in pregnancy reduces neural tube defects. Given alone in B12 deficiency it corrects the blood picture but the neurological damage worsens, because the small B12 store is diverted to haemopoiesis. Folinic acid (already reduced) is reserved for methotrexate toxicity; it is not needed for simple folate deficiency.

front: Outline the evolution of India's tuberculosis control programme.
back: Treatment of TB in India is free for all patients under a national programme. The Revised National Tuberculosis Control Programme (RNTCP) began in 1997 and revised its treatment guidelines several times, most recently (in KDT) in 2016. TB became a notifiable disease in 2012, so every treating doctor must notify cases. After the WHO End TB Strategy (2014), RNTCP was renamed the National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme (NTEP).

front: What is DOTS, and what principles of short-course chemotherapy underlie it?
back: Directly observed treatment, short course, recommended by WHO in 1995, used 6-8 month multidrug regimens with weight-based standard doses. All first-line drugs are given as a single daily dose; an intensive phase of 4-6 drugs rapidly kills bacilli and converts sputum, and a continuation phase of 3-4 drugs removes the remaining bacilli to prevent relapse. Directly observed treatment remains NTEP's patient-friendly way of monitoring adherence.

Free high-sensitivity diagnostics; active case finding; private-sector engagement
Universal drug-resistance testing; screening of high-risk groups; vulnerability mapping
