front: How did the RNTCP 2016 regimen for new drug-sensitive TB differ from the 2010 regimen, and why?
back: The 2016 regimen is 2HRZE followed by 4HRE (6 months). Ethambutol was added to the continuation phase (2010 used RH only), as WHO advises where primary isoniazid resistance is common (up to 18%). Dosing was changed from thrice weekly to daily in both phases, because thrice-weekly dosing had been an operational compromise.

front: Why does the TB programme use fixed-dose combination tablets in weight bands?
back: FDCs make sure the patient takes all the drugs together, so bacilli are never exposed to only one or two drugs and resistance is not fostered. For operational ease the programme supplies separate FDC tablets for the intensive and continuation phases, with the number of tablets set by body-weight band.

front: How did the TB programme extend to drug-resistant TB?
back: RNTCP began DOTS-Plus in 2000 for diagnosis and treatment of MDR-TB, updated it in 2010 per WHO, and revised it again in 2016 with extensive drug-susceptibility testing: liquid culture DST, line probe assay (R and H resistance) and cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test (CBNAAT, R resistance). A standard MDR regimen is used unless DST or patient factors call for an individualised regimen.

front: Trace the history of leprosy control in India.
back: The National Leprosy Control Programme began in 1955 and became the National Leprosy Eradication Programme (NLEP) in 1982. Following the WHO Action Programme, multidrug therapy (introduced by WHO in 1981) was implemented through NLEP in 1982. India reached elimination as a public health problem (prevalence below 1 per 10,000) in December 2005, although some states remain above that level.

front: What is the aim of MDT in a mass programme, and how does it differ from institutional care?
back: Mass programmes (WHO Action Programme, NLEP) aim to make patients non-contagious and cut transmission, so fixed-duration therapy (12 months for multibacillary, 6 months for paucibacillary) is accepted; the few relapses are retreated with the same MDT, since persisters stay drug-sensitive. Private or institutional care aims to cure each patient and may continue up to about 4 years in highly bacillated cases.

front: What has MDT achieved in India, as recorded in KDT?
back: Prevalence fell from 57.6 per 10,000 in 1981 to 0.66 per 10,000 in 2016; total cases fell from 3.95 million (1981) to about 0.127 million new cases detected in 2015-16. Relapses were few, and lepra reactions did not become more common with MDT. India still has the largest number of leprosy patients in the world.

front: What does the National Strategic Plan and Roadmap for Leprosy 2023-2027 aim for?
back: A leprosy-free India with zero infection and disease, zero disability, and zero stigma and discrimination. Strategies: stronger leadership and partnerships, early case detection, quality services, prevention of disease, disability and discrimination, and digital surveillance of individual patient records (Nikusth 2.0). The Sparsh Leprosy Awareness Campaign targets stigma.

text: The National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme covers six diseases: {{malaria}}, {{filariasis}}, {{kala-azar}}, {{dengue}}, {{Japanese encephalitis}} and {{chikungunya}}.

front: How did India's antimalaria programme evolve?
back: The National Malaria Eradication Programme (NMEP, 1958) nearly eliminated malaria in the 1960s, but insecticide resistance and other factors brought it back by the mid-1970s. NMEP was renamed the National Anti-Malaria Programme and then absorbed into the wider NVBDCP. Use of artemisinin-based combination therapy has since cut falciparum cases and deaths.

front: Short note: National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016-2030)

Keep malaria-free areas free and prevent reintroduction

Integrated vector management: insecticides, larvicides, malathion fogging, biological control, personal protection
Community participation; environmental management
Epidemic preparedness and rapid response; partnerships
Planning, monitoring and evaluation
Districts placed in four categories by annual parasite incidence (API)

front: Complete: NVBDCP antimalarial drug policy (as in KDT)
text: All P. falciparum cases receive {{artemisinin-based combination therapy}} (first line: artesunate plus {{sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine}}) with a single gametocidal dose of {{primaquine}} on day 2, regardless of chloroquine sensitivity; in the {{North-eastern}} states {{artemether-lumefantrine}} is used because of S/P resistance. The national drug policy makes artesunate compulsory with S/P to slow {{S/P resistance}}. Severe malaria is treated only with {{intravenous artesunate}}. Vivax malaria gets chloroquine for 3 days plus primaquine for {{14}} days.

front: Describe the kala-azar programme in India.
back: The Kala-azar Control Programme began in 1990 and was upgraded in 2000 to aim at elimination; it runs under NVBDCP with its own treatment guidelines and free treatment. Only confirmed cases (rapid diagnostic test or splenic aspirate) are treated. The disease is endemic in Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal and eastern Uttar Pradesh.

Reduce cases in vulnerable endemic populations
Reduce post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis to break transmission
Prevent KA-HIV and KA-TB coinfection
Diagnosis with rK39 rapid kits, then oral miltefosine
Vector control; synthetic pyrethroid against sandflies
Human resources; monitoring and evaluation; research guidelines

front: Which antileishmanial drugs does NVBDCP use, and how does its miltefosine dosing differ from WHO's?
back: Miltefosine is first line (orally for 28 days; supplied in India only through NVBDCP) and amphotericin B is second line because of its toxicity and need for hospital infusions; sodium stibogluconate is no longer used because of resistance in Bihar. NVBDCP gives 100 mg/day to all adults over 25 kg, whereas WHO advises 150 mg/day for adults over 50 kg. WHO gives liposomal amphotericin B its highest preference, but cost limits its use in India.

front: Outline India's programme against lymphatic filariasis.
back: The National Filaria Control Programme (1955) used larval control, case and carrier treatment and complication prevention; it merged with the urban malaria scheme in 1978. The elimination strategy adds annual mass drug administration (MDA) of DEC with albendazole, or DEC with ivermectin, aiming to cover more than 80% of the population, plus home care of lymphoedema and hydrocele surgery.

front: Why does annual single-dose mass drug administration control filariasis?
back: DEC is mainly microfilaricidal; a yearly single dose of DEC (6 mg/kg) with albendazole (400 mg) lowers microfilaraemia across the population and so cuts transmission by mosquitoes. Ivermectin (0.2 mg/kg) with albendazole yearly for 5-6 years is an alternative. MDA does not reverse established elephantiasis, which is due to irreversible lymphatic fibrosis.

front: Complete: Japanese encephalitis control under NVBDCP
text: Strategies are early case detection and management, {{vaccination}} of children aged {{1 to 15}} years, health education, avoiding mosquito bites, keeping {{pigs}} away from homes, and {{malathion}} spraying in affected areas.

front: What has the National AIDS Control Programme achieved, and what is its current vision?
back: HIV prevalence and deaths in India fell steadily only after 2004, when NACO began giving free combination ART; by 2015 new infections were 32% lower and AIDS deaths 54% lower than in 2007. The National Strategic Plan for HIV/AIDS and STI (2017-2024) aims at an AIDS-free India: no new infections, no AIDS deaths and no discrimination.

front: When does NACO start antiretroviral therapy?
back: Immediately after HIV infection is confirmed, irrespective of CD4 count, viral load or clinical stage, and continued for life. Earlier guidelines waited until CD4 fell below 350 cells/microlitre; WHO's 2016 "treat all" advice was accepted by the Government of India and is implemented by NACO.

front: What principles shape NACO antiretroviral regimens (as in KDT)?
back: Lamivudine is part of most first-line triple regimens; first line contains an NNRTI (nevirapine or efavirenz); protease inhibitors are kept for failure, and a ritonavir-boosted PI is nearly always in second line; stavudine is no longer used except in exceptional cases. On failure, change the whole regimen (lamivudine may continue), never add or switch a single drug. For pregnant women NACO (2013) uses tenofovir + lamivudine + efavirenz once daily as an FDC, with nevirapine syrup to the infant for 6 weeks.

back: It began as the Expanded Programme on Immunization in 1978 and was renamed UIP in 1985. It gives uniform, high-quality vaccines free to all sections of society. Objectives: raise coverage in a time-bound way, improve service quality including a reliable cold chain, monitor the programme, and build self-sufficient vaccine production.

front: What drug strategy does the National Diarrhoeal Disease Control Programme use?
back: Launched in 1983 to cut deaths and malnutrition from childhood diarrhoea, it combines zinc with oral rehydration solution: 10 mg dispersible tablets for infants aged 2-6 months and 20 mg for children over 6 months, for 2 weeks. Prevention includes safe water, hand hygiene, food safety, sanitation and rotavirus vaccination.

front: Which dengue vaccine does Sarkar describe, and for whom is it approved?
back: A live tetravalent vaccine (Dengvaxia) against dengue serotypes 1 to 4. It is approved for people with laboratory-confirmed past dengue infection who live in endemic areas. It is not approved for people never infected, who are at higher risk of severe dengue if vaccinated.

front: Define pharmacovigilance and state its purpose.
back: WHO (2002): the science and activities for detecting, assessing, understanding and preventing adverse effects or any other drug-related problem. The word joins Greek pharmakon (drug) and Latin vigilare (to keep watch). Its purpose is to reduce drug-related harm, inform doctors and regulators, support rational use, and guard against ineffective, substandard or counterfeit medicines.

front: Define a signal, an adverse drug reaction and an adverse event.
back: Signal: reported information on a possible causal link between an adverse event and a drug that was previously unknown or incompletely documented. ADR: a noxious, unintended effect at doses normally used in humans for prophylaxis, diagnosis or therapy. Adverse event: any untoward occurrence during treatment, not necessarily caused by the drug.

front: Short note: Why premarketing trials cannot establish drug safety

points: Pivotal trials often involve only hundreds to a few thousand patients (median about 467): rare reactions are missed, e.g. nefazodone liver failure
Few patients with uncommon genetic variants (TPMT, HLA-B*5701, CYP2D6)
Median duration about 24 weeks; late effects missed (bisphosphonate jaw necrosis, atypical femoral fractures)
Children, pregnant women, the very old and patients with comorbidity are excluded
Mostly placebo-controlled; few active comparators
Surrogate endpoints can mislead: flecainide and encainide (CAST), rosiglitazone
High-dose rofecoxib approved for 5 days of acute pain was used long-term, increasing MI risk

front: Which landmark US laws were triggered by drug disasters?
back: 1938 Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act after more than 100 deaths from sulfanilamide elixir made with diethylene glycol (pre-marketing safety testing). 1962 Kefauver-Harris amendment after thalidomide (proof of efficacy, reporting of serious adverse effects). 2007 FDA Amendments Act after rofecoxib (population surveillance, mandatory label changes, post-approval studies, REMS and public trial registration).

front: Complete: drugs withdrawn or restricted after postmarketing surveillance
text: Terfenadine, astemizole, cisapride and grepafloxacin: {{QT prolongation}} and torsades. Fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine: {{cardiac valve}} abnormalities. Rofecoxib: {{myocardial infarction}} and stroke. Cerivastatin: fatal {{rhabdomyolysis}}. Lorcaserin: increased {{cancer}} risk. Thalidomide: {{phocomelia}}, though now used again under risk controls for multiple myeloma.

points: Voluntary reporting of suspected ADRs by health professionals (yellow card scheme in the UK, MedWatch/FAERS in the USA); mandatory for manufacturers
Cheap, covers all users from marketing onwards
Can detect rare and dramatic reactions quickly (thalidomide, fen-phen valvulopathy)
Massive under-reporting (only about 10% of ADRs reported; median under-reporting about 94%)
Denominator (number exposed) unknown, so incidence cannot be calculated
Reports often incomplete
Cannot detect small rises in common events such as MI
Reporting distorted by media, litigation and time on market

front: When are individual case reports most convincing for causality?
back: When the event is otherwise rare, has few other risk factors, follows exposure closely in time (anaphylaxis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome), and the drug carries a large excess risk (e.g. rhabdomyolysis with cerivastatin, far higher per million prescriptions than other statins).

front: How are signals detected in large spontaneous-report databases?
back: Quantitative disproportionality methods compare how often a particular event is reported for a drug with how often it would be expected from the whole database; they need no exposure denominator but rest on unverifiable assumptions, so signals always need further evaluation.

A UK postmarketing method that follows cohorts of usually at least 10,000 patients on a new drug: questionnaires are sent to the prescribing general practitioners to record all significant events over about 6-12 months after starting the drug.

text: Pharmacovigilance uses {{spontaneous reporting}} and published case reports, {{prescription-event monitoring}}, computerised {{record linkage}}, observational {{cohort}} and case-control studies, {{targeted clinical investigations}} (PK, PD, genetic and interaction studies) and postmarketing {{clinical trials}}.

front: What is the FDA Sentinel System?
back: A distributed network of the FDA and more than 30 data partners covering over 100 million people. Each site analyses its own data under a common data model and reusable tools (e.g. propensity score matching) and returns results centrally, protecting privacy. It has evaluated signals such as olmesartan-associated sprue-like enteropathy and rotavirus vaccine intussusception, sometimes avoiding costly trials.

front: Short note: Evolution of pharmacovigilance in India

points: 1986: ADR monitoring system with 12 regional centres proposed
1989: six regional centres set up under the Drugs Controller
1997: India joined the WHO Programme for International Drug Monitoring (Uppsala Monitoring Centre)
National Pharmacovigilance Programme launched November 2004 with World Bank funding; suspended when funding ended in 2009
Launched 14 July 2010 with AIIMS New Delhi as National Coordination Centre
NCC moved to the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, Ghaziabad on 15 April 2011
Run with CDSCO under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

front: What are the goal and objectives of the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India?
back: Goal: ensure that the benefits of medicines outweigh their risks for the Indian population. Objectives: a nationwide patient-safety reporting system; identify and analyse new signals; assess benefit-risk of marketed drugs; generate evidence on medicine safety; support regulatory decisions; communicate safety information; collaborate with and train other national centres; become a centre of excellence.

front: Under PvPI, what should be reported and who may report (as given in Sarkar)?
back: All suspected adverse events, including those from herbal, traditional or alternative remedies; especially all events with new drugs and drugs of current interest, all suspected interactions, and reactions causing death, life-threat, hospitalisation, disability, congenital anomaly or needing intervention. Health care professionals (doctors, dentists, nurses, pharmacists) report; the source states lay reports are not accepted.

front: Trace the flow of an ADR report in PvPI.
back: The ADR monitoring centre (AMC, mostly medical colleges) collects the report, follows up for completeness and enters it into VigiFlow with source documents; causality is assessed (e.g. Naranjo algorithm, Hartwig severity scale); the National Coordination Centre at IPC Ghaziabad analyses the data and forwards it to the WHO Uppsala Monitoring Centre; CDSCO takes regulatory decisions and reports to DTAB.

front: How is an individual case safety report (ICSR) assessed?
back: For quality of documentation; coding of drugs (WHO Drug Dictionary based on ATC) and reactions (WHO-ART, MedDRA); relevance (new drug, i.e. within 4 years of first approval, unknown reaction not in the product information, or serious reaction); duplicate reports; and causality.

front: Which drugs does Sarkar list as banned in India following PvPI data?
back: Rosiglitazone, sibutramine, rimonabant, nimesulide in children under 12, cisapride, lorcaserin, phenylpropanolamine, gatifloxacin and tegaserod.

front: Short note: Risk evaluation and mitigation strategies (REMS)

points: FDA-mandated measures, pre- or postmarketing, to manage serious drug risks
Medication guides, patient package inserts
Patient registries, documented safe-use conditions, laboratory testing
Communication to, education and certification of prescribers and pharmacies
Isotretinoin programme to prevent fetal exposure
About 60 drugs have REMS; effectiveness little evaluated

front: How do regulators communicate new drug safety information, and how effective is it?
back: Quarterly postings of potential signals, label changes, boxed (black-box) warnings, drug safety communications and public health alerts; also drug alerts and advisories sent to doctors. Evidence suggests communications are often ineffective: monitoring advice changes little, warnings affect new more than existing patients, work best when specific, repeated and with alternatives, and may cut prescribing in untargeted groups.

front: What ethical problems arise in postmarketing safety trials?
back: Randomising patients to a drug with a suspected serious harm and no expected extra benefit is hard to justify (e.g. rosiglitazone versus pioglitazone). An IOM review advised mandating such trials only when observational studies cannot answer a critical public health question, after reviewing all existing data, with heightened informed consent. Comparative studies early in a drug's life avoid the problem.

front: Define pharmacoeconomics and the ECHO model.
back: The branch of health economics that measures and compares the costs and consequences of drug therapy (cost-benefit, cost-effectiveness, cost-minimisation, cost-utility and cost-of-illness analyses) to find best value for money. Drug decisions should balance Economic, Clinical and Humanistic Outcomes (ECHO). Regulators increasingly require economic analysis for licensing decisions.

front: Classify: pharmacoeconomic analyses by how outcome is measured
text: Cost-minimisation: outcomes proven {{equivalent}}, only costs compared. Cost-effectiveness: outcome in {{natural units}} (life-years gained, mmHg, cases cured). Cost-utility: outcome in {{QALYs}}. Cost-benefit: both costs and outcomes in {{money}}.

points: Costs and benefits (costs averted, productivity gained, valued health gains) both converted to money at present value
Benefit-to-cost ratio = PV of benefits / PV of costs; net benefit = benefits minus costs
Ratio above 1: worthwhile; equal to 1: break-even; below 1: not economically beneficial
Allows comparison of programmes whose costs and benefits occur at different times
Putting a money value on health is controversial; avoid if benefits cannot be monetised properly
Costs in money, outcomes in natural clinical units (life-years gained, cases cured, BP fall)
Total cost divided by outcome: cost per unit of outcome for one option
Extra cost divided by extra effect when moving to the next-best alternative
Most cost-effective is not always cheapest: aims at cost optimisation
Supports formularies, essential medicine lists and policy

back: Only when two or more options are already proven equivalent in efficacy and safety (e.g. two equally effective antiulcer drugs, generics, me-too drugs or alternative regimens of one drug). Costs then compared should include acquisition, preparation, administration and storage. If equivalence is unproven, use cost-effectiveness analysis.

front: What is cost-utility analysis and what is a QALY?
back: CUA compares cost per quality-adjusted life-year (QALY), weighting survival by health-related quality of life on a utility scale from 1 (perfect health) to 0 (death); QALYs = time in a health state x its utility. It suits life-extending treatments with serious toxicity (cancer chemotherapy) and morbidity-reducing therapies (arthritis). Limits: no consensus on measuring utilities and difficulty comparing across populations.

Framing medication policy and formularies, selecting essential medicines and devices, allocating limited resources, guiding individual prescribing, reimbursement decisions by insurers and government, and prescription audit to cut cost burden and polypharmacy. Example: the large price gap between bevacizumab and ranibizumab for macular degeneration with similar outcomes.

front: Essay: Pharmacoeconomics: principles, methods and applications

front: What is Mendelian randomisation and how did it predict a statin adverse effect?
back: Grouping people by genetic variants that mimic a drug's action; since genes are fixed at conception, the comparison avoids biases of drug choice. Variants lowering HMG-CoA reductase activity mimic statins and predicted the higher diabetes risk with statins that clinical use took decades to reveal.

front: What are pragmatic trials and their drawbacks?
back: Large, simple, often open-label trials with remote enrolment and outcomes from health records, close to usual care. They suit relatively safe interventions. Poor adherence and uncontrolled co-therapy blur results: in ADAPTABLE (aspirin 81 vs 325 mg) many switched to the lower dose, so intention-to-treat showed no difference.

front: How are drug names and adverse events coded when an ICSR is assessed?
back: Drug names are registered in the WHO Drug Dictionary, which is based on the ATC classification. Adverse events are coded with WHO-ART or MedDRA.

front: What does a drug utilisation study investigate?
back: Why and how drugs are prescribed, delivered, consumed and self-medicated, together with the non-clinical factors that drive drug use. Clinical pharmacologists at tertiary care centres conduct these studies.

front: How often must a periodic safety update report (PSUR) be filed during post-marketing surveillance of a new drug?
back: Every 6 months for the first 2 years, then yearly for the next 2 years. Post-marketing surveillance itself is mandatory.

front: Which study designs does Sarkar list for observing drug safety after marketing?
back: Non-interventional (observational) studies, post-marketing surveillance, adverse drug monitoring, case-control studies of ADRs, drug utilisation studies and observational registries.

front: Classify: the four scales of measurement
text: {{Nominal}} data are labels without order (e.g. sex, hair colour; a two-category nominal variable is dichotomous); {{ordinal}} data are ranked but the gaps are unknown (e.g. satisfaction scores, visual analogue scale); {{interval}} data have equal known gaps but no true zero (e.g. temperature in Celsius); {{ratio}} data have equal gaps and a true zero (e.g. weight, height).

front: Which summary measures can be used on each scale of data?
back: Nominal: mode only. Ordinal: mode or median, not the mean, because ranks cannot be added. Interval: mode, median, mean and SD (addition and subtraction allowed, ratios not, since there is no true zero). Ratio: all of these plus ratios and the coefficient of variation. Interval and ratio data suit parametric tests; nominal and ordinal data need non-parametric tests.

front: Distinguish discrete from continuous, and qualitative from quantitative data.
back: Continuous variables can take any value on a scale and be subdivided indefinitely (e.g. temperature, litres of fuel); discrete variables take fixed countable values (e.g. number of heads in 100 tosses). Quantitative data are measured numerically and can be computed; qualitative data describe attributes (e.g. honesty, creativity) that are observed but not calculated.

front: Define mean, median and mode. When is the median the better summary?
back: Mean: sum of values divided by their number. Median: middle value of ordered data (average of the two middle values when n is even). Mode: most frequent value. The median is better when outliers are present, e.g. for 1, 2, 3, 4 and 10,000 the mean is 2002 but the median is 3. In a normal distribution mean, median and mode are equal and half the values lie on each side of the mean.

front: What is standard deviation and how is it calculated?
back: A measure of how widely values are spread around the mean; a small SD means values cluster near the mean. Steps: find the mean; find each deviation from it; square and sum the deviations; divide by n - 1 to get the variance; take the square root. In a normal distribution, mean plus or minus 1 SD covers about 68% and plus or minus 2 SD about 95% of values. SD is also used to derive the standard error and to plan sample size.

front: Why is the sample variance divided by n - 1 rather than n?
back: Dividing by n - 1 makes the sample variance an unbiased estimate of the population variance: averaged over all possible samples it equals the population value, whereas dividing by n underestimates it.

front: Distinguish standard deviation from standard error of the mean.
back: SD describes the spread of individual observations in one sample. The standard error of the mean (SEM) is the SD of the sampling distribution of means, i.e. how much sample means scatter around the population mean. SEM = SD divided by the square root of n, so it shrinks as sample size grows.

front: Define prevalence. How do point and period prevalence differ?
back: Prevalence is the proportion of a population with a condition at a given time: all existing cases (old and new) divided by the population. It is cross-sectional. Point prevalence uses the population at one moment; period prevalence uses the average or mid-period population over a defined interval and is mainly used for chronic disease, insurance and hospital statistics.

front: Distinguish incidence proportion (cumulative incidence) from incidence rate (incidence density).
back: Both count only new cases. Incidence proportion = new cases during a stated period divided by the number initially at risk; it is a risk (0 to 1), needs a closed cohort and a stated follow-up time. Incidence rate = new cases divided by person-time at risk (e.g. per 1000 person-years); it is a rate (0 to infinity) and can be measured in an open population.

front: What is an odds ratio, how is it calculated and interpreted?
back: The odds of exposure among cases divided by the odds of exposure among controls; from a 2x2 table (a, b = exposed cases, controls; c, d = unexposed cases, controls), OR = (a/c)/(b/d) = ad/bc. It is the measure of association in case-control studies. OR = 1: no association; above 1: exposure linked to the outcome; below 1: possibly protective. It needs no population denominator, but association does not prove causation.

front: What is relative risk and from which study design is it obtained?
back: Risk of the outcome in the exposed divided by risk in the unexposed: [a/(a+b)] / [c/(c+d)]. It needs incidence, so it comes from cohort studies, not case-control studies. RR = 1: no effect; above 1: exposure raises risk; below 1: exposure lowers risk. It is a descriptive measure and does not by itself test significance.

front: Complete: when the odds ratio approximates relative risk
text: In case-control and cohort studies the odds ratio approximates the relative risk when the outcome occurs in less than {{10%}} of the unexposed (i.e. a {{rare}} outcome); when the outcome is commoner, the OR {{overestimates}} the RR.

front: What is the number needed to treat (NNT), and why is it more informative than relative risk reduction?
back: The number of patients who must be treated for one to show a defined effect, beneficial or harmful. It reflects baseline severity: a drug that halves mortality from 50% to 25% has an NNT of 4, while one that halves mortality from 5% to 2.5% has an NNT of 40, so 40 patients face adverse-effect risk for each life saved. NNTs for benefit and for minor or major harm can be set side by side to guide choice.

front: What is a P value, and how are P values conventionally interpreted?
back: The probability, calculated from the test statistic, of getting the observed result if the null hypothesis were true. It is compared with a significance level (alpha) chosen in advance, usually 5% (also 1% or 0.1%); P below alpha leads to rejecting the null hypothesis. Rough guide: P > 0.10 no evidence against the null; 0.05-0.10 weak; 0.01-0.05 moderate; 0.001-0.01 strong; < 0.001 very strong.

front: Distinguish the null hypothesis, alternative hypothesis and research hypothesis.
back: Null hypothesis (H0): no difference between a sample and the population, or between samples; it can be rejected but never proved. Alternative hypothesis (H1): there is a difference (greater, smaller or simply different). Research hypothesis: a specific, clear, predictive and testable statement about the expected outcome based on background knowledge.

front: What does a 95% confidence interval mean, and why is it reported alongside the P value?
back: For a large sample, mean plus or minus 1.96 SE gives a range expected to contain the population mean in 95% of samples; values outside it would occur by chance only 5% of the time. Unlike a P value alone, a CI shows the direction and size of the effect and its precision. In a forest plot a study whose CI crosses the line of no effect is not statistically significant.

front: When is the t test used instead of the Z test, and what are its requirements?
back: Both test whether two means differ more than chance allows. For small samples (n < 30) Z values do not follow the normal distribution, so Student's t test (W.S. Gosset, pen-name "Student") is used, with probability read from the t table at the right degrees of freedom. Requirements: random sample, quantitative data, normally distributed variable.

text: The {{unpaired}} (independent) t test compares means of two separate groups, df = {{n1 + n2 - 2}}; the {{paired}} t test compares before-and-after values in the same subjects, df = {{n - 1}}; the {{one-sample}} t test compares a sample mean with a known or hypothesised population mean.

front: When is ANOVA used, what are its assumptions, and what statistic does it give?
back: To compare means of more than two groups, where repeated t tests become unreliable (for two groups it gives the same result as the t test). Assumptions: each group from a normal population, equal variances, independent samples, random independent observations. It splits total sum of squares into between- and within-group parts and gives the F ratio (between-group mean square divided by within-group mean square), read from the F table.

text: {{One-way}} ANOVA tests one factor with three or more levels; {{two-way}} ANOVA tests two factors and their interaction (equal numbers per cell needed); {{factorial}} ANOVA (e.g. 2x2 design) studies several factors and their interactions in one experiment; {{repeated measures}} ANOVA compares related means, e.g. the same patients at three time points, extending the paired t test.

back: Parametric tests assume a normal distribution, equal variances, interval or ratio data and independence, and use the mean; they have more power. Non-parametric (distribution-free) tests suit ordinal or nominal data, small samples or non-normal data, use the median and resist outliers, but have lower power, so type II error is more likely. Data that violate normality should be analysed non-parametrically.

front: Define meta-analysis and outline how one is done.
back: Statistical analysis of results from many studies to integrate their findings (Glass, 1976); a quantitative alternative to a narrative review. Steps: frame the question as PICO(T); search databases and grey literature (e.g. MEDLINE, EMBASE, theses, congress abstracts); screen abstracts and full papers against inclusion criteria; extract data and assess study quality; compute effect sizes; examine their spread and moderators; interpret and report.

front: What are the strengths and weaknesses of meta-analysis?
back: Strengths: greater power and precision from pooled data, resolves conflicting trials, quantifies inconsistency, allows subgroup analysis, and pooled RCTs give the highest level of evidence. Weaknesses: selective reporting and publication bias (negative studies are less often published), double counting of the same data, heterogeneity of populations, time-consuming search and complex statistics.

Diamond: centre = pooled estimate, width = its 95% CI; touching the no-effect line = overall result not significant

front: What is evidence-based medicine (EBM), and how is the evidence obtained?
back: Using the best available research evidence, after critical appraisal, together with the doctor's clinical skill and the patient's preferences to make care decisions. It aims to improve outcomes, reduce harm, improve cost-effectiveness and support shared decisions. Evidence is found by literature search (e.g. the TRIP database) and synthesised by systematic reviews and meta-analysis.

front: Classify: methods of random allocation and sampling
text: Methods include {{simple}} (lottery or random numbers), {{systematic}} (every kth unit), {{stratified}} (random within homogeneous strata), {{multistage}} (random at successive levels, e.g. district then village), {{cluster}} (natural groups such as villages), {{multiphase}} (sub-samples of a sample), {{block}} (equal numbers per block), unequal and {{minimisation}}.

front: What does randomisation achieve, and what are the criteria of a good method?
back: It removes selection bias (with allocation concealment), balances known and unknown covariates between arms, and provides the basis for statistical tests. A good method is unpredictable (each participant has the same chance of any arm), produces balanced groups, and is simple to use.

front: How do block randomisation and minimisation keep groups balanced?
back: Block randomisation assigns equal numbers to each arm within small blocks (e.g. AABB, ABAB in blocks of 4), so groups stay equal in size even if the trial stops early; with fixed blocks, staff may predict the next allocation. Minimisation assigns each new patient to the arm that best reduces imbalance in key factors (e.g. sex, age, disease stage) and suits very small trials (about 50 patients).

front: How is cluster sampling used to estimate immunisation coverage?
back: Natural groups such as villages are listed with their populations; 30 clusters are chosen systematically by a sampling interval and random start. In each, houses are surveyed from a random first house until 7 eligible children are found, giving 210 children. Cluster sampling is cheaper and quicker but has higher sampling error and may miss diversity.

front: Which pairs of central value and spread does a results section use?
back: Mean with standard deviation or standard error, or median with interquartile range.

front: What does a Kaplan-Meier plot show in the rizatriptan example?
back: The probability of relief from migraine pain, plotted against hours after dosing, for 10 mg rizatriptan and for placebo, so the two groups can be compared over time.

front: How do glucocorticoids produce their slow, gene-mediated effects?
back: The steroid enters the cell and binds a high-affinity cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor. The activated complex moves into the nucleus, binds glucocorticoid response elements and alters transcription, so protein synthesis changes. This takes roughly 30 to 60 minutes, and the effects last longer than the drug because the proteins it switches on persist. A few fast actions, such as suppression of ACTH release, may work through membrane receptors instead.

front: Compare hydrocortisone with prednisolone for duration and glucocorticoid potency.
back: Hydrocortisone is short acting and has glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity of roughly equal strength, so it is also the replacement drug in adrenal insufficiency. Prednisolone is about four times as potent as a glucocorticoid and has an intermediate duration, which makes it suitable for alternate-day or single-morning dosing.

front: Which oral doses are roughly equal in anti-inflammatory effect to 20 mg of hydrocortisone?
back: Prednisolone 5 mg, methylprednisolone 4 mg, triamcinolone 4 mg, deflazacort 6 mg, and dexamethasone or betamethasone 0.75 mg. Relative to hydrocortisone, dexamethasone and betamethasone are about 25 times as potent as anti-inflammatory agents and have practically no salt-retaining action.

front: Why is DOCA not given by mouth, and what is it used for?
back: DOCA is almost purely mineralocorticoid, but it is not effective when swallowed, so it is given sublingually or by intramuscular injection. It is used occasionally for replacement in Addison's disease.

It is an orally active, potent mineralocorticoid with some glucocorticoid action. Uses: replacement in Addison's disease when sodium is still being lost, salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and idiopathic postural hypotension.

front: What is the first-line emergency treatment for acute adrenal insufficiency?
back: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV as a bolus, then given by continuous infusion (KDT: about 100 mg every 8 hours; GG14: 50 to 100 mg every 8 hours). IV isotonic saline with glucose is given, with the volume guided by central venous pressure because these patients handle a water load poorly; a short vasopressor infusion may be needed. Dexamethasone is an alternative (KDT gives 8 to 16 mg IV; GG14 suggests 4 mg when the diagnosis is not yet confirmed, because it does not interfere with the cortisol assay). The precipitating cause (infection, trauma, haemorrhage) must be treated.

front: Why are dexamethasone or betamethasone preferred over prednisolone in cerebral oedema?
back: They have little sodium-retaining activity, so they do not worsen fluid retention when brain swelling must be controlled. Corticosteroids are also useful in oedema from tumours and in tubercular meningitis.

front: What antenatal steroid regimen is used when preterm delivery is expected, and why?
back: Betamethasone 12 mg IM, two doses 18 to 24 hours apart (KDT: betamethasone or dexamethasone 12 mg IM, two doses 24 hours apart), when delivery is expected before 34 weeks. Glucocorticoids speed fetal lung maturation and surfactant production, so respiratory distress syndrome and neonatal death fall. These two steroids are chosen because they cross the placenta well (less maternal protein binding and placental metabolism than cortisol).

front: What is the current role of corticosteroids in septic shock?
back: High-dose corticosteroid therapy for septic shock has been abandoned because it worsens outcome. Low-dose hydrocortisone (100 mg every 8 hours as an IV infusion for 5 to 7 days) is used in patients with relative adrenal insufficiency who respond poorly to fluids and vasopressors. GG14 describes this state as critical illness-related cortisol insufficiency, treated with hydrocortisone 50 to 100 mg every 6 hours or a 10 mg/hour infusion.

front: How does metyrapone work, and how is it used diagnostically?
back: Metyrapone blocks 11-beta-hydroxylase in the adrenal cortex, so cortisol synthesis falls. Pituitary ACTH output rises, and 11-deoxycortisol accumulates and is excreted in urine. The response is used to test whether the pituitary can mount an ACTH response. Related enzyme inhibitors such as ketoconazole are also tried in Cushing's disease when surgery is not an option.

Deflazacort is a slightly less potent glucocorticoid than prednisolone (6 mg is roughly 5 mg prednisolone) and lacks mineralocorticoid activity. It is claimed to cause fewer adverse effects, but this may simply reflect its lower potency. Some trials found less growth retardation in children, so it has been recommended for paediatric patients. It is used mainly for inflammatory and immunological disorders.

front: Which enzyme converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, and why does DHT matter?
back: 5-alpha reductase converts testosterone to DHT, which binds the androgen receptor more tightly. DHT mediates androgen action on the external genitalia, prostate, genital skin and hair follicles, while testosterone itself mediates feedback inhibition of LH, effects on muscle, erythropoiesis and spermatogenesis. Type 2 5-alpha reductase predominates in the urogenital tract and genital skin, which is why finasteride (mainly type 2) shrinks the prostate.

front: Why is free testosterone not given orally or as a simple injection?
back: Oral testosterone is inactivated by first-pass hepatic metabolism, and a plain intramuscular dose lasts only minutes to hours. Slowly released esters given intramuscularly last weeks, and oral testosterone undecanoate is absorbed through lymphatics, bypassing the liver.

front: Which androgens cause cholestatic jaundice, and why are injectable esters preferred?
back: The 17-alkyl derivatives such as methyltestosterone, fluoxymesterone, oxymetholone and stanozolol cause dose-related cholestatic jaundice, which reverses when the drug is stopped. Parenteral testosterone esters do not cause this, so they are preferred for long-term replacement.

front: How does cyproterone acetate reduce androgen action, and what is it used for?
back: It is a weak androgen receptor blocker related to progesterone. Its progestational action suppresses LH, which lowers testosterone and adds to the direct antiandrogen effect. Uses include precocious puberty, inappropriate sexual behaviour in men, and acne or hirsutism in women, given with an estrogen. Hepatotoxicity limits its use.

front: Why is flutamide given together with a GnRH agonist in metastatic prostate cancer?
back: Flutamide is a nonsteroidal androgen receptor blocker, but blocking feedback raises LH and testosterone, which partly offsets it, so monotherapy is poor. It is therefore used with a GnRH agonist or after orchidectomy (combined androgen blockade). KDT advises starting it about 3 days before the agonist to block the initial testosterone flare. Its main toxicity is hepatic; gynaecomastia and breast tenderness are common, while libido and potency are largely preserved. Bicalutamide is now preferred: once daily and less hepatotoxic.

front: What does finasteride do, and how is it used?
back: It is a competitive inhibitor of 5-alpha reductase, mainly type 2, which lowers DHT in the prostate. It shrinks the prostate and improves urinary flow in benign prostatic hyperplasia, but benefit takes about 6 months. It works best in large glands, and 1 mg daily can help male-pattern baldness. Typical side effects are reduced libido, impotence and lower ejaculate volume.

front: Complete the note on anabolic steroids.
text: Anabolic steroids include {{nandrolone}}, {{oxymetholone}}, {{stanozolol}} and {{methandienone}}. Their anabolic selectivity is only modest, and the 17-alkyl ones, such as oxymetholone and stanozolol, can cause {{cholestatic jaundice}} and adverse lipid changes.

front: Complete the note on PDE-5 inhibitors.
text: The PDE-5 inhibitors used for erectile dysfunction are {{sildenafil}}, {{tadalafil}} and {{vardenafil}}. Of these, {{tadalafil}} has the longest action (half-life about 18 hours), so nitrates are contraindicated for up to {{3 days}} after it, and {{vardenafil}} can prolong the QT interval.

front: Classify the antiandrogens and related agents.
text: {{Cyproterone acetate}} is a progesterone-related steroid antagonist; {{flutamide}} and {{bicalutamide}} are nonsteroidal androgen receptor blockers; {{finasteride}} inhibits 5-alpha reductase type 2; {{GnRH agonists}} suppress gonadal androgen output.

front: How do estrogens act at the cell level?
back: Estradiol binds nuclear estrogen receptors, ERalpha and ERbeta. The receptor dimerises, binds estrogen response elements and changes gene transcription with the help of coactivators or corepressors. ERalpha predominates in uterus, breast, bone and blood vessels, while ERbeta predominates in the prostate and ovary. Some rapid membrane-initiated effects also exist.

front: Why is ethinylestradiol used by mouth when natural estradiol is not?
back: Natural estrogens are inactivated by rapid first-pass metabolism in the liver, so oral estradiol is weak and short acting. Ethinylestradiol is metabolised slowly, so it is orally active and more potent, which is why it is used in oral contraceptives and oral hormone therapy.

front: What is the usual cyclical oral HRT regimen for a woman with an intact uterus?
back: Conjugated estrogens 0.625 mg daily for 3 weeks, then 1 week off. A progestin is added for the last 10 to 12 days of each cycle to protect the endometrium from hyperplasia and carcinoma. Lower estrogen doses of about 0.3 to 0.45 mg are also used now. In women without a uterus, estrogen is given alone.

front: What effects do estrogens have on clotting and lipids?
back: They increase synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and lower PAI-1, which raises the thrombotic tendency despite increased fibrinolysis. They lower LDL and raise HDL and triglycerides. They also raise SHBG, TBG and CBG levels in the liver.

front: How does clomiphene induce ovulation, and what are its main adverse effects?
back: It blocks estrogen negative feedback on the pituitary, so more LH and FSH is released with each pulse; the ovaries enlarge and ovulate if they can respond. Course: 50 mg daily for 5 days from cycle day 5, monthly; if no conception after 1 to 2 cycles the dose may be doubled, and no more than 6 cycles are tried. Adverse effects: polycystic ovaries, multiple pregnancy, hot flushes, gastric upset and vertigo. GG14: letrozole gives a higher pregnancy and live-birth rate than clomiphene in PCOS; KDT notes India banned letrozole for ovulation induction in 2011.

front: Why is tamoxifen called a SERM, and where does it act as an agonist?
back: It is an estrogen antagonist in breast tissue and blood vessels, but a partial agonist in uterus, bone, liver and pituitary. Its antiestrogenic action inhibits breast cancer cells and causes hot flushes; its agonist action stimulates the endometrium (hyperplasia, carcinoma risk), improves bone density, lowers LDL and raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis 2 to 3 fold.

front: What is the tissue profile of raloxifene, and what is it used for?
back: It is an estrogen agonist in bone and lipid metabolism, but an antagonist in breast and endometrium. It prevents postmenopausal bone loss and vertebral fracture and reduces the risk of ER-positive breast cancer. It does not relieve hot flushes, and it raises the risk of venous thrombosis.

front: Why are aromatase inhibitors not used in premenopausal women with functioning ovaries?
back: They block estrogen synthesis from androgens, but functioning ovaries keep making estrogen, so the block is incomplete. They are used in premenopausal women only after ovarian removal or with GnRH suppression. In postmenopausal women, extraglandular aromatisation is the main estrogen source, so they nearly abolish estrogen.

front: What is the textbook mifepristone and misoprostol regimen for medical termination of early pregnancy?
back: Mifepristone 600 mg as a single oral dose, followed 48 hours later by misoprostol 400 microgram orally, up to 7 weeks (49 days from the last menstrual period). This gives over 90 percent complete abortion; mifepristone alone gives 60 to 85 percent. Indian kits give mifepristone as three 200 mg tablets on day 1 and misoprostol as two 200 microgram tablets on day 3. Problems: prolonged bleeding and failed abortion; also cramps, nausea and loose stools.

front: What is the dose and time window for ulipristal as emergency contraception?
back: Ulipristal 30 mg as a single oral dose, taken within 120 hours of unprotected intercourse. It is as effective as levonorgestrel when taken within 72 hours and more effective than levonorgestrel from 72 to 120 hours. It is a selective progesterone receptor modulator.

front: What is the mechanism of danazol?
back: Danazol is an orally active ethisterone derivative with weak androgenic, anabolic, progestational and glucocorticoid activity. Its main action is suppression of the mid-cycle gonadotropin surge, so ovarian or testicular function falls; it also directly inhibits steroidogenic enzymes (not aromatase). As a 17-alkylated steroid it raises C1 esterase inhibitor levels, so it prevents hereditary angioedema attacks. Other uses: endometriosis (now second line because of androgenic and hepatic adverse effects), menorrhagia and fibrocystic breast disease.

front: Why are desogestrel and gestodene preferred in some combined pills?
back: They are potent gonane progestins with strong antiovulatory action and little or no androgenic activity. Because they are potent, the ethinylestradiol dose in the pill can be reduced. Because they are weakly androgenic, they do not oppose estrogen's favourable effect on the lipid profile, so they are preferred in women with hyperandrogenism. Desogestrel and norgestimate are prodrugs.

Androgenic 19-nortestosterone types lower HDL

front: Classify the selective estrogen receptor agents.
text: Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) include {{tamoxifen}}, {{raloxifene}} and {{toremifene}}. {{Fulvestrant}} is a pure antagonist that down-regulates the estrogen receptor, so it is called a selective estrogen receptor down-regulator (SERD).
Nonsteroidal, reversible: {{letrozole}} and {{anastrozole}}. Steroidal, irreversible (suicide substrate): {{exemestane}}.

front: Complete the note on drug interactions with oral contraceptives.
text: Enzyme inducers such as {{rifampicin}}, {{phenytoin}}, {{phenobarbitone}} and {{carbamazepine}} speed the metabolism of contraceptive steroids and can cause contraceptive failure. The woman should switch to a pill containing {{50 microgram}} ethinylestradiol or use {{another method}} of contraception.

front: Complete the note on long-acting progestin injectables.
text: Depot {{medroxyprogesterone acetate}} 150 mg is given intramuscularly every {{3 months}}; {{norethisterone enanthate}} 200 mg is given every {{2 months}}. The main drawback is disruption of menstrual bleeding or total {{amenorrhoea}}, and return of fertility after stopping is {{delayed by several months}}.

front: How do oxytocin and vasopressin differ?
back: Both are nine-amino-acid peptides made in the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior pituitary, and they differ at positions 3 and 8. Oxytocin acts mainly on the uterus and breast, while vasopressin mainly controls water excretion. Very high doses of oxytocin can show some antidiuretic effect.

front: How does oxytocin stimulate the uterus, and what changes its sensitivity?
back: It acts on G-protein-coupled receptors on the myometrium, raising intracellular calcium through depolarisation and IP3-mediated release. It also stimulates prostaglandin release from the endometrium. Estrogens increase receptor numbers, so sensitivity rises toward term and falls after delivery. Progestins reduce it.

front: Which conditions must be checked before starting an oxytocin infusion for induction of labour?
back: Correct presentation, mature fetal lungs, no cephalopelvic disproportion, no placenta praevia, no fetal distress, and no previous uterine scar. The infusion is started slowly and titrated to the response, with contractions monitored closely, and it is stopped once contractions are strong enough.

front: What serious adverse effect of oxytocin is linked to its antidiuretic action?
back: Water intoxication, which can be fatal. It occurs when large doses are given with intravenous fluids, especially in toxaemia of pregnancy and renal insufficiency. Over-strong uterine contractions from injudicious use can also cause uterine rupture and fetal asphyxia.

front: How are ergometrine and methylergometrine used to control postpartum haemorrhage?
back: Give 0.2 to 0.3 mg IM at delivery of the anterior shoulder to prevent PPH in women prone to bleed (for example grand multipara, uterine inertia), or 0.5 mg IV if PPH is occurring; in severe bleeding 0.5 mg can be combined with oxytocin 5 IU. Routine use in all deliveries is not justified, and multiple pregnancy must be excluded first. GG14 describes oxytocin 10 units IM immediately after delivery as the standard measure to keep the uterus contracted.

front: In which conditions should ergometrine be avoided?
back: Hypertension, toxaemia, vascular or cardiovascular disease, sepsis (risk of gangrene), liver or kidney disease, and in pregnancy before the third stage of labour. In hypertensive women, oxytocin is the preferred uterotonic.

front: What are the obstetric uses of prostaglandins?
back: PGE2, PGF2alpha and 15-methyl PGF2alpha are potent uterine stimulants, especially late in pregnancy, and they also soften the cervix. Misoprostol, a PG analogue with fewer side effects, is increasingly used for obstetric indications such as cervical ripening and induction.

Likely to work only if cervix is under 4 cm and the lower segment is barely taken up

Uterotonics give sustained contraction that compresses the vessels running through the myometrial mesh

Preferred in hypertensive women, in whom ergometrine is contraindicated
0.2 to 0.3 mg IM at delivery of the anterior shoulder; 0.5 mg IV if PPH is occurring
Methylergometrine is more potent on the uterus with milder other actions

front: Complete the note on ergot alkaloids in obstetrics.
text: Ergometrine and methylergometrine raise the force, rate and duration of uterine contraction, and high doses can cause {{contracture}}. Ergometrine given for many days after delivery can reduce milk through {{dopaminergic inhibition of prolactin release}}.

front: Complete the note on oxytocin pharmacokinetics.
text: Oxytocin is inactive by mouth and is given IM or IV. It is broken down by {{oxytocinase}} from the placenta, with a plasma half-life of about {{6 to 12 minutes}}. {{Carbetocin}} is a long-acting analogue used to prevent uterine atony after caesarean section.

Beta-2 agonists: {{ritodrine}}, {{salbutamol}}, {{terbutaline}}. Calcium channel blocker: {{nifedipine}}. Oxytocin receptor antagonist: {{atosiban}}. {{Magnesium sulfate}} also relaxes the uterus but is no longer recommended for this purpose. COX inhibitors such as {{indomethacin}} are used off-label (GG14), while KDT lists them among unreliable uterine depressants.

front: How does tadalafil differ from sildenafil?
back: Tadalafil is more potent and longer acting: half-life about 18 hours and duration 24 to 36 hours, with peak levels at 30 to 120 minutes, so onset may be slower. Because of its long action, nitrates are contraindicated for up to 3 days after it (GG14: more than 24 hours, especially with tadalafil). It has lower PDE-6 affinity, so visual disturbance is less frequent, but it can cause back pain. Dose: 10 mg at least 30 minutes before intercourse (maximum 20 mg). It is also approved for pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Also has antiglucocorticoid and antiandrogenic activity
Follicular phase: blunts the mid-cycle gonadotropin surge and delays ovulation

Termination of pregnancy up to 7 weeks: 600 mg, then misoprostol 400 microgram 48 hours later

Avoid in women on long-term glucocorticoids

front: Which newer drugs block androgen action in advanced prostate cancer, and how?
back: GnRH antagonists (degarelix by injection; relugolix orally) cut LH, FSH and testosterone quickly without the initial testosterone surge seen with GnRH agonists. Abiraterone acetate inhibits CYP17A1, blocking the synthesis of androgen precursors, and is given with prednisone. Enzalutamide, apalutamide and darolutamide are second-generation nonsteroidal androgen receptor antagonists; enzalutamide binds the receptor 5 to 8 times more tightly than older antiandrogens, and the bound receptor interacts poorly with coactivators and androgen response elements on DNA. These are used with androgen deprivation in metastatic and castration-resistant prostate cancer.

front: How does isoniazid act, and why is it selective for mycobacteria?
back: It is a prodrug activated inside the bacillus by the catalase-peroxidase KatG. The activated form binds NAD and blocks InhA and KasA, stopping mycolic acid synthesis in the cell wall. Human cells lack this activation step, so the drug is selective. A second adduct inhibits mycobacterial DHFR and disrupts DNA synthesis.

front: How does rifampicin kill mycobacteria, and why is it selective?
back: It binds the beta subunit of the bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (the rpoB gene product) and blocks chain elongation. Mammalian RNA polymerase binds it poorly, which gives selectivity. Resistance is almost always an rpoB mutation.

front: Why is pyrazinamide useful despite being a weak drug, and how does it act?
back: Bacterial pyrazinamidase (pncA) converts it to pyrazinoic acid, which accumulates in an acidic environment. Its activity at acidic pH suits intracellular bacilli and inflamed sites, so it gives sterilising activity and allows the course to be shortened. It is most useful in the first 2 months.

front: What does ethambutol inhibit, which gene mutation causes resistance, and why is it given?
back: It inhibits arabinosyl transferases (embAB) that make arabinogalactan, so mycolic acids cannot be incorporated into the cell wall. Resistance develops slowly, mostly through embB mutation. It is bacteriostatic; its main role is to prevent resistance when added to RHZ.

front: Classify: the five first-line anti-TB drugs and their activity.
text: The first-line drugs are {{isoniazid}}, {{rifampicin}}, {{pyrazinamide}}, {{ethambutol}} and {{streptomycin}}. Isoniazid and rifampicin are the most potent {{bactericidal}} drugs, {{ethambutol}} is {{bacteriostatic}}, and streptomycin acts only on {{extracellular}} bacilli.

Blocks mycolic acid synthesis (InhA, KasA)
Selective: no activity against other organisms
Completely absorbed; penetrates cavities, placenta and meninges

front: Why does isoniazid acetylator status matter?
back: INH is acetylated by NAT2. Fast acetylators (about 30 to 40 percent of Indians) clear it in about 1 hour; slow acetylators (60 to 70 percent) take about 3 hours. Daily dosing works in both groups, but twice-weekly regimens are less effective in fast acetylators. Slow acetylators get peripheral neuritis more often.

front: Isoniazid neurotoxicity: cause, prophylaxis and treatment?
back: It interferes with formation of active pyridoxal phosphate and increases urinary loss of pyridoxine. Prophylaxis is pyridoxine 10 mg/day, and it is essential in diabetics, alcoholics, malnourished, pregnant, lactating and HIV-infected patients and with high-dose INH. Treatment is pyridoxine 100 mg/day.

front: Rifampicin: main adverse effects and the harmless finding patients notice first
back: Orange-red urine, sweat, tears and secretions, which is harmless. Flushing, pruritus, rash, flu-like symptoms and GI upset, commoner with intermittent dosing. Hepatitis is dose-related, rare below 600 mg/day, and worse in pre-existing liver disease. Rarely purpura, haemolysis, shock or renal failure.

front: Why does rifampicin lower the levels of other drugs?
back: It induces microsomal CYP450 enzymes (CYP3A4, CYP2C, CYP2D6, CYP1A2), speeding up its own metabolism (AUC down about 35 percent) and that of warfarin, oral contraceptives, corticosteroids, sulfonylureas, HIV protease inhibitors, NNRTIs, theophylline, metoprolol, azoles, clarithromycin and phenytoin. Contraceptive failure has occurred; use a pill with 50 mcg estrogen or another method.

front: Which drugs' levels rise with isoniazid, and what lowers isoniazid levels?
back: INH inhibits CYP2C19 and CYP3A4, raising phenytoin, carbamazepine, diazepam, theophylline and warfarin. Aluminium hydroxide reduces its absorption. PAS competes for acetylation and prolongs its half-life. Rifampicin counteracts INH's inhibition, but the net effect on many drugs is unpredictable.

front: Ethambutol: main toxicity, monitoring and what to do
back: Retrobulbar neuritis: loss of visual acuity and colour vision, and central field defects. It is dose- and duration-dependent and largely reversible if stopped early. Patients must report any visual change at once; young children may not report it, so monitor them carefully. Stop at the first sign of optic neuritis, and use with caution in renal disease.

front: Pyrazinamide: main toxicities, contraindication and dose limit
back: Dose-related hepatotoxicity, so the daily dose is limited to 25 to 30 mg/kg (less common in Indians than in Western patients). Contraindicated in liver disease. Hyperuricaemia from reduced renal urate secretion can cause gout. Also abdominal upset, arthralgia, and it can disturb glucose control in diabetics. It is now considered safe in pregnancy.

front: Which fluoroquinolone is most active against M. tuberculosis, and why is its use restricted?
back: Moxifloxacin is most active, followed by levofloxacin, ofloxacin and ciprofloxacin. They are oral bactericidal drugs that also kill bacilli inside macrophages. Use is restricted to drug-resistant TB to preserve them. Used alone they select resistance quickly by gyrase mutation, although resistance to moxifloxacin develops more slowly.

A D-alanine analogue. It blocks the enzymes that make D-alanine and join two D-alanine residues, so cell wall peptide cross-linking fails. Toxicity is mainly neuropsychiatric (sleepiness, headache, tremor, psychosis, with seizures less often). Give pyridoxine 100 mg/day. Contraindicated in mental illness or seizure disorders.

front: Classify: WHO grouping of drugs for MDR/RR-TB regimens (GG14), and the older grouping
text: Group A (include all three): {{levofloxacin or moxifloxacin}}, {{bedaquiline}} and {{linezolid}}. Group B (add both): {{clofazimine}} and {{cycloserine or terizidone}}. Group C (to complete the regimen when A and B drugs cannot be used): {{ethambutol}}, {{delamanid}}, {{pyrazinamide}}, meropenem with amoxicillin-clavulanate, {{amikacin}}, ethionamide or prothionamide, and PAS. The older RNTCP grouping in KDT put first-line oral drugs in group I, {{injectables}} in group II, fluoroquinolones in group III and bacteriostatic oral drugs in group IV.

front: Bedaquiline: mechanism and why it is selective
back: A diarylquinoline that inhibits subunit c of mycobacterial ATP synthase, cutting the bacillus's energy supply. Human ATP synthase is far less sensitive, which gives selectivity. It kills both multiplying and dormant bacilli. Resistance arises from ATP synthase mutation or from efflux pump mutations; GG14 notes that efflux-based resistance gives cross-resistance with clofazimine. WHO now classes it as a Group A drug for MDR-TB.

front: Bedaquiline: adverse effects and why background drugs must continue after it stops
back: Nausea, headache, arthralgia, QTc prolongation (caution with other QT-prolonging drugs) and potential hepatotoxicity. It accumulates in tissues and has a terminal half-life of about 5.5 months, so it persists for months after stopping. KDT therefore stresses continuing the background drugs to the end of the course, so that surviving bacilli are not left exposed to bedaquiline alone.

front: Bedaquiline dosing in pulmonary MDR-TB (as licensed)
text: 400 mg daily for {{2 weeks}}, then 200 mg {{three times a week}} for {{22 weeks}}. Maximum course {{24 weeks}}, with each tablet swallowed whole with meals. Use only in adults over 18 who are not pregnant, with at least 3 active background drugs.

front: Linezolid in drug-resistant TB: role, dose in the book regimen and key toxicities
back: The RNTCP XDR-TB regimen in KDT lists linezolid 600 mg daily for adults of 46 to 70 kg. GG14 states that WHO now classes linezolid as a Group A drug for MDR-TB and that it is part of the 6-month bedaquiline + pretomanid + linezolid regimen approved for XDR-TB, although adverse effects are frequent. It inhibits bacterial protein synthesis at the 50S ribosome. Main toxicities are bone marrow suppression, peripheral and optic neuropathy and lactic acidosis, so blood counts and vision are monitored.

front: Regimen for new drug-sensitive pulmonary TB (RNTCP 2016 in KDT, and GG14)
text: Intensive phase: {{2 months}} of daily HRZE. Continuation phase: {{4 months}} of daily HRE under RNTCP 2016 (GG14 gives daily HR). Total duration: {{6 months}}. GG14 notes that {{daily}} dosing is preferred over intermittent dosing because it gives the best chance of cure without relapse.

front: Regimen for previously treated pulmonary TB, presumed drug-sensitive (RNTCP 2016).

front: Standard RNTCP regimen for MDR-TB (2016), and how WHO practice has changed
text: RNTCP 2016 intensive phase (6 to 9 months): {{kanamycin}}, {{levofloxacin}}, {{ethionamide}}, {{cycloserine}}, {{pyrazinamide}} and {{ethambutol}}. Continuation phase ({{18 months}}): levofloxacin, ethionamide, cycloserine and ethambutol, with {{pyridoxine}} throughout. GG14: injectable agents (kanamycin, amikacin, capreomycin) have now largely been {{phased out}}, and WHO builds MDR-TB regimens from Group A, B and C drugs given for 18 to 20 months.

front: Rifampicin-resistant TB with isoniazid sensitivity: how is it treated?
back: It is managed as MDR-TB, with isoniazid added to both phases without changing the duration or the other drugs. The intensive phase (6 months) has seven drugs: kanamycin, levofloxacin, ethionamide, cycloserine, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and isoniazid. The continuation phase (18 months) has five: levofloxacin, ethionamide, cycloserine, ethambutol and isoniazid.

front: Low-level versus high-level isoniazid resistance: when is high-dose INH used?
back: Low-level resistance (on LC-DST) or inhA mutation can be overcome with high-dose INH: 900 mg/day for 46 to 70 kg body weight, with pyridoxine. High-level resistance, or resistance from a katG mutation, makes INH ineffective, so it must not be given.

front: Initial regimens for mono-drug and poly-drug resistant TB (RNTCP 2016)
back: Mono-resistant (not rifampicin): rifampicin, two susceptible first-line drugs, one injectable second-line drug and one fluoroquinolone, daily for 3 to 6 months. Poly-resistant: rifampicin, an injectable, a fluoroquinolone, a susceptible first-line drug and one oral second-line drug (ethionamide, cycloserine or PAS). Both: stop the injectable after the intensive phase and give four oral drugs for 6 more months, for a total of 9 to 12 months.

front: TB in pregnancy: which drugs are safe and what supplement is needed?
text: {{Isoniazid}}, {{rifampicin}}, {{ethambutol}} and {{pyrazinamide}} are considered safe, so the standard 6-month regimen is given in full and treatment is not delayed. {{Streptomycin}} is contraindicated because it is ototoxic to the foetus. Pregnant women on INH take {{pyridoxine 10 to 25 mg/day}}.

front: When are corticosteroids used in TB, and when are they contraindicated?
back: Not routinely. Used only under effective chemotherapy cover: in severe or miliary TB (to buy time), for drug hypersensitivity, and in meningeal, renal or pericardial TB or pleural effusion (to reduce exudation and adhesions). GG14 calls steroids standard care in TB meningitis; in TB pericarditis a large trial showed no overall benefit on the main outcome, though constrictive pericarditis was reduced. Contraindicated in intestinal TB because of the risk of silent perforation. Taper once the patient improves.

front: Anti-TB drug hepatitis: what is the first step?
back: Stop all anti-TB drugs and let the reaction subside. Isoniazid, rifampicin or pyrazinamide (one or more) are the usual culprits, and combination therapy raises the risk. If TB is severe, start streptomycin, ethambutol and one fluoroquinolone (all non-hepatotoxic) while the liver recovers.

Stop the last-added drug permanently and rebuild the regimen

front: Dapsone: mechanism and why it is selective for M. leprae
back: It is a sulfone that blocks folate synthase, so PABA cannot be used to make folic acid; PABA reverses its action. The folate synthase of M. leprae binds dapsone with much higher affinity than that of most other bacteria, so it works at very low leprostatic levels. Doses needed for pyogenic infections are too toxic to use.

front: Dapsone resistance: primary versus secondary, and why dapsone still works
back: Primary resistance is found in a patient never treated with dapsone, meaning the infection came from a resistant source. Secondary resistance develops during monotherapy, in up to about 20 percent of patients. Mutated folate synthase has lower affinity. Peak serum levels still exceed the MIC by about 500 times, so relapse from resistance is only about 2 to 3 percent. Dormant persisters are a separate problem.

front: Dapsone adverse effects: which are dose-related and which depend on G6PD status?
back: Mild haemolytic anaemia is common and dose-related, from its oxidising action. G6PD-deficient patients haemolyse at doses above 50 mg/day. Also methaemoglobinaemia, early nausea and anorexia, headache, paraesthesia, drug fever, rashes, fixed drug eruption, hypermelanosis and phototoxicity. Hepatitis and agranulocytosis are rare.

front: Sulfone syndrome: timing, features and treatment
back: It starts 4 to 6 weeks after dapsone is begun: fever, malaise, lymph node enlargement, skin desquamation, jaundice and anaemia. It is commoner in malnourished patients and has become more frequent since MDT was introduced. Treatment: stop dapsone, give corticosteroids and supportive care.

front: Dapsone: contraindications and uses beyond leprosy
back: Avoid in severe anaemia (Hb below 7 g/dL), G6PD deficiency and hypersensitivity. KDT lists its combination with pyrimethamine for chloroquine-resistant malaria, toxoplasmosis and Pneumocystis jirovecii infection; GG14 states that dapsone is no longer used for malaria, but it is used for Pneumocystis treatment and prophylaxis, Toxoplasma prophylaxis, and for its anti-inflammatory action in conditions such as pemphigoid.

front: Clofazimine: proposed mechanisms, absorption and why it can be given intermittently
back: A dye with leprostatic and anti-inflammatory action. Proposed actions: interference with DNA template function, disruption of membrane structure and transport, and disruption of the mitochondrial electron transport chain. About 40 to 70 percent is absorbed orally. It accumulates in macrophages as crystals in fat and other tissues, with a half-life of about 70 days, which allows intermittent dosing.

The main problem is reddish-black skin discolouration, especially on exposed areas. Hair, body secretions and the conjunctiva may also be pigmented. Dryness, itching, acneiform eruptions and phototoxicity occur. GI upset, weight loss and enteritis are seen mainly at higher doses. Avoid in early pregnancy and in liver or kidney damage.

front: Rifampicin in leprosy: why a monthly dose is used and when it must be withheld
back: A 600 mg dose kills up to 99.99 percent of M. leprae within 3 to 7 days, so patients become non-infectious quickly. The monthly MDT dose is nearly non-toxic and causes no significant enzyme induction. Withhold it in hepatic or renal dysfunction, and during erythema nodosum leprosum or reversal reactions, because rapid killing releases large amounts of antigen.

Used mainly as alternatives when rifampicin cannot be given

front: NLEP 2009 classification of leprosy for treatment.
text: Paucibacillary (PB): {{1 to 5}} skin lesions, with no nerve or only {{one}} nerve involved, and skin smear {{negative}} at all sites. Multibacillary (MB): {{6 or more}} skin lesions, more than one nerve involved, or skin smear {{positive}} at any site.

front: NLEP multidrug therapy (MDT) regimens for leprosy, by type.
text: Multibacillary: rifampicin {{600 mg}} once a month (supervised), dapsone {{100 mg}} daily (self-administered), and clofazimine {{300 mg}} once a month (supervised) plus {{50 mg}} daily (self-administered), for {{12 months}}. Paucibacillary: rifampicin {{600 mg}} monthly plus dapsone {{100 mg}} daily, for {{6 months}}.

front: Why was multibacillary leprosy treatment shortened to 12 months?
back: Dapsone monotherapy had caused resistance and relapse in up to 20 percent of patients. Fixed-duration therapy of 24 months gave relapse rates similar to standard MDT, and a WHO committee (1997) found 12 months gave similar relapse rates over 3 to 5 years. So mass programmes use 12 months for MB and 6 months for PB. Private or institutional care may treat longer, up to 4 years in highly bacillated patients.

front: Leprosy relapse and leprosy-TB coinfection: what is the management?
back: Relapse: restart the same MDT (12 months for MB, 6 months for PB), because dormant bacilli remain sensitive to these drugs. Coinfection with TB: continue the leprosy MDT but give rifampicin daily, as for TB. HIV: there is no association with leprosy, and MDT can be given safely to HIV-positive patients and those on antiretroviral therapy.

Oligonucleotide drugs are also grouped with biopharmaceuticals, although some (e.g. antisense oligonucleotides) are made synthetically, so the biological/small-molecule boundary is not sharp.

front: How are monoclonal antibodies named, and what change did WHO make in 2021?
back: Names end in -mab. The syllable before it shows origin: -omab mouse (murine), -ximab chimeric (human constant Fc fused to mouse variable Fv domains), -zumab humanised (only the antigen-binding CDRs are non-human, inserted into a human IgG scaffold), -umab fully human (from transgenic mice carrying human Ig genes, or phage display). Another syllable can show function, e.g. -li- immunomodulatory (nivolumab, cemiplimab). Examples: cetuximab, trastuzumab, bevacizumab. In October 2021 WHO changed the scheme for newly named antibodies: the single -mab stem is being replaced by four distinct stems that describe the antibody's composition; names assigned up to 2021 keep the old pattern.

Murine: whole mouse antibody
Chimeric: mouse variable regions, human constant regions

Fully human: transgenic mice with human Ig loci, or phage display
Lower antigenicity and a longer half-life
Cetuximab (chimeric) still provokes HAMA in about 4% of patients

front: Ligand blockade versus receptor blockade: how do they differ, with one example each?
back: Ligand blockade: the antibody binds the soluble ligand so it cannot reach its receptor (bevacizumab binds VEGF-A; anti-TNF antibodies neutralise TNF-alpha). Receptor blockade: the antibody binds the receptor's extracellular domain and prevents ligand binding (trastuzumab on HER2, cetuximab on EGFR).

front: What is antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC), and which cells mediate it?
back: The antibody's Fc region engages Fc receptors on NK cells or phagocytes, which then kill the antibody-coated target cell. IgG1 interacts with Fc receptors more strongly than IgG2 or IgG4, and Fc engineering can enhance or suppress ADCC. Examples: elotuzumab (SLAMF7 on myeloma cells); rituximab, ofatumumab and obinutuzumab (CD20, together with complement-dependent lysis).

front: What is complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC), and which antibody shows it?
back: Antibody bound to the target cell activates complement; the membrane attack complex (C5b to C9) then lyses the cell. IgG1 activates complement better than IgG2 or IgG4. Rituximab (anti-CD20) kills B cells mostly by CDC and ADCC; daratumumab (anti-CD38) may kill myeloma cells by CDC, ADCC or apoptosis.

text: Ipilimumab blocks {{CTLA-4}}, nivolumab and pembrolizumab block {{PD-1}}, and atezolizumab blocks {{PD-L1}}. Blocking these brakes releases antitumour T cells.

front: What is a bispecific T-cell engager (BiTE)? Give one example and its main toxicities.
back: A bispecific antibody with one arm binding a tumour antigen and the other binding CD3 on T cells, bringing T cells close to tumour cells so they kill them. Blinatumomab (CD19 x CD3) is used in relapsed or refractory B-cell precursor ALL and in ALL with minimal residual disease; teclistamab (BCMA x CD3) in multiple myeloma. Monitor for cytokine release syndrome, neurological toxicity and infections.

front: What is an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC), and how is its payload released?
back: A monoclonal antibody chemically linked to a cytotoxic payload (toxin or drug; radionuclides are used similarly). The antibody binds its tumour antigen, the complex is internalised, and the payload is released inside the cell by proteolytic cleavage. Payloads include microtubule disruptors (emtansine, MMAE) and topoisomerase inhibitors (deruxtecan).

front: Trastuzumab emtansine: target, payload and key toxicity
back: Anti-HER2 antibody linked to mertansine (emtansine), a microtubule disruptor. Used in HER2-positive breast cancer that recurred or progressed after trastuzumab and a taxane. Its toxicities include those of trastuzumab plus hepatotoxicity from the payload.

front: Brentuximab vedotin: target, payload and main indications
back: Chimeric anti-CD30 IgG1 linked to monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE), a microtubule disruptor released inside the cell by proteolytic cleavage. Used in Hodgkin lymphoma after failed autologous stem cell transplant or after at least two prior regimens, and in systemic anaplastic large cell lymphoma after at least one prior multiagent regimen. Monitor mainly for neutropenia and peripheral sensory neuropathy.

front: What is cytokine release syndrome (CRS), which biologics cause it, and how is it treated?
back: A systemic reaction to a large release of cytokines (TNF, interleukins including IL-6, interferons). Features: fever, chills, rigors, nausea, headache, tachycardia, hypotension, dyspnoea and wheezing; can be life-threatening. Seen with CAR T cells, bispecific T-cell engagers (blinatumomab), immune checkpoint inhibitors, and the first doses of muromonab-CD3. Management: tocilizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor) with or without corticosteroids; corticosteroid pretreatment attenuates the muromonab reaction.

Rang and Dale also contrast biosimilars with 'biobetters' (similar function, superior pharmacology or toxicity).
