front: What are the main viral vectors used in gene therapy, and which one is used to make CAR-T cells?
back: Retroviruses (including lentivirus) integrate into host DNA, giving permanent expression passed to daughter cells, but random insertion can disrupt genes; a lentiviral vector is used to transduce T cells when making CAR T cells. Adenovirus is highly infective but immunogenic, with transient expression needing repeated doses. Adeno-associated virus is less immunogenic but hard to mass-produce and cannot carry large genes. Non-viral options (liposomes, DNA cassettes) are safer but less efficient.

text: Antisense oligonucleotides are short ({{15 to 25}} bases) nucleic-acid chains that bind a complementary region of {{mRNA}} and promote its breakdown by {{ribonuclease H}}. Mipomersen, the first licensed antisense drug, suppresses {{apolipoprotein B}}; volanesorsen, an apo C-III antisense, is available in Europe for severe chylomicronaemia.

front: How does a small interfering RNA (siRNA) silence a gene, and what is one clinical example?
back: Short double-stranded RNA recruits the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC), which selectively degrades the complementary messenger RNA, so the protein is not made. It silences genes more efficiently than antisense oligonucleotides. Example: inclisiran, an siRNA against PCSK9, given twice yearly, reduces LDL-cholesterol by about 50%.

They deliver messenger RNA encoding an antigen, packaged in lipid nanoparticles. Antigen-presenting cells take up the nanoparticles and make the protein, which triggers an immune response. Example: the Pfizer/BioNTech and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines encode the full-length SARS-CoV-2 spike protein and are given as two doses (21 and 28 days apart respectively).

front: What are the aims, subjects and dose strategy of a phase I trial?
back: First-in-human study of safety, tolerability and human PK. Subjects are mostly healthy volunteers; when the drug is expected to be toxic (e.g. cancer or AIDS therapy) volunteer patients are used instead. Size: about 20 to 80 subjects (KDT); 10 to 100 (GG14); 20 to 100 (Katzung). Done by trained clinical pharmacologists with vital functions monitored and resuscitation at hand. Subjects receive the drug one by one, starting at about 1/100 to 1/10 of the highest dose that was non-toxic in animals, escalated stepwise to find the dose range for later study. Open label (no blinding).

front: What does a phase II trial aim to establish?
back: Therapeutic exploration and dose ranging: the first study in patients with the target disease ('proof of concept'). Size: about 100 to 500 patients (KDT); 50 to 500 (GG14); 100 to 200 (Katzung). Patients are selected by inclusion and exclusion criteria. Aims: therapeutic efficacy, dose range and ceiling effect; tolerability and PK are extended from phase I. Mostly controlled and randomised, blinded or open, generally at 2 to 4 centres. A candidate drug may be dropped here if efficacy is inadequate.

front: What is a phase III trial, and what does its completion lead to?
back: Therapeutic confirmation: randomised, usually double-blind comparison with existing therapy, done at many centres by specialists in the disease. Size: about 500 to 3000 patients (KDT); a few hundred to a few thousand (GG14); usually thousands (Katzung). It confirms efficacy, assesses safety on a wider scale, finalises indications and may add PK data. Some immunologically mediated toxicities first appear here. Completion leads to the marketing application: NDA, or BLA for biologics. Toxic but valuable drugs may receive restricted marketing permission (e.g. hospital use only).

front: What do phase IV studies detect that earlier phases cannot?
back: Postmarketing studies in the general treated population, with far larger numbers and everyday prescribing. They pick up uncommon or idiosyncratic adverse effects, effects of long-term use and unsuspected drug interactions, and show real patterns of use. They also study groups excluded from earlier trials (children, elderly, pregnant or lactating women, renal or hepatic disease), and new formulations, routes or fixed-dose combinations.

front: Classify: phases of a drug trial
text: Phase {{I}} is the first-in-human study in about {{20 to 80}} subjects, usually {{healthy volunteers}}, and open label; phase {{II}} explores dose and efficacy in about 100 to 500 patients; phase {{III}} is a {{randomised, double-blind}} multicentre comparison in about 500 to 3000 patients that supports the marketing application; phase {{IV}} is {{postmarketing}} surveillance.

front: Why is randomisation used, and when is stratified randomisation chosen?
back: Subjects are allocated by a preselected random number table or computer programme, so each has an equal chance of entering the test or control group. Neither investigator nor patient can influence allocation, so that source of bias is removed. When groups may end up ill-matched (especially small groups), stratified randomisation is used: subjects are first divided by age, sex, disease severity or other variables, and randomised within each stratum. Too many strata defeat the purpose.

front: Compare parallel-group and crossover trial designs.
back: Parallel: test and control groups run at the same time, each with different patients. Crossover: the same patients receive both treatments in a random order, so each serves as its own control. Crossover reduces between-patient variation and the sample size needed, but carry-over and order effects can occur, and it suits only chronic diseases that stay stable over time.

front: What is an adaptive trial design?
back: Conventional statistical methods may fail to give a clear answer when trials meet unexpected confounders, loss of subjects or marked subgroup differences. Adaptive statistical methods allow the study design to be changed when interim data show the need. They may permit decisions on superiority as well as non-inferiority, shorten the trial, reveal new benefits and give more reliable conclusions.

front: Short note: Bias in clinical trials and how it is minimised

points: Conscious and unconscious bias of investigators and subjects, for or against the test drug
Eliminating bias is the greatest challenge in a trial; credibility depends on it
Randomisation, stratified where groups may be unbalanced
Blinding: single (subject) or double (subject and investigator); identical-looking medicines in unlabelled packets; code held by a third party
Rigorous follow-up and outcome assessment; assessors unaware of treatment if full blinding is impossible
Proper control group: placebo if ethical, otherwise standard treatment
Inclusion and exclusion criteria fixed in advance
Primary and secondary end points and the statistical method pre-specified

front: Short note: Surrogate versus clinical endpoints

points: Clinical end point: patient-relevant outcome such as myocardial infarction, fracture or death
Surrogate end point: an easily measured marker thought to predict the clinical outcome, e.g. LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, bone mineral density, HbA1c, blood pressure
Trials are cheaper and quicker

Ezetimibe was approved on LDL lowering; ENHANCE then found no reduction in carotid intima-media thickness despite extra LDL lowering; the later IMPROVE-IT trial showed reduced MI and stroke with ezetimibe plus statin
Torcetrapib raised HDL but increased cardiovascular deaths
CAST: antiarrhythmics suppressed ventricular arrhythmias (the surrogate) but increased sudden cardiac death
Regulators are cautious about surrogate end points; the marker must truly reflect patient benefit

front: Classify: errors and power in a trial
text: A type {{I}} error is a {{false positive}} result, declaring a difference that does not exist; a type {{II}} error is a {{false negative}}; the {{power}} of a trial is 1 minus the type II error rate.

front: What factors determine the sample size of a clinical trial?
back: Four inputs: the significance level (type I error, usually 0.05); the power (1 minus type II error); the smallest clinically meaningful difference expected between groups; and the variability of the primary endpoint. A smaller expected difference, greater variability, higher power or a stricter significance level all increase the number needed. Sample size is calculated in advance because it must be minimal for both ethical and financial reasons.

front: Short note: Interim analysis and early stopping of trials

points: Analysis of accumulating results at intervals while a large trial is still running
An independent committee, not the investigators
Early termination once a decisive result, positive or negative, is reached
Otherwise the trial continues
Unethical to keep giving remaining patients a treatment already shown to be inferior
Sequential trial: matched pairs scored continuously until a preset boundary of superiority, inferiority or no difference is reached; suits drugs whose end points are reached quickly

front: What is a non-inferiority trial, and why would one be done?
back: A trial designed to show that a new drug is not inferior to existing treatment, rather than better. It is worthwhile when the new drug may offer other advantages: tolerability, safety, convenience, cost, or use in a particular patient subgroup. Many phase II and III studies are designed this way. The sample size calculation differs depending on whether the aim is to show equivalence or non-inferiority, or a significant difference.

front: Essay: Design of a non-inferiority phase III trial

points: Aim: show the new drug is not inferior to standard treatment
Justified by expected gains in tolerability, safety, convenience, cost or use in a subgroup
Randomised, parallel-group trial against the existing standard treatment (active control)
Double blind with identical-looking medicines where possible
Inclusion and exclusion criteria and the dosage regimen fixed in advance
Primary and secondary end points specified in advance
Surrogate end points only if they reliably reflect clinical benefit
Calculated beforehand from significance level, power, the clinically relevant difference and variability of response
Calculation depends on aiming for non-inferiority rather than a difference
Pre-specified statistical method
Interpretation is hard with confounders, loss of subjects or subgroup differences
Independent ethics committee approval and written informed consent
Interim analysis by an independent committee
Standards laid down by the International Conference on Harmonization (ICH) for trial design, ethics, conduct, monitoring, auditing, recording, analysis and reporting
Assures that data and reported results are credible and accurate
Protects the rights, integrity and confidentiality of trial subjects
Principles of the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association)
National guidelines too: in India, ICMR ethical guidelines for biomedical research on human participants
Every trial needs prior approval by an independent ethics committee as per GCP

front: What are the roles of the sponsor, the investigators and the institutional review board in a drug trial?
back: Sponsor (usually a pharmaceutical company): files the Investigational New Drug (IND) application describing preclinical data and the protocol before human testing, and applies for marketing (NDA or BLA) after phase III. Investigators: run the trial; in phase III they are usually specialists in the disease. Institutional review board (ethics committee) at each facility: an interdisciplinary body that must review and approve the scientific and ethical plan before testing in humans.

front: Recall: who does what before and during a drug trial
text: The {{sponsor}} files the {{IND}} application before human testing; an {{institutional review board}} at each site approves the plan; after phase III the sponsor applies for marketing by an {{NDA}} (or a BLA for biologics).

front: Short note: Ethics committee in clinical trials

points: Independent body; every trial needs its scrutiny and approval as per GCP
Weighs safety and ethical issues as well as the scientific importance of the study
Autonomy: freedom, dignity and confidentiality; right to choose whether to join or continue
Beneficence: intent to do good to the subject or society
Non-maleficence: no harm or undue risk
Justice: fairness, honesty and impartiality in obtaining, analysing and reporting data
Interdisciplinary institutional review board at each trial facility

front: What must trial subjects be told, and what are the limits of informed consent?
back: Subjects must be told that the drug is investigational, the nature and risks of the trial, and that they may be randomly and unknowingly assigned to test or control. They must be free to decline, or to stop participating (autonomy), and confidentiality is protected. Consent is proper and written. Limits: unconscious, demented or mentally ill patients cannot consent, and trials in children and the elderly raise similar concerns, yet such groups still need trials.

front: Classify: components of valid informed consent
text: Consent must be {{voluntary}}, informed and {{written}}; the subject keeps the right to decide whether to {{continue}} in the trial (autonomy).

back: A drug or biological product for diagnosis, treatment or prevention of a rare disease, or of a commoner disease endemic only in resource-poor areas, for which there is no reasonable expectation that development and marketing costs will be recovered from sales. Under the US Orphan Drug Amendment (1983), a rare disease affects fewer than 200,000 people in the USA. Governments offer tax benefits and other incentives. Examples given orphan status: clofazimine, paromomycin, sodium stibogluconate, rituximab, bortezomib.

front: Why do orphan drugs need special incentives?
back: Proving safety and efficacy in small populations is complex; little basic research is done on rare diseases, so rational targets are few; and development cost weighs heavily when the target population is small. Excessive product-liability costs (e.g. failure-to-warn claims for rare harms not detected in small trials) are a further disincentive. Hence tax benefits and other incentives, and support from not-for-profit foundations.

front: Why can spontaneous adverse-event reports not give the true incidence of a drug reaction?
back: The denominator is unknown, because the number of patients exposed to the drug is not recorded. The numerator is also incomplete: most reactions go unreported, reporting patterns change over the life of the product, and reports often lack dose, concomitant drugs or outcome. Media attention and litigation further distort reporting, so reports cannot be used to compare rates between drugs.

front: What is a safety signal and how is it detected?
back: A signal is a possible link between a drug and an adverse event that needs evaluation. Signals are found by disproportionality analysis, which compares how often an event is reported with the drug against its frequency across the whole database. These methods need no drug-use denominator but rely on assumptions that are hard to verify, so a signal almost always needs confirmation from controlled studies.

front: When is a single case report strong evidence that a drug caused an event?
back: When the event is rare or unlikely from other causes, appears close in time after exposure, has few other risk factors, and the drug carries a large excess risk. Examples are anaphylaxis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and rhabdomyolysis with cerivastatin. Otherwise a case report only raises suspicion.

front: How is pharmacovigilance organised in India and internationally (as given in KDT)?
back: Pharmacovigilance centres exist in most countries, with the Uppsala Monitoring Centre (Sweden) as the international collaborating centre. In India, CDSCO coordinates the pharmacovigilance programme, with peripheral, regional and zonal monitoring centres and a National Pharmacovigilance Advisory Committee. Centres collect, communicate and disseminate ADR data by linking with hospitals and practitioners, and assess causality (Naranjo algorithm) and severity (modified Hartwig scale).

text: A {{cohort}} study follows users and non-users of a drug to find uncommon adverse effects; a {{case-control}} study compares the frequency of drug use in cases with an adverse response against controls.

front: Essay: From a suspected adverse drug reaction to regulatory action

points: Premarketing trials are too small to detect rare ADRs; safety knowledge evolves over the drug's life cycle
Spontaneous reports (e.g. FAERS via MedWatch in the US; CDSCO-coordinated programme in India)
Published case reports
Observational cohort and case-control studies
Postmarketing clinical trials
Disproportionality methods on the spontaneous report database
Causality judged by temporal relation, previous knowledge, dechallenge and rechallenge; Naranjo algorithm
Denominator unknown
Heavy underreporting
Incomplete reports; confounding in observational studies
Safety communication and label change, including boxed warning
Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (REMS)
Withdrawal from the market

front: Short note: New Drugs and Clinical Trials (NDCT) Rules, 2019

points: In force from 25 March 2019 (the chapter on ethics committees for biomedical and health research from 21 September 2019)
Replaced Part XA and Schedule Y of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945 (older texts, e.g. KDT8, still describe Schedule Y)
Apply to new drugs, investigational drugs, ethics committees, BA/BE studies and clinical trials
Not used in India to any significant extent and not approved by the Central Licensing Authority (CLA) for its claims
Also: approved drug with new claims (indication, route, dose, dosage form); new fixed-dose combination or changed ratio; modified-release or novel delivery form
Also: vaccines, rDNA products, monoclonal antibodies, stem-cell products, gene therapy products, xenografts; phytopharmaceutical drugs added
Decision within 90 days for drugs developed outside India, 30 days for new drugs developed in India; no reply means deemed approval
Trial permission valid 2 years
Rejected applicant may seek reconsideration within 60 days
Two types: for clinical trials and BA/BE studies, and for biomedical and health research
Registration valid 5 years
CLA (DCGI) informed of EC approval within 15 working days
6-monthly trial status report to DCGI through the SUGAM portal; enrolment status every 3 months
Termination notified to CLA within 30 days with reasons
Post-trial access to the drug free of cost, on investigator recommendation and EC approval
Academic trials need EC approval only

front: What is an academic clinical trial under the NDCT Rules 2019?
back: A trial intended solely for academic research. It needs only Ethics Committee approval; no permission from the DCGI is required. Its results must not be used for promotional purposes or to seek regulatory approval.

front: How do the NDCT Rules 2019 define a serious adverse event (SAE) in a clinical trial?
back: An untoward medical occurrence during a clinical trial that results in death; in-patient hospitalisation (if the study was on out-patients) or prolonged hospitalisation (if on in-patients); persistent or significant disability or incapacity; a congenital anomaly or birth defect; or is otherwise life-threatening. The NDCT Rules amended the earlier Schedule Y rule (Rule 122DAB).

front: Recall: SAE reporting timelines under the NDCT Rules 2019
text: The investigator reports every SAE to the CLA, the sponsor and the EC within {{24 hours}}. For SAE of death, the sponsor and investigator send analysed reports to the CLA and head of institution within {{14 days}}; the EC sends its report with an opinion on compensation within {{30 days}}; the expert committee recommends cause and compensation within {{60 days}}; the CLA decides compensation within {{90 days}}; the sponsor pays within {{30 days}} of the order.

front: Short note: Medical management and compensation for trial injury under the NDCT Rules 2019

points: Sponsor gives free medical management for as long as required in the investigator's opinion, or until the injury is shown to be unrelated to the trial or BA/BE study
Payable for clinical trial-related injury or death
Quantum determined by the CLA using the formula in the Seventh Schedule
Paid by the sponsor or its representative
Investigator reports the SAE within 24 hours
EC forwards its analysed report with an opinion on compensation
CLA may constitute an independent expert committee, which recommends cause and quantum within 60 days
CLA passes the order within 90 days of the SAE report
Sponsor pays within 30 days of the order and submits payment details to the CLA

front: Short note: Ethics committee for clinical trials under the NDCT Rules 2019

points: At least 7 members from medical, non-medical, scientific and non-scientific areas
At least one lay person, one woman, one legal expert, and one independent member (social scientist, NGO representative, philosopher, ethicist or theologian)
At least half not associated with the institution; chairperson unaffiliated; member secretary from the institution
Medical scientists and clinicians need postgraduate qualification; all members trained in GCP
Registered by the CLA; valid 5 years
Renewal applied for 90 days before expiry
Changes in membership intimated to the CLA within 30 days
At least 5 members, including a medical scientist (preferably a pharmacologist), a clinician, a legal expert, and a social scientist, NGO representative or lay person
Invited subject experts cannot vote
Protect rights, safety and well-being of subjects, with extra care for vulnerable groups (e.g. prisoners, students, the impoverished, minors)
Ongoing review; may revoke approval with recorded reasons
Report on SAEs with opinion on compensation
Schedule Y also required at least 7 members, but without the detailed composition rules

front: How do the NDCT Rules 2019 define an orphan drug, and what concessions do they give?
back: An orphan drug is one intended to treat a condition affecting not more than five lakh (500,000) persons in India. Concessions: fast-track approval and special status, including a complete fee waiver for clinical trial filing; expedited review where safety and efficacy evidence is established even before all trial phases are complete (post-marketing trials may then be required); and waiver of the local clinical study and phase IV if the CLA is satisfied. Marketing still needs CDSCO authorisation to import or manufacture.

front: Short note: Pharmacovigilance Programme of India (PvPI)

points: 1989: six regional ADR centres
1997: India joined the WHO Programme for International Drug Monitoring (Uppsala Monitoring Centre)
2004: National Pharmacovigilance Programme
14 July 2010: PvPI launched with AIIMS, New Delhi as National Coordination Centre (NCC)
15 April 2011: NCC shifted to the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC), Ghaziabad
Conducted by CDSCO (Directorate General of Health Services, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare); coordinated by IPC as NCC
ADR Monitoring Centres (AMCs), mostly in medical colleges, send reports to the NCC through VigiFlow
Data go to the WHO-UMC global database; CDSCO takes regulatory decisions on NCC recommendations
Suspected ADR reporting form (voluntary, by healthcare professionals)
Report all suspected reactions to new drugs, all suspected interactions, and serious reactions (death, life-threatening, hospitalisation, disability, congenital anomaly)
KDT8 describes the older CDSCO-coordinated programme with peripheral, regional and zonal centres

front: Define bioassay and explain why a standard is run alongside the unknown.
back: Bioassay measures the potency of a drug or unknown mediator from the size of the biological effect it produces. The unknown (U) is compared with a standard (S) on the same test system, because absolute 'units' (e.g. pigeon or mouse units) differ between laboratories, whereas the relative potency of U and S can be agreed. The assay estimates the dose of U that gives the same effect as a known dose of S.

front: What is a 2 + 2 (parallel-line) bioassay, and why is it used?
back: The minimal parallel-line design: two doses of standard (S1, S2) and two of unknown (U1, U2), chosen to fall on the linear part of the log dose-response curve. Doses are given repeatedly in random order, which measures the variability of the test system and lets the confidence limits of the potency ratio be calculated. Example: a modified 2 + 2 assay in patients showed morphine to be about 13 times as potent an analgesic as codeine.

front: Short note: Requirements of a valid bioassay

points: Compare unknown with a standard on the same preparation
Compare equi-effective doses from dose-response curves, not responses to equal doses
Log dose-response lines of standard and unknown must be parallel
Maximal responses must be similar; differing mechanisms or a partial agonist invalidate a simple potency ratio
Biological variation is the main problem
Minimise variation, avoid systematic error, and estimate limits of error
Randomised order of doses; observer (and subject) unaware of the dose
Graded or quantal responses need different statistics

front: Parallel-line assay: how is potency read?
text: In a parallel-line assay the potency ratio is read from the {{horizontal distance}} between the standard and unknown log dose-response lines. A simple ratio is invalid if the lines are not {{parallel}} or the maximal responses differ.

front: Graded vs quantal dose-response: how do they differ?
back: Graded responses are continuous (e.g. fall in BP, strength of contraction) and are measured in each individual, giving a sigmoidal curve of response against log dose. Quantal responses are all-or-none (e.g. death, convulsion). The proportion of a population responding is plotted against dose, giving a cumulative curve from which median doses (ED50, LD50) are read.
ED50: the dose producing the specified therapeutic effect in 50% of subjects. TD50: the dose producing a defined toxic effect in 50% of subjects. LD50: the dose that kills 50% of the test animals.

front: Potency vs efficacy: define each and give one example.
back: Potency is the dose or concentration needed for a given effect (its position on the dose axis). Efficacy is the maximal effect a drug can produce (the height of the plateau). Morphine is more efficacious than aspirin as an analgesic; pethidine is less potent than morphine but equally efficacious.

front: What is the dose ratio, and how does a Schild plot measure competitive antagonist affinity?
back: Dose ratio (r): the factor by which agonist concentration must be raised in the presence of an antagonist to restore a given response. With a reversible competitive antagonist the log concentration-effect curve shifts right without change in slope or maximum, and r increases linearly with antagonist concentration. A Schild plot of log(r - 1) against log antagonist concentration gives the antagonist's equilibrium dissociation constant (KB) from the abscissal intercept, e.g. propranolol on isolated guinea-pig atria. Antagonist affinity measured this way is used to classify receptors.

front: Short note: Therapeutic index and margin of safety

points: Gap between therapeutic and adverse-effect dose-response curves = safety margin or therapeutic index
Animals: TI = LD50 / ED50
Humans: TI = TD50 / ED50
Measurable only in animals (LD50 form)
LD50 does not reflect adverse effects at therapeutic doses
ED50 depends on the effect chosen (aspirin for headache vs as antirheumatic)
Individual variation in efficacy and toxicity is not captured
Clinically the therapeutic window (minimal therapeutic dose to maximal acceptable dose) is more relevant
Narrow-margin drugs need individualised dosing and monitoring

text: Therapeutic index in animals = {{LD50}} / {{ED50}}. In humans the index uses {{TD50}} in place of LD50, because TD50 is the dose producing a defined toxic effect in 50% of people.

front: Frog rectus abdominis: what phenomenon does it demonstrate?
back: Repeated or high doses of acetylcholine produce progressively smaller contractions; shortly after a high (100-fold) dose the response is markedly reduced and returns only after time is allowed. This illustrates receptor desensitisation at the nicotinic end plate. The preparation is also a classical system for studying acetylcholine responses at nicotinic receptors.

front: Classify: isolated tissues and what each tests
text: Guinea pig ileum is used to show {{muscarinic}} actions of acetylcholine blocked by atropine, and its contraction is a standard bioassay for {{histamine}} (H1). Frog rectus abdominis shows {{nicotinic}} end-plate desensitisation. Isolated guinea pig {{atria}} are used to measure competitive antagonism of isoprenaline by propranolol.

front: Short note: Isolated organ bath preparations

points: A strip of smooth muscle or other tissue is held in an organ bath, and contraction or relaxation is recorded
Response is plotted against concentration as a concentration-effect curve
Estimate maximal response and potency of agonists
Detect specific activity early in screening (e.g. antihistaminic, vasodilator)
Measure antagonist affinity by dose ratio and Schild analysis
The classical technique of pharmacology, still widely used alongside molecular and cellular assays

front: Rat paw oedema: what does it screen, and what are its limits?
back: Irritant chemicals injected into a rat's paw make it swollen and tender. Drugs that reduce this swelling predict well the symptomatic relief of inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, so it is used to screen anti-inflammatory drugs. Limit: it lacks construct validity for rheumatoid arthritis, which is an autoimmune disease.

front: MES vs PTZ anticonvulsant screens: what does each predict?
back: MES: a brief high-intensity shock to the rodent head gives tonic flexion, tonic extension and clonic convulsions. Drugs that abolish the tonic (extensor) phase (e.g. phenytoin, carbamazepine) are effective in GTCS and complex partial seizures; activity reflects action on seizure spread. PTZ: injection produces clonic seizures, prevented by drugs effective in absence and myoclonic seizures (e.g. ethosuximide, valproate, clonazepam); activity reflects action on the seizure focus. Other models: chronic focal seizures (alumina cream on monkey cortex) and kindling.

front: Animal models of depression: principle and limitations.
back: Mild stress procedures, such as the forced swim test or inescapable foot shock, produce behavioural states (social withdrawal, loss of appetite, reduced motor activity) that mimic aspects of human depression and are used to test antidepressants. Limitation: no known animal condition corresponds to inherited human depression, and no clear brain pathology is defined, so face and construct validity are poor; models selected on response to known drugs may miss new mechanisms.

front: What makes a good animal model of human disease?
back: It should resemble the human disease in pathophysiological phenotype (face validity), causation (construct validity) and response to treatment (predictive validity). Difficulties: many psychiatric diseases cannot be observed in animals; causes of degenerative diseases are complex; selecting models by response to known drugs may miss new mechanisms; transgenic models can mislead (cystic fibrosis gene defect affects mainly the intestine in mice).

front: Classify: animal models of human disease used in drug screening
text: Examples include {{kindled}} seizures in rats, {{spontaneously hypertensive}} rats (genetic model), experimental tuberculosis in mice, and {{alloxan}}-induced diabetes in rats or dogs.

front: Essay: Preclinical pharmacological screening of a new analgesic and anti-inflammatory drug

points: Animal tests expose the whole pharmacological profile before human use
Rodent first, then a larger animal; unfavourable compounds are rejected at each step
Simple rapid screening tests for the sought activity (e.g. analgesic activity)
Isolated organ tests for specific activities
Rat paw oedema from irritant chemicals predicts anti-inflammatory benefit
Models need face, construct and predictive validity
Detailed confirmatory tests; related activities such as antipyretic and anti-inflammatory action of an analgesic
Systemic pharmacology on major organ systems; mechanism of action
Dose-response relationship, maximal effect, potency and efficacy compared with existing drugs
Pharmacokinetics, then toxicity testing
Animal efficacy may not translate (e.g. substance P antagonists were analgesic in animals but inactive in humans)

front: Acute toxicity study: design and endpoint.
back: Single escalating doses are given to small groups of animals (usually two species, two routes) and observed for overt effects and mortality for 1 to 3 days. Goals: the no-effect dose, the maximum tolerated dose and, where needed, the LD50, now estimated with the smallest possible number of animals. Organ toxicity is examined by histopathology.

front: Subacute and chronic toxicity studies: duration and parameters.
back: Subacute (subchronic): repeated doses for about 2 to 12 weeks (Katzung: 2 weeks to 3 months), usually three doses in two species; the longer the intended human use, the longer the test. Doses are chosen from ED50 and LD50. Chronic: a rodent and at least one non-rodent for 6 to 12 months, required when the drug will be used long term, and usually run alongside early clinical trials. Both record overt effects, food intake, body weight, haematology, biochemistry and organ histopathology.

points: At least two species, one rodent and one non-rodent, by oral and parenteral routes
Acute, subacute and chronic studies
Effects on spermatogenesis, ovulation, fertility, mating, parturition and the developing foetus (teratogenicity)
Two species, usually one rodent and rabbits
Carcinogenicity: dosing for 2 years or the whole life of the animal, required for drugs used long term
Mutagenicity: bacteria (Ames test), mammalian cells and intact rodents
Conducted under Good Laboratory Practice (GLP)
Thalidomide disaster led to more extensive teratogenicity testing
Ames test: detects mutations in bacteria
Mutations and genetic stability in mammalian cells in culture
Intact rodents: dominant lethal test and clastogenicity (chromosome damage) in mice
Part of the preclinical safety package with carcinogenicity testing
Rare effects may still be missed for statistical reasons

front: Classify: species and routes in toxicity testing
text: Toxicity testing uses at least {{two}} species, one {{rodent}} and one {{non-rodent}}, dosed by the {{oral}} and {{parenteral}} routes.

front: Essay: Preclinical safety evaluation of a new drug candidate

points: Aim: identify likely human toxicities and those to monitor in trials
Two species, two routes
No-effect dose, maximum tolerated dose, LD50 if needed
Subacute and chronic designs with haematology, biochemistry and histopathology
Reproduction and teratogenicity
Mutagenicity (Ames, mammalian cells, rodents)
Carcinogenicity where long-term use is planned
First human dose usually 1/100 to 1/10 of the no-effect (non-toxic) dose in animals
Time-consuming and expensive (2 to 6 years)
Large numbers of animals
Extrapolation to humans imperfect; rare effects missed
GLP-compliant data package before human trials

front: How is the use of animals in preclinical testing being reduced?
text: Progress has been made in {{reducing the number}} of animals needed while keeping data valid; {{cell and tissue culture}} in vitro methods and {{computer modelling}} are increasingly used, though their {{predictive value}} is still limited.

front: Essay: Use of animals in pharmacological research: value, limits and alternatives

points: Animal studies expose the pharmacological and toxicological profile before human use
Simple models often predict human efficacy (ferret motion-sickness model, rat paw oedema)
Safety testing in two species is required before trials
Many human diseases have no animal counterpart
Validity (face, construct, predictive) often incomplete
Animal-to-human extrapolation imperfect; rare effects missed; large numbers of animals
Isolated organ, cell and tissue culture methods
Computer modelling
Human microdosing (phase 0) studies give early human PK
Reduce animal numbers while keeping data valid; Good Laboratory Practice standards

front: What is CPCSEA, and what are its functions?
back: The Committee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals: a statutory body under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, formed in 1964 and revived in 1998. Sarkar lists its member secretary under the Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying. Functions: register establishments that experiment on or breed animals; appoint nominees to Institutional Animal Ethics Committees (IAECs); approve animal house facilities after inspection; permit experiments on animals; recommend import of animals; act against violations; and train nominees.

front: Short note: Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (IAEC)

points: Every animal study (including tissue or cell collection from animals) must be approved by the IAEC first
Constituted in every CPCSEA-registered laboratory; CPCSEA guidelines govern animal maintenance
Held at scheduled intervals, with expedited review if needed
Decisions by consensus; dissent minuted; unresolved cases referred to CPCSEA
Multiple surgical procedures on one animal only if specified in the protocol and approved by the IAEC
Knows CPCSEA guidelines and the 4Rs; reviews proposals for humane issues and animal numbers
Visits the animal house at least once a year and submits an inspection report
Informs CPCSEA if no meetings are held for 6 months

front: Short note: The 3Rs and the 4th R in animal experimentation

points: Russell and Burch defined alternatives as the three Rs: Replacement, Reduction, Refinement
CPCSEA introduced the 3Rs in India in 1999 and adopted a 4th R, Rehabilitation, in 2006 (others use Responsibility)
Absolute: no animals (human cells, computer models, dummies); relative: animal cells or tissues
Using lower organisms (microorganisms, invertebrates, eggs) instead of higher animals
Fewer animals where use is essential: better skills, pilot studies, proper design and statistics
Modify methods to minimise pain and distress; define humane endpoints
After-care of experimental animals until natural death; aseptic procedures; one major procedure per animal; proper post-operative care

back: Pharmacogenetics studies the genetic basis of variable drug response and often involves a small number of DNA variants with large effects. Pharmacogenomics studies larger numbers of variants, in an individual or across a population, to explain genetic influence on drug response.

front: Short note: Star alleles and metaboliser phenotypes

points: Gene name, asterisk, then a number for the haplotype
*1 is the functional allele by convention
CYP2C19*2 and *3 have no function; CYP2C19*17 increases expression
Poor: no enzyme activity (two no-function alleles)
Intermediate: reduced activity (e.g. one functional and one no-function allele)
Normal: two functional alleles
Rapid and ultrarapid: greatly increased activity, e.g. from promoter variants or extra gene copies (CYP2D6 duplication)
Phenotype reflects the combined effect of the maternal and paternal alleles
One gene can carry over 100 variants, plus deletions and duplications (e.g. CYP2D6)

text: A single-base substitution is a {{single-nucleotide variant (SNV)}}; deletion or duplication of a whole gene or a large DNA segment is a {{copy number variant (CNV)}}; variants that are inherited together on a chromosome are in {{linkage disequilibrium}}.

front: Name the three situations in which a single pharmacogene produces a large effect on drug response.
back: 1) The drug's key metabolic or transport step depends on one enzyme or transporter with variable function (e.g. codeine and CYP2D6). 2) The drug acts on a target, or an off-target protein, that varies (e.g. aminoglycosides and MT-RNR1). 3) The drug's effect depends on the wider biological setting (e.g. antimalarials and rasburicase in G6PD deficiency).

front: What is the two-sided risk of codeine with CYP2D6 variation?
back: Codeine is a prodrug that CYP2D6 converts to morphine. Poor metabolisers make little morphine, so analgesia is absent. Ultrarapid metabolisers make excess morphine, which can cause respiratory depression and death.

front: Which enzyme's variants are linked to breast cancer recurrence on tamoxifen, and why?
back: CYP2D6. Tamoxifen relies on CYP2D6 for metabolic activation to endoxifen, a metabolite with high oestrogen-receptor affinity. The CYP2D6 poor metaboliser phenotype correlates with a higher risk of relapse in breast cancer treated with tamoxifen.

front: Clopidogrel: how does CYP2C19 status change the antiplatelet plan?
back: Clopidogrel is a prodrug: about 85% of a dose is hydrolysed by esterases to an inactive acid, and about 15% is converted (mainly by CYP2C19) to the active thiol metabolite. Carriers of the no-function CYP2C19*2 allele have more serious cardiovascular events and stent thrombosis after ACS treated with PCI. Poor metabolisers (about 2-3% of European and over 10% of East Asian ancestry) should get an alternative antiplatelet, because even large dose increases do not work. GG14: intermediate metabolisers may reach adequate effect with a higher dose. Katzung (CPIC, ACS with PCI): use prasugrel or ticagrelor in both poor and intermediate metabolisers; the FDA label recommends alternatives for poor metabolisers.

front: Classify: CYP2C19 and proton pump inhibitors
text: Omeprazole and lansoprazole are inactivated by {{CYP2C19}}. CYP2C19 poor metabolisers have higher {{parent drug}} exposure, stronger acid suppression and a higher chance of {{ulcer cure}} than rapid or ultrarapid metabolisers.

front: Which transporter variant is linked to simvastatin myopathy, and how was it found?
back: SLCO1B1, which encodes OATP1B1, an uptake transporter on the sinusoidal (blood) side of hepatocytes that takes up statins, methotrexate and bilirubin. The common reduced-function variant rs4149056 (Val174Ala) lowers hepatic uptake, raising systemic statin exposure and myopathy risk. It was found by a GWAS of only 85 simvastatin myotoxicity cases and 90 controls; the exact mechanism of muscle toxicity is undefined. CPIC advice for reduced-function genotypes: lower simvastatin dose or an alternative statin (e.g. pravastatin, rosuvastatin), with CK monitoring.

front: Essay: Loss-of-function and gain-of-function metabolic variants and their effect on drug action

points: Drugs with a narrow margin, cleared by a single enzyme, are the highest-risk group
Outcome depends on whether the parent drug or a metabolite is the active species
Parent drug and upstream metabolites rise, so toxicity or overdose-like effects follow
Downstream metabolites fall
If the active species is a metabolite formed by the enzyme, efficacy is lost
Parent drug falls, so efficacy can be lost
Downstream active metabolites rise, which can cause adverse effects
Loss of activation gives inefficacy (clopidogrel, codeine analgesia)
Gain of activation can give excess active drug (codeine and morphine)
Codeine and CYP2D6
Clopidogrel and CYP2C19
Tacrolimus and CYP3A5: functional alleles lower exposure, so higher doses are needed
Omeprazole and CYP2C19: poor metabolisers get a stronger acid-suppressing effect
Genotype the enzyme before using a narrow-margin drug that depends on it
Interpret results with ancestry in mind, since allele frequencies vary between populations
CYP2C9 metabolises the more active S-enantiomer
CYP2C9 poor and intermediate metabolisers need lower steady-state doses and have more bleeding
Target VKORC1 is needed to recycle vitamin K to its active reduced form
Promoter variants that lower VKORC1 expression need lower doses (more common in Asian ancestry)
Rare coding variants cause partial or complete resistance and higher dose needs
CYP4F2 inactivates vitamin K by hydroxylation
CYP2C9, VKORC1 and CYP4F2 together explain over 50% of the dose variability

front: How do MT-RNR1 variants raise the risk of aminoglycoside hearing loss?
back: Aminoglycosides bind bacterial 16S rRNA, but in the inner ear they also bind human mitochondrial ribosomes (off-target). MT-RNR1 variants make human mitochondrial rRNA resemble bacterial rRNA, increasing binding affinity. Hearing loss can then occur even when serum levels are judged non-toxic.

front: Why must tumour genotype be checked before some targeted anticancer drugs?
back: Response depends on somatic (tumour) mutations as well as germline DNA. EGFR activating mutations predict response to gefitinib, and BRAF V600E predicts response to vemurafenib. Trastuzumab helps only HER2-expressing breast cancers, yet it can cause cardiomyopathy, and HER2-negative patients carry that risk without benefit.

front: Classify: drug targets and variant-specific drug action
text: Warfarin's target is {{VKORC1}}; ivacaftor partly corrects the gating defect of the CFTR {{G551D}} variant; lumacaftor improves surface expression of the commonest CFTR variant, {{F508}}; vemurafenib inhibits {{BRAF V600E}} kinase.

front: Why is NUDT15 testing relevant to thiopurine toxicity in East Asian patients?
back: TPMT and NUDT15 variants both alter the levels of active thiopurine metabolites and the risk of bone marrow toxicity. TPMT poor metabolisers are rare in East Asian populations, but NUDT15 poor and intermediate metabolisers are more frequent there. Thiopurine toxicity is more common in Asian patients, and NUDT15 was found by GWAS, so TPMT testing alone can miss risk.

front: What does the UGT1A1*28 allele do, and which drugs does it affect?
back: UGT1A1*28 has seven TA repeats in the promoter instead of the common six, which lowers UGT1A1 expression. The allele frequency can reach about 30%, with up to 10% of people homozygous depending on ancestry. Reduced activity raises SN-38, the active metabolite of irinotecan, and so raises the risk of serious toxicity. It also causes Gilbert syndrome and atazanavir-related hyperbilirubinaemia.

front: Acetylator (NAT2) polymorphism: what are the consequences of slow and fast acetylation?
back: NAT2 variants give slow and fast acetylators; slow acetylation is autosomal recessive and results from less NAT2 enzyme. About 60-70% of Indians are slow acetylators (isoniazid half-life about 3 h, versus 1 h in fast acetylators). Slow acetylators: isoniazid peripheral neuropathy; hydralazine- and procainamide-induced lupus; sulfonamide hypersensitivity; amonafide toxicity. The historical account in GG14 also links NAT deficiency with isoniazid hepatotoxicity (the hepatotoxic metabolite is formed from acetylhydrazine by CYP2E1). Fast acetylators: acetylator status does not matter with daily isoniazid, but biweekly regimens are less effective.

front: Short note: G6PD deficiency and drug response

points: Oxidant drugs lower the antioxidant glutathione in G6PD-deficient red cells, raising fragility and causing haemolysis
X-linked; commoner in Mediterranean, African and Southeast Asian people; severity varies with the variant and is largely dose related
Primaquine and other antimalarials; tafenoquine
Dapsone (haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia)
Rasburicase
Others: sulfonamides, cotrimoxazole, nitrofurantoin, methylene blue, fluoroquinolones, chloramphenicol
Breaks uric acid down to allantoin and hydrogen peroxide
G6PD-deficient cells cannot handle the oxidative stress: haemolytic anaemia and methaemoglobinaemia
Methaemoglobin cannot carry oxygen; can cause arrhythmias, seizures and death
Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency
G6PD is neither the drug's metabolic enzyme nor its target; it changes the biological background (pharmacodynamic modifier)

text: TPMT and NUDT15: {{azathioprine}} and mercaptopurine cause marrow toxicity; DPYD (dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase): {{capecitabine}} and {{fluorouracil}} cause toxicity; UGT1A1: {{irinotecan}} causes toxicity; NAT2: {{isoniazid}} causes neurotoxicity; G6PD: {{rasburicase}} causes haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia.

front: Essay: Pharmacogenetic approach to severe toxicity from antimetabolite and cytotoxic drugs

points: Many of these drugs have a narrow therapeutic margin, and toxicity can be life-threatening
Germline variants affect the host; somatic variants affect the tumour
TPMT and NUDT15 variants raise marrow toxicity risk
The same variants alter the risk of second cancers
NUDT15 matters more in Asian ancestry, where TPMT variants are less common
DPYD variants predict toxicity with fluorouracil and capecitabine
Reduced UGT1A1 activity raises SN-38 exposure
Higher SN-38 is linked to serious toxicity
TYMS enhancer repeat: two copies rather than three raises host toxicity and tumour susceptibility to TYMS inhibitors
Somatic markers such as EGFR and BRAF V600E select patients for targeted drugs
Genotype before prescribing where a validated test exists
Ancestry determines which variants are informative for a given patient

front: How does HLA-B*57:01 testing change abacavir treatment?
back: Carriers of HLA-B*57:01 are at risk of severe abacavir hypersensitivity, described as skin reactions particularly Stevens-Johnson syndrome. A randomised trial showed that genotyping before treatment eliminated this risk, and abacavir is contraindicated in HLA-B*57:01-positive patients. Proposed mechanism: non-covalent binding of the drug or a metabolite to HLA or the T-cell receptor, altering the peptides presented; the immune details are not fully characterised.

front: Which HLA allele predicts carbamazepine skin reactions in East Asian and in European-ancestry patients?
back: HLA-B*15:02 in East Asian individuals. In European-ancestry individuals, a GWAS of patients with Stevens-Johnson-type reactions (65 cases, 3987 controls) identified HLA-A*31:01.

front: Why check both CYP2C9 and HLA-B genotype before starting phenytoin?
back: Phenytoin (and fosphenytoin) is metabolised by CYP2C9, so poor metabolisers have higher plasma levels and more toxicity. Phenytoin can also cause life-threatening Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis; the risk appears especially high when a CYP2C9 variant occurs together with an HLA-B risk allele such as HLA-B*15:02. Knowing both genotypes helps predict response.

front: Classify: HLA alleles and drug hypersensitivity
text: HLA-B*57:01 with {{abacavir}}; HLA-B*58:01 with {{allopurinol}}; HLA-B*15:02 with {{carbamazepine}} (East Asian), oxcarbazepine and {{phenytoin}}; HLA-A*31:01 with {{carbamazepine}} (European ancestry).

front: Short note: HLA testing for drug hypersensitivity and its limits

points: HLA-A, -B and -C encode MHC class I proteins that let the immune system tell self from foreign proteins
HLA-B is among the most polymorphic genes in the genome
HLA-B*15:02 is most prevalent in East Asian and Central/South Asian populations, carried by up to about 20% in some
It is absent or very rare in European and sub-Saharan African populations
Other regional phenytoin risk alleles include HLA-B*15:21, B*15:11, B*15:08 (Asian) and B*56:02 (Aboriginal Australian)
A negative result is reassuring only if the correct allele panel for the patient's population was tested
Incomplete panels give false reassurance
The immune mechanism is incompletely understood

front: Why has the candidate-gene approach worked well in pharmacogenetics when it often fails elsewhere?
back: Pharmacogenetic candidate genes were chosen from known drug disposition or action pathways, and the variants found often have large effects that replicate. Elsewhere, candidate-gene findings frequently failed to replicate. GWAS is now used without a prior hypothesis and can give clear signals even with small samples when the effect is large (e.g. carbamazepine and HLA-A*31:01).

front: Why are the results of warfarin genotyping trials mixed?
back: Trials using time in therapeutic range over the first 30 to 90 days gave inconsistent results, none showing a large effect, and these studies had few bleeding events. An RCT with bleeding as the primary endpoint did show a significant benefit of genotype-guided dosing. EHR-based case-control studies link CYP2C9 and CYP4F2 variants to bleeding.

front: Short note: Clinical implementation of pharmacogenomic testing

points: Point-of-care: genotype when the drug is prescribed; each drug needs its own assay
Multi-gene panel stored in the EHR, with clinical decision support when a relevant drug is prescribed
Strongest: RCTs comparing a genotype-guided strategy with standard care
HLA-B*57:01 with abacavir: genotyping eliminated severe skin reactions
Clopidogrel: genotype-guided care gave fewer bleeding events without more stent thrombosis
Warfarin: mixed results overall
Non-randomised data are weaker, and RCTs for rare variants may be impractical
The variant must link to a clinically important outcome, and the test must lead to actionable advice (change drug or dose)
Evidence strength varies by drug-gene pair
CPIC publishes peer-reviewed, genotype-based prescribing guidance across drugs
Allele panels must suit the target population

front: Essay: Role of human genomics in new drug discovery and development

points: Genetic pathways in physiology and disease point to new drug targets
Drugs with human genetic support are about three times more likely to be marketed
Brown and Goldstein's FH studies identified a defect in regulation of HMG-CoA reductase, the enzyme statins inhibit
PCSK9 gain-of-function variants raise LDL and cause FH; loss-of-function variants (African American subjects) lower LDL and coronary risk; PCSK9 antibodies (alirocumab, evolocumab) followed
Loss-of-function variants in APOC3, SLC30A8 and HSD17B13 reduce risk of common diseases
SCN9A loss of function causes insensitivity to pain, suggesting an analgesic target
After a negative phase III trial of dalcetrapib, a GWAS found an ADCY9 variant that predicted efficacy
Polygenic risk scores may pick patients most likely to benefit from costly LDL-lowering drugs
Phenome-wide association studies link variants to phenotypes, suggesting new indications
Such studies can also predict adverse effects of drugs
Variants are often population specific, so diverse cohorts are needed
Ancestry diversity drives discovery in all populations

front: Classify: genomic evidence in drug development
text: Loss-of-function variants in {{PCSK9}} lower LDL cholesterol and point to it as a target; a GWAS found that an {{ADCY9}} variant predicts response to {{dalcetrapib}}; PheWAS can suggest {{repurposing}} of existing drugs; drugs with human genetic support are about {{three-fold}} more likely to be marketed.

front: Atypical plasma cholinesterase: what happens with succinylcholine, and how is it detected?
back: Plasma pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase, BCHE) normally hydrolyses succinylcholine, so its action lasts only 5 to 8 minutes. Some people inherit an abnormal enzyme with low affinity for succinylcholine, or a deficiency of it. Homozygotes (about 1 in over 3000) develop prolonged block with muscle paralysis and apnoea lasting 4 to 6 hours; heterozygotes (about 1 in 50) show only a 2- to 3-fold prolongation. Succinylcholine also readily produces phase II block in these patients. The apnoea can only be managed by mechanical ventilation.

front: What is the genetic basis of malignant hyperthermia, and which drugs trigger it?
back: Variants in RYR1 (the ryanodine receptor calcium-release channel of skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum) and CACNA1S. Triggers: volatile anaesthetics (halothane, isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane, enflurane, methoxyflurane) and succinylcholine, which release massive intracellular calcium, causing persistent muscle contraction and heat production. Treatment: rapid external cooling, bicarbonate, 100% oxygen and IV dantrolene, which acts on RYR1 to block calcium-induced calcium release.

front: DPYD testing before fluoropyrimidines: why, and how is the dose changed?
back: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD, gene DPYD) is the rate-limiting step of pyrimidine catabolism and eliminates about 80% of a fluorouracil dose; capecitabine and tegafur are oral prodrugs of 5-FU. Deficiency sharply lowers 5-FU clearance, causing severe toxicity. Clinically recognised variants: DPYD*2A and *13 (no function), rs67376798 and HapB3 (reduced function); all are rare. CPIC: intermediate metabolisers start at a reduced dose (50% reduction, then titrate by toxicity); complete deficiency calls for a non-fluoropyrimidine drug. Genotype-guided dose reduction lowered the risk of severe toxicity.

front: What does the WHO mean by rational use of medicines?
back: Patients receive medicines suited to their clinical needs, in doses that match their own requirements, for an adequate period, and at the lowest cost to them and their community. It covers the whole supply-use chain, though prescribing is the clinical core.

front: Which criteria show that a prescription is appropriate?
back: A sound indication; a drug that suits the patient for efficacy, tolerability, safety and cost; a dose, route and duration fitted to the patient; no contraindication, the drug acceptable to the patient, and expected benefit greater than likely harm; correct dispensing with instructions; and follow-up of adherence, benefit and adverse effects.

points: Prescriber habits, copied from teachers or popular doctors
Heavy patient load leading to routine symptom-based prescribing
Imprecise diagnosis, so several drugs are given to cover every possibility
Industry promotion, unrealistic claims and inducements
Patient demand for a 'pill for every ill'; knowledge alone does not fix this
Drug given when none is needed (antibiotic for viral fever or non-specific diarrhoea); compulsive vitamins and tonics
Drug unrelated to the diagnosis (PPI for any abdominal symptom); wrong drug (tetracycline for pharyngitis)
Doubtful-efficacy drugs; wrong route (injection when oral would do); wrong dose or duration (stopping TB treatment early; prolonged post-operative antibiotics)
Unnecessary combinations, costly new drugs where cheaper ones work, unsafe use (corticosteroid for fever), polypharmacy with interaction risk
Delayed relief or cure; more adverse effects; longer hospital stay, more morbidity and mortality
Emergence of microbial resistance
Financial loss to patient and community; loss of trust in the doctor; lower community health standards
Follow the stepwise process of rational prescribing, including monitoring
Use the essential medicines list for procurement and supply, which improves availability, saves cost and promotes rational use
Knowledge alone has not been enough to change prescribing; the other influences above must also be addressed

text: Antibiotic for a viral fever is {{use when no drug is needed}}; tetracycline for pharyngitis is {{wrong drug selection}}; corticosteroid for fever is {{unsafe use}}; ciprofloxacin plus tinidazole for any diarrhoea is {{unnecessary combination}}; an injection where tablets would do is {{incorrect route}}.

front: Why should a drug be prescribed by its generic (non-proprietary) name, and when is a brand name better?
back: A generic name is uniform, shorter and easier to remember than many brand names, and it lets the pharmacist supply any manufacturer's product, which is usually cheaper because no brand promotion is paid for. A brand name is safer when product consistency in quality and bioavailability matters and official quality control is weak.

front: Classify: the three names of a drug
text: A {{chemical}} name describes the molecule and is too cumbersome for prescribing; a {{non-proprietary}} name is the accepted generic name, and the WHO recommends {{rINN}} names for new drugs; a {{brand}} name is the manufacturer's trademark and can differ between countries.

front: What are the steps of rational prescribing?
back: 1) Establish at least a provisional diagnosis. 2) Define the therapeutic problem and goals (symptom relief, cure, prevention of complications). 3) Select the drug class for each goal. 4) Choose the drug on efficacy, safety, suitability for this patient and cost. 5) Decide route, dose and duration for this patient. 6) Give information and instructions. 7) Monitor adherence, goal achievement and adverse effects, and change therapy as needed.

front: What information must a patient receive when a drug is prescribed?
back: What effect to expect and when; whether the disease is cured or only controlled; what happens if doses are missed; common side effects, told without alarming the patient; how and how long to take it, and which tests are needed; precautions such as not driving after sedating antihistamines or not drinking alcohol with metronidazole. The patient should repeat the instructions back to confirm understanding.

points: Name, professional degree, address and telephone number, so the pharmacist can verify and contact
Signature and licence or registration number
Date written (and time for hospital orders)
Patient's full name and address; age or date of birth and sex are often added
Drug name (generic or brand), strength in metric units, quantity to dispense
Directions for use that are specific to the drug and patient, including purpose and duration; avoid 'take as directed'
Refills and warning labels (e.g. may cause drowsiness, avoid alcohol)
Legible, unambiguous and complete; omissions such as 'continue eye drops' cause errors
Always put a zero before a decimal point (0.1) and never add a trailing zero (1 mg, not 1.0 mg)
Write out 'units', 'microgram' and 'daily' rather than abbreviating; safest to avoid abbreviations altogether
Check for contraindications, interacting drugs (including OTC) and physicochemical incompatibilities

front: How does the WHO define essential medicines?
back: Medicines that satisfy the priority health care needs of a population. They are chosen for public health relevance, evidence of efficacy and safety, and comparative cost-effectiveness. They should be available at all times in working health systems, in adequate amounts and suitable dosage forms, with assured quality, adequate information and a price the individual and community can afford.

front: Essay: Selection criteria for essential medicines

points: Only a small set of medicines meets most health needs
Cheaper, well-tested drugs are often as good as newer, costlier ones
Concentrating resources on this set gives better value
Adequate efficacy and safety data from clinical studies
Quality, including bioavailability, and stability on storage must be assured
Pattern of prevalent diseases
Facilities and trained personnel; financial resources
Genetic, demographic and environmental factors
Compare efficacy, safety, quality, price and availability
Cost-benefit ratio is a major consideration
Pharmacokinetic properties and local manufacturing capacity also count
Mostly single compounds; fixed-ratio combinations only with proven advantage
List is reviewed continuously as disease patterns, evidence and drugs change
Selection should follow rationally developed treatment guidelines

front: Short note: WHO and National List of Essential Medicines

points: First Model List of Essential Drugs in 1977; revised periodically
KDT 8e quotes the 20th list (2017): 433 medicines, including 25 FDCs; GG14 cites the 21st list (2019)
Member countries adapt it to local needs
First National Essential Drugs List 1996; revised 2011, then 2015 as the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM)
NLEM 2015 (as given in KDT 8e): 376 medicines, of which 20 are FDCs
Medicines are marked for primary, secondary and tertiary care levels
Basis for procurement and supply, especially in the public sector
Improves availability, saves cost and promotes rational use

front: What is an orphan drug, and why do governments support it?
back: A drug or biological for a rare disease, or for a commoner disease endemic only in resource-poor areas, where the cost of developing and marketing it is not expected to be recovered from sales. Under the US Orphan Drug Amendment Act (1983), a rare disease affects fewer than 0.2 million people in the USA. Governments give tax benefits and other incentives to encourage development.

front: What are over-the-counter (OTC) drugs, and how is prescription status regulated in India?
back: OTC drugs can be bought without a prescription because they are relatively harmless, e.g. paracetamol, aspirin, antacids, senna, lactulose, vitamins and ferrous salts. Most drugs, including all antibiotics, are prescription-only; in India they are placed in Schedule H of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules.

front: When is a fixed-dose combination (FDC) rational? Give the main advantages.
back: When every component is needed at the stated doses. Advantages: better adherence and convenience; synergy (sulfamethoxazole plus trimethoprim, levodopa plus carbidopa); components with different mechanisms add their effect while side effects differ (amlodipine plus atenolol); one component offsets another's side effect (thiazide plus a potassium-sparing diuretic); a single drug cannot be given alone in TB, HIV or falciparum malaria; sometimes cheaper than separate tablets.

text: The patient may receive {{unneeded}} components; one ingredient's dose cannot be changed without altering the other; components may have different {{time courses}} and renal or hepatic handling; an adverse effect is hard to {{attribute}} to one drug; a {{contraindication}} to one part bars the whole product; and a false sense of {{superiority}} may follow.

front: Classify: examples of rational fixed-dose combinations
text: Sulfamethoxazole + {{trimethoprim}} (synergy); levodopa + {{carbidopa}} (synergy); {{isoniazid}} + rifampin (single-drug use avoided in TB); amlodipine + {{atenolol}} (different mechanisms, antihypertensive); thiazide + {{potassium-sparing diuretic}} (side effect offset).

points: Contains an ingredient the patient does not need
Fixed ratio prevents individual dose adjustment
Components with different pharmacokinetics given at one interval
No proven advantage over the single agents
Antimicrobial combinations used without need, adding toxicity and resistance risk
Tonic or vitamin add-ons with no clear benefit
Products containing doubtful-efficacy ingredients
Use a combination only if every component is needed at that dose
Prescribe separate drugs when individual dosing matters
Know the exact composition of any FDC used
Corticosteroids must never be combined with other drugs for internal use (inhalers excepted in the banned list)
Banned examples: penicillin with sulfonamide, tetracycline with vitamin C, vitamins with analgesics or tranquillisers, antihistamines with antidiarrhoeals, more than one antihistamine in one product
KDT 8e: besides the earlier bans, 344 more irrational FDCs were banned in India
The 2017 WHO list has only 25 FDCs and NLEM 2015 only 20

front: Which drug class must not be given as a fixed-dose combination with other drugs for internal use?
back: Corticosteroids. The reference states they should never be combined with any other drug meant for internal use, because the steroid dose can then not be adjusted on its own.

points: Narrow safety margin: digoxin, anticonvulsants, antiarrhythmics, theophylline, aminoglycosides, lithium, tricyclic antidepressants
Large individual variation: antidepressants, lithium
Toxic drugs in renal failure: aminoglycosides, vancomycin
Poisoning, to confirm it and track clearance
Unexplained treatment failure (antimicrobials); checking compliance (psychotropics)
Response is easily measured: antihypertensives, hypoglycaemics, diuretics, oral anticoagulants, inhalational anaesthetics
Drug is a prodrug needing activation (levodopa)
Effect outlasts plasma level ('hit and run'): reserpine, MAO inhibitors, omeprazole
Action is irreversible: organophosphates, phenoxybenzamine
Dose adjustment of long-acting drugs: trough level just before the next dose
Short-acting intermittent drugs (ampicillin, gentamicin): sample about 1-2 hours after dosing
Poisoning: sample early and repeat to judge clearance

text: Pharmacoeconomics is the branch of {{health economics}} that expresses the {{cost and benefit}} of therapeutic drugs in economic terms; regulators increasingly ask for an {{economic analysis}} alongside evidence of benefit, and phase III trials may now include a {{pharmacoeconomic}} analysis.

front: What is a QALY and how is it used?
back: Quality-adjusted life years combine survival time with health-related quality of life into a single overall measure of benefit. They are used as a clinical outcome measure in trials and in economic assessment of treatments. Valuing quality of life against length of life is contentious.

Rang & Dale use the term 'antibiotic stewardship' for sensible clinical use of existing antibacterials, based on understanding how resistance arises and spreads under the selection pressure of heavy drug use. In practice (GG14): prefer narrower-spectrum drugs when other factors are equal; de-escalate (streamline) from broad empirical cover once the pathogen and sensitivity are known; use monotherapy for definitive treatment unless combination has a proven role; and weigh prophylaxis against resistance, microbiome damage, toxicity and cost.

front: What principles guide empirical antimicrobial therapy before culture results are known?
back: Make at least a tentative clinical diagnosis; guess the likely organism from the clinical features and local experience; start a specific drug. Use broad cover only when the infection is severe or diagnostic services are unavailable. Review the response and narrow or change treatment on bacteriological findings, avoiding hasty, arbitrary switches.

front: Why are antimicrobial combinations discouraged outside specific indications?
back: They encourage a casual approach to diagnosis; they increase adverse effects (e.g. vancomycin with an aminoglycoside causes excess nephrotoxicity); they raise the risk of superinfection; underdosed non-synergistic drugs can select resistance; and they cost more. Combinations are justified for mixed infections, for empirical cover in severe infection until cultures are known, and for topical use.

front: Essay: Antimicrobial stewardship as rational use

points: Rational antimicrobial use means the right drug, dose, route and duration
Goal: best outcome with least harm, resistance and cost
Make at least a tentative clinical diagnosis; collect specimens before starting treatment in serious infection
Guess the likely organism from clinical features and local experience
No antibiotics for viral fevers or non-specific diarrhoea
Prefer a specific, narrower-spectrum drug when other factors are equal
Give full doses; adjust for renal impairment where needed
Never a single drug where multidrug therapy is standard (TB, leprosy, HIV)
Combinations only for synergy, preventing resistance, mixed infections, or temporary empirical cover in severe infection
Prophylaxis only for established indications; avoid prolonged post-operative courses
Review when culture results return; de-escalate to the definitive regimen
Avoid hasty, arbitrary switching of drugs
Irrational use promotes resistance, superinfection, toxicity and cost

front: SGLT2 inhibitors beyond glucose lowering: main indications and key adverse effect?
back: They block Na+-glucose reabsorption by SGLT2 in the proximal tubule. All reduce hospitalisation for heart failure; dapagliflozin reduced heart failure hospitalisation and cardiovascular death in HFrEF with or without diabetes. Canagliflozin, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin slowed progression of kidney disease in patients with reduced GFR and albuminuria. Adverse effects: genital mycotic infections (3-5% excess), urinary tract infections, volume depletion and hypotension; euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis has been reported.

front: Finerenone: class, key use and key adverse effect?
back: A non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (FDA approved 2021) that competitively blocks aldosterone binding; it binds androgen and progesterone receptors less than spironolactone and distributes equally to heart and kidney. Use: CKD with type 2 diabetes, to reduce kidney function decline, non-fatal MI, heart failure hospitalisation and cardiovascular death. Key adverse effect: hyperkalaemia, less than with spironolactone or eplerenone but still significant. Metabolised by CYP3A4 (half-life about 2 h).

front: Sacubitril-valsartan: what does each component do, and what is the key safety rule?
back: Valsartan blocks AT1 receptors. Sacubitril is a prodrug whose active metabolite inhibits neprilysin, the enzyme that breaks down ANP and BNP (and also angiotensin II and bradykinin), so natriuretic peptide effects are enhanced. In HFrEF the combination was superior to enalapril, reducing cardiovascular death and hospitalisation. Because neprilysin also degrades bradykinin, angioedema is a concern, as with ACE inhibitors.

text: Steroidal MRAs are {{spironolactone}} and {{eplerenone}}; the non-steroidal MRA is {{finerenone}}.

front: Short note: Heart failure and CKD drugs beyond the ACE inhibitor

points: ARB plus neprilysin inhibitor
Raises natriuretic peptide effects
Superior to enalapril in HFrEF

front: Tirzepatide: mechanism, key use and key adverse effect?
back: A dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist: a modified GIP analogue given once weekly by subcutaneous injection. It raises glucose-dependent insulin release, lowers glucagon, slows gastric emptying and reduces appetite. In type 2 diabetes it lowered HbA1c by about 1.9-2.6% with weight loss of about 6-13 kg. front: Inclisiran: how does it lower LDL-cholesterol, and how is it given?
back: A small interfering RNA (FDA approved 2021) that targets PCSK9 mRNA in the liver and blocks PCSK9 synthesis. Fewer LDL receptors are degraded, so LDL-cholesterol falls by about 50%. Low-volume subcutaneous injections give effects lasting over 180 days, allowing twice-yearly dosing. Common adverse effects: injection-site reactions and bronchitis.

front: Bempedoic acid: where does it act, and what adverse effects follow?
back: An oral inhibitor of ATP-citrate lyase, acting in the liver in the cholesterol synthesis pathway at a step before HMG-CoA reductase; LDL receptors increase. Monotherapy lowers LDL-C by 15-25%; about 30% with ezetimibe (fixed combination available) and more with a statin. Adverse effects: hyperuricaemia (competition for renal OAT2) raising gout risk, tendon rupture, and rises in CK, creatinine and transaminases. Limit simvastatin to 20 mg and rosuvastatin to 40 mg when combined (myopathy).

front: Romosozumab: target, effect on bone, and key warning?
back: A monoclonal antibody against sclerostin, an osteocyte protein that inhibits Wnt signalling and bone formation. Blocking it increases bone formation and also suppresses resorption. Given monthly by subcutaneous injection for one year, followed by an antiresorptive to keep the bone gained. Boxed warning: do not use in patients at risk of stroke or coronary vascular disease.

front: Gepants: what are they, and which are used for acute treatment versus prevention of migraine?
back: Small-molecule CGRP receptor antagonists. Trigeminal nerves release CGRP, an extremely powerful vasodilator, in migraine. First-generation gepants (olcegepant, telcagepant) worked but were limited by liver toxicity. Second generation: ubrogepant and rimegepant for acute attacks; rimegepant and atogepant for prevention.

front: Aducanumab: target, use and main safety issue?
back: A monoclonal antibody that reduces amyloid-beta plaques; the first disease-modifying therapy for Alzheimer disease (FDA 2021). Approval was via the Accelerated Approval Program on a surrogate (plaque burden) and was controversial, as clinical benefit was modest. Indication: mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to AD, with amyloid confirmed by PET or CSF. Given as monthly IV infusions. Main safety issue: amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) in almost half of trial patients: cerebral oedema (ARIA-E) or microhaemorrhages (ARIA-H), often asymptomatic and reversible; MRI before starting and every 6 months. Donanemab is a newer anti-amyloid antibody.

front: Bedaquiline: mechanism, use and key adverse effect?
back: A diarylquinoline that inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, stopping energy production. Used in multidrug-resistant pulmonary TB as part of a combination. Metabolised by CYP3A4 to M2 (less active); terminal half-life about 5.5 months from tissue redistribution; strong CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers interact. Adverse effects: nausea, arthralgia, headache; hepatotoxicity; boxed warning for QTc prolongation and associated mortality.

front: Pretomanid: how is it activated, what is its spectrum, and what is a key interaction?
back: A nitroimidazole prodrug activated inside M. tuberculosis by a deazaflavin (F420)-dependent nitroreductase. In replicating bacilli it blocks mycolic acid synthesis; in non-replicating anaerobic bacilli it releases nitric oxide. Active against M. tuberculosis only, not other mycobacteria. Used with bedaquiline and linezolid for 6 months in XDR, pre-XDR or non-responsive MDR pulmonary TB. Partly metabolised by CYP3A4, so avoid potent CYP3A4 inducers (rifampicin lowers its levels). Can raise liver enzymes.

front: Cefiderocol: how does it enter bacteria, and when is it reserved?
back: A siderophore cephalosporin. Unlike other beta-lactams, which diffuse through porins, it is bound by bacterial active iron transporters and pumped into the cell, then binds PBPs to inhibit cell wall synthesis. It is stable to all beta-lactamase types, including metallo-beta-lactamases, and is active against drug-resistant Enterobacterales (including carbapenem-resistant), Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii, but not Gram-positives or anaerobes. Warning: increased mortality in carbapenem-resistant infections in one trial, so reserve it for cases with limited or no alternatives.

front: Baloxavir marboxil: target, dosing principle and key adverse effect?
back: An oral prodrug hydrolysed to baloxavir acid, which inhibits the influenza cap-dependent endonuclease, blocking initiation of viral mRNA synthesis. Active against influenza A and B, including oseltamivir-resistant virus. Single-dose treatment of uncomplicated influenza within 2 days of symptoms in patients 12 years and older, and post-exposure prophylaxis. Long half-life (about 80 h). Avoid co-administration with dairy products or polyvalent cations. Resistance: polymerase acidic protein I38T/M/F variants emerged in about 10% of treated patients.

front: CTLA-4 and PD-1 checkpoint inhibitors: where do they act, and which agents block each?
back: CTLA-4 competes with CD28 for B7 ligands on antigen-presenting cells, damping T-cell priming. Anti-CTLA-4 antibodies (ipilimumab, tremelimumab) release this brake early, in lymphoid tissue. PD-1 on activated T cells binds PD-L1 and PD-L2, exhausting T cells within tumours. Anti-PD-1 (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, cemiplimab) and anti-PD-L1 (atezolizumab, durvalumab, avelumab) restore antitumour activity.
